title: Respond to a Text with Simple Judgment
body: A simple judgment says what you think about an action, choice, idea or event in a text and supports that view with evidence. First understand what happened. Then decide whether an action was sensible, fair, helpful, harmful or appropriate. Finally, explain your judgment using a relevant detail from the text.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Read: "Kojo found a wallet near the school gate. He took it to the headteacher instead of keeping it. The owner later collected it." A supported judgment is: "Kojo made a responsible choice because he handed the lost wallet to someone who could return it to its owner."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Identify the action or idea you are judging. Step 2: find a detail that shows what happened. Step 3: state your judgment clearly. Step 4: give a reason linked to the evidence. Step 5: check that your response evaluates the text rather than merely retelling it.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not give an opinion with no evidence from the text. Do not only retell what happened when the question asks for a judgment. Do not base your judgment on an unrelated personal preference.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Réagir à un texte par un jugement simple
body: Un jugement simple exprime ce que tu penses d'une action, d'un choix, d'une idée ou d'un événement dans un texte et appuie ce point de vue par des indices. Comprends d'abord ce qui s'est passé. Décide ensuite si une action était raisonnable, juste, utile, nuisible ou appropriée. Enfin, explique ton jugement à l'aide d'un détail pertinent du texte.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Lis : "Kojo found a wallet near the school gate. He took it to the headteacher instead of keeping it. The owner later collected it." Un jugement justifié est : "Kojo made a responsible choice because he handed the lost wallet to someone who could return it to its owner."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Identifie l'action ou l'idée que tu juges. Étape 2 : trouve un détail qui montre ce qui s'est passé. Étape 3 : exprime clairement ton jugement. Étape 4 : donne une raison liée aux indices. Étape 5 : vérifie que ta réponse évalue le texte au lieu de simplement le raconter.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne donne pas une opinion sans indice tiré du texte. Ne raconte pas seulement ce qui s'est passé lorsque la question demande un jugement. Ne fonde pas ton jugement sur une préférence personnelle sans rapport avec le texte.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Relate Ideas in a Text
body: To relate ideas, explain how two or more ideas connect. They may show cause and effect, problem and solution, similarity, contrast, sequence, or a shared message. You can also make a personal connection, but it must clearly link your experience to an idea in the text.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Read: "The school garden dried during a week without rain. The pupils began carrying water to the beds each morning. Soon the vegetables looked healthier." The dry garden created a problem, watering was the response, and healthier vegetables were the result.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Identify the important ideas. Step 2: ask how they are connected. Step 3: name the relationship, such as cause and effect or problem and solution. Step 4: point to details that prove the connection. For a personal connection, explain exactly how an experience reminds you of the text.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not connect ideas merely because they contain the same word. Do not mention a personal experience without explaining its link to the text. Do not treat ideas as separate when the passage clearly shows a relationship between them.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Relier des idées dans un texte
body: Pour relier des idées, explique comment deux ou plusieurs idées sont liées. Elles peuvent montrer une cause et un effet, un problème et une solution, une ressemblance, un contraste, une suite ou un message commun. Tu peux aussi faire un lien personnel, mais ton expérience doit être clairement reliée à une idée du texte.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Lis : "The school garden dried during a week without rain. The pupils began carrying water to the beds each morning. Soon the vegetables looked healthier." Le jardin sec a créé un problème, l'arrosage a été la réponse et l'amélioration des légumes a été le résultat.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Identifie les idées importantes. Étape 2 : demande-toi comment elles sont liées. Étape 3 : nomme la relation, par exemple cause et effet ou problème et solution. Étape 4 : indique les détails qui prouvent ce lien. Pour un lien personnel, explique exactement comment une expérience te rappelle le texte.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne relie pas des idées simplement parce qu'elles contiennent le même mot. Ne mentionne pas une expérience personnelle sans expliquer son lien avec le texte. Ne traite pas des idées comme séparées lorsque le passage montre clairement une relation entre elles.

title: Recognise Introduction, Body and Conclusion
body: Many texts have an introduction, a body and a conclusion. The introduction opens the topic or situation. The body develops it with events, explanations or supporting details. The conclusion closes the text by giving an outcome, final thought or summary. The job of each part matters more than its position alone.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Read: "Our class wanted a cleaner compound. First, groups collected litter and swept the paths. Next, they emptied the bins and cleared leaves from the drain. In the end, the compound looked neat, and the class agreed to keep it clean." The first sentence introduces the aim, the middle sentences form the body, and the final sentence concludes with the result and future decision.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Ask how the text opens its topic. Step 2: find the events, reasons or details that develop the topic. Step 3: identify how the writer closes the text. Step 4: summarise each part briefly. Step 5: use connectives such as "first", "next", "therefore" and "finally" to join the summaries into one clear account.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not call a sentence an introduction merely because it comes first. Do not mistake a supporting detail in the body for the conclusion. Do not leave separate part summaries disconnected when you need to explain the whole text.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Reconnaître l'introduction, le développement et la conclusion
body: De nombreux textes comportent une introduction, un développement et une conclusion. L'introduction présente le sujet ou la situation. Le développement l'approfondit avec des événements, des explications ou des détails. La conclusion ferme le texte avec un résultat, une idée finale ou un résumé. La fonction de chaque partie compte davantage que sa position seule.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Lis : "Our class wanted a cleaner compound. First, groups collected litter and swept the paths. Next, they emptied the bins and cleared leaves from the drain. In the end, the compound looked neat, and the class agreed to keep it clean." La première phrase introduit l'objectif, les phrases du milieu forment le développement et la dernière phrase conclut avec le résultat et la décision future.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Demande-toi comment le texte présente son sujet. Étape 2 : repère les événements, raisons ou détails qui développent le sujet. Étape 3 : identifie comment l'auteur termine le texte. Étape 4 : résume brièvement chaque partie. Étape 5 : utilise des connecteurs comme "first", "next", "therefore" et "finally" pour réunir les résumés en un ensemble clair.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: N'appelle pas une phrase introduction simplement parce qu'elle vient en premier. Ne confonds pas un détail du développement avec la conclusion. Ne laisse pas les résumés des différentes parties séparés lorsque tu dois expliquer l'ensemble du texte.

title: Use Prefixes and Suffixes to Interpret Unfamiliar Words
body: A prefix is added to the beginning of a base word, while a suffix is added to the end. Affixes can change a word's meaning or its grammatical role. When you meet an unfamiliar word, separate the affix from the base, recall what each part contributes, combine the meanings, and check the result in the sentence.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: In "Ama misunderstood the instruction," the prefix "mis-" means wrongly or badly and the base "understand" means to grasp the meaning. "Misunderstood" therefore means understood wrongly. In "The child was careless with the glass," "-less" means without, so "careless" means without enough care.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Find the base word. Step 2: identify the prefix or suffix. Step 3: state what the affix contributes. Step 4: combine it with the base meaning. Step 5: reread the sentence and check whether your interpretation makes sense in context.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not treat an affix as a separate unrelated word. Do not state only the meaning of the affix without combining it with the base. Do not guess an unfamiliar word from the sentence while ignoring the useful prefix or suffix.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Utiliser les préfixes et suffixes pour comprendre des mots inconnus
body: Un préfixe s'ajoute au début d'un mot de base, tandis qu'un suffixe s'ajoute à la fin. Les affixes peuvent modifier le sens d'un mot ou sa fonction grammaticale. Lorsque tu rencontres un mot inconnu, sépare l'affixe du mot de base, rappelle-toi ce que chaque partie apporte, combine les sens et vérifie le résultat dans la phrase.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Dans "Ama misunderstood the instruction," le préfixe "mis-" signifie de manière incorrecte et le mot de base "understand" signifie comprendre. "Misunderstood" signifie donc compris de manière incorrecte. Dans "The child was careless with the glass," "-less" signifie sans, donc "careless" signifie sans assez de soin.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Trouve le mot de base. Étape 2 : identifie le préfixe ou le suffixe. Étape 3 : indique ce que l'affixe apporte. Étape 4 : combine-le avec le sens du mot de base. Étape 5 : relis la phrase et vérifie si ton interprétation convient au contexte.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne traite pas un affixe comme un mot séparé sans rapport avec le mot de base. Ne donne pas seulement le sens de l'affixe sans le combiner avec celui du mot de base. Ne devine pas un mot inconnu à partir de la phrase en ignorant le préfixe ou le suffixe utile.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Comprendre un mot avec préfixe
body: Lis : "Kofi miscounted the oranges, so he counted them again." Que signifie "miscounted" ?

title: Infer Meaning from Texts
body: An inference is a meaning you work out from clues in a text even when the writer does not state it directly. During silent reading, notice important details, connect them, and ask what they suggest. If your attention drifts and meaning is disrupted, stop, return to the last part you understood, reread, and rebuild the meaning.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Read silently: "When Esi reached the classroom, she shook water from her umbrella and wiped her sandals on the mat. Several pupils near the window were closing it." The text never says, "It was raining," but the wet umbrella, sandals and closing window allow us to infer that rain was falling outside.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Read silently for overall meaning. Step 2: mark two or more useful clues. Step 3: ask what those clues suggest together. Step 4: choose an inference supported by the clues. Step 5: if meaning breaks down, pause and reread the relevant sentence before continuing.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not merely copy a detail when the question asks what the details imply. Do not invent an inference that has no support in the text. When concentration breaks, do not continue reading without understanding; pause and reread.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

Nothing in the text supports that specific inference.","Kojo should ignore the earlier sentences and continue reading even if he does not understand why the pot is empty."]

title: Déduire le sens d'un texte
body: Une inférence est un sens que tu déduis à partir d'indices dans un texte, même lorsque l'auteur ne l'exprime pas directement. Pendant la lecture silencieuse, repère les détails importants, relie-les et demande-toi ce qu'ils suggèrent. Si ton attention se détourne et que le sens est interrompu, arrête-toi, retourne à la dernière partie comprise, relis et reconstruis le sens.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Lis silencieusement : "When Esi reached the classroom, she shook water from her umbrella and wiped her sandals on the mat. Several pupils near the window were closing it." Le texte ne dit jamais "It was raining", mais le parapluie mouillé, les sandales et la fenêtre qu'on ferme permettent de déduire qu'il pleuvait dehors.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Lis silencieusement pour comprendre le sens général. Étape 2 : repère au moins deux indices utiles. Étape 3 : demande-toi ce que ces indices suggèrent ensemble. Étape 4 : choisis une inférence soutenue par les indices. Étape 5 : si tu perds le sens, arrête-toi et relis la phrase concernée avant de continuer.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne copie pas simplement un détail lorsque la question demande ce que les détails suggèrent. N'invente pas une inférence sans appui dans le texte. Lorsque ta concentration est interrompue, ne continue pas à lire sans comprendre ; arrête-toi et relis.

title: Find the Meaning of Words in Context
body: A word can have more than one meaning. To find the meaning intended in a passage, read the whole sentence and nearby sentences. Look for examples, descriptions, actions, contrasts or results that give clues. Then test the possible meaning in the sentence.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Read: "The pupils formed a line outside the library and waited quietly for their turn." Here, "line" means a row of people, not a mark drawn with a pencil. The words "pupils", "waited" and "turn" reveal the intended meaning.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Notice the unfamiliar or multiple-meaning word. Step 2: read the entire sentence. Step 3: collect two useful context clues. Step 4: consider possible meanings. Step 5: choose the meaning that makes the whole sentence sensible.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not choose a familiar dictionary meaning without checking the passage. Do not guess from only one nearby word. When a word has several meanings, use the whole context to decide which one the writer intends.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Trouver le sens des mots en contexte
body: Un mot peut avoir plusieurs sens. Pour trouver le sens voulu dans un passage, lis toute la phrase ainsi que les phrases voisines. Cherche des exemples, des descriptions, des actions, des contrastes ou des résultats qui donnent des indices. Ensuite, vérifie si le sens possible convient à la phrase.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Lis : "The pupils formed a line outside the library and waited quietly for their turn." Ici, "line" signifie une rangée de personnes, et non un trait dessiné au crayon. Les mots "pupils", "waited" et "turn" révèlent le sens voulu.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Repère le mot inconnu ou ayant plusieurs sens. Étape 2 : lis toute la phrase. Étape 3 : relève deux indices utiles du contexte. Étape 4 : envisage les sens possibles. Étape 5 : choisis le sens qui rend toute la phrase logique.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne choisis pas un sens familier du dictionnaire sans vérifier le passage. Ne devine pas à partir d'un seul mot voisin. Lorsqu'un mot a plusieurs sens, utilise tout le contexte pour décider lequel l'auteur veut exprimer.

title: Answer Questions Based on a Passage
body: Good comprehension answers come from careful reading of the passage. First understand what the question asks. Then return to the relevant part of the text, select evidence that answers that exact question, and use it to form your response. Some answers are stated directly, while others require a reasonable inference from clues.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Passage: "Akosua noticed that the class reading corner was untidy. She asked two friends to help her arrange the books by size and subject. By break time, pupils could find books more easily." Question: Why did Akosua arrange the books? A strong answer is: "She wanted to make the reading corner orderly so pupils could find books more easily." It uses the problem and result in the passage.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Read the question and identify its focus, such as who, what, why or how. Step 2: find the relevant sentence or clues. Step 3: reject details that do not answer the question. Step 4: answer clearly. Step 5: for an inference, check that the passage provides enough evidence.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not answer from your own memory when the passage gives the needed information. Do not choose a true detail that fails to answer the question. Do not present an unsupported guess as if the writer stated it.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

This is in the passage but does not answer what they did every morning.","They planned to sell all the tomatoes at the market. The passage gives no evidence for that claim."]

title: Répondre aux questions à partir d'un passage
body: De bonnes réponses de compréhension viennent d'une lecture attentive du passage. Comprends d'abord ce que demande la question. Ensuite, retourne à la partie pertinente du texte, choisis les indices qui répondent exactement à la question et utilise-les pour formuler ta réponse. Certaines réponses sont données directement, tandis que d'autres demandent une inférence raisonnable à partir d'indices.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Passage : "Akosua noticed that the class reading corner was untidy. She asked two friends to help her arrange the books by size and subject. By break time, pupils could find books more easily." Question : Why did Akosua arrange the books? Une bonne réponse est : "She wanted to make the reading corner orderly so pupils could find books more easily." Elle utilise le problème et le résultat donnés dans le passage.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Lis la question et identifie ce qu'elle demande, par exemple qui, quoi, pourquoi ou comment. Étape 2 : trouve la phrase ou les indices pertinents. Étape 3 : écarte les détails qui ne répondent pas à la question. Étape 4 : réponds clairement. Étape 5 : pour une inférence, vérifie que le passage fournit assez d'indices.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne réponds pas à partir de tes souvenirs personnels lorsque le passage donne l'information nécessaire. Ne choisis pas un détail vrai qui ne répond pas à la question. Ne présente pas une supposition sans preuve comme si l'auteur l'avait affirmée.

title: Read with Good Speed and Accuracy
body: Fluent reading means reading a grade-level text accurately, at a suitable pace and in meaningful phrases so that the message remains clear. Good speed does not mean racing. A fluent reader recognises words correctly, groups related words together, observes punctuation and adjusts pace when a sentence is difficult.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Read: "After the morning bell, / the pupils gathered under the neem tree / for assembly." The slashes show sensible phrase groups. Reading every word separately sounds broken. Racing through the sentence may cause errors. A steady pace with correct words and natural phrasing supports comprehension.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Preview unfamiliar words. Step 2: read the sentence accurately. Step 3: group words that belong together. Step 4: pause at punctuation. Step 5: keep a steady pace. Step 6: if an error changes the meaning, correct it and continue.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not judge fluency by speed alone. Do not read one isolated word at a time when words form a meaningful phrase. Do not skip, replace or misread words merely to finish faster.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Use Punctuation for Fluent Reading

title: Lire avec une bonne vitesse et précision
body: La lecture fluide consiste à lire un texte adapté au niveau avec précision, à un rythme convenable et en groupes de mots porteurs de sens afin que le message reste clair. Une bonne vitesse ne signifie pas lire le plus vite possible. Un lecteur fluide reconnaît correctement les mots, regroupe les mots liés, respecte la ponctuation et ralentit lorsqu'une phrase est difficile.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Lis : "After the morning bell, / the pupils gathered under the neem tree / for assembly." Les barres indiquent des groupes de mots logiques. Lire chaque mot séparément donne une lecture saccadée. Lire trop vite peut provoquer des erreurs. Un rythme régulier, des mots correctement lus et un groupement naturel favorisent la compréhension.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Repère les mots inconnus. Étape 2 : lis la phrase avec précision. Étape 3 : regroupe les mots qui vont ensemble. Étape 4 : fais une pause à la ponctuation. Étape 5 : garde un rythme régulier. Étape 6 : si une erreur change le sens, corrige-la puis continue.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne juge pas la fluidité uniquement par la vitesse. Ne lis pas un mot isolé à la fois lorsque plusieurs mots forment un groupe porteur de sens. Ne saute pas, ne remplace pas et ne lis pas mal des mots simplement pour finir plus vite.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Use Context and Self-Correction
body: Good readers notice when a word or sentence does not make sense. They stop, reread and use the surrounding words, punctuation, sentences and paragraph links to correct the reading. Self-correction is not simply changing a word. The corrected reading must fit the text and restore meaning.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Read: "The farmer filled the bucket at the well and carried the water to the goats." If a learner reads "wall" instead of "well", the sentence becomes strange. The clues "filled the bucket" and "water" help the learner return to the word and correct it to "well".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Read for meaning. Step 2: notice when meaning breaks. Step 3: return to the difficult word or sentence. Step 4: use context and punctuation to test a correction. Step 5: reread the whole phrase or sentence. Step 6: check that the corrected version connects logically with what comes before and after.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not continue with a misread word when the sentence stops making sense. Do not replace a word and assume the problem is solved without rereading. Do not ignore punctuation or connecting words that show how ideas fit together.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Utiliser le contexte et l'autocorrection
body: Les bons lecteurs remarquent lorsqu'un mot ou une phrase n'a pas de sens. Ils s'arrêtent, relisent et utilisent les mots voisins, la ponctuation, les phrases et les liens entre les paragraphes pour corriger leur lecture. S'autocorriger ne consiste pas simplement à changer un mot. La lecture corrigée doit convenir au texte et rétablir le sens.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Lis : "The farmer filled the bucket at the well and carried the water to the goats." Si un élève lit "wall" au lieu de "well", la phrase devient étrange. Les indices "filled the bucket" et "water" l'aident à revenir au mot et à le corriger en "well".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Lis pour comprendre. Étape 2 : remarque lorsque le sens est interrompu. Étape 3 : retourne au mot ou à la phrase difficile. Étape 4 : utilise le contexte et la ponctuation pour vérifier une correction. Étape 5 : relis tout le groupe de mots ou toute la phrase. Étape 6 : vérifie que la version corrigée s'enchaîne logiquement avec ce qui précède et ce qui suit.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne continue pas avec un mot mal lu lorsque la phrase cesse d'avoir du sens. Ne remplace pas un mot en supposant que le problème est résolu sans relire. N'ignore pas la ponctuation ni les mots de liaison qui montrent comment les idées s'enchaînent.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Summarise a Text Orally
body: An oral summary gives the most important ideas of a text in your own words. It is shorter than the original. For a story, identify the main characters, setting, central problem or event, and important outcome. For an informational text, identify the main idea and the key details that explain it. Leave out minor details and personal opinions.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Text: "A storm damaged the roof of the community library. Residents contributed materials, and local carpenters repaired the roof over two days. The library reopened on Monday." Oral summary: "After a storm damaged the community library roof, residents and carpenters worked together to repair it, allowing the library to reopen."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Read or listen for the main idea. Step 2: identify the most important characters, events or facts. Step 3: remove repeated and minor details. Step 4: put the key ideas in a sensible order. Step 5: retell them briefly in your own words without adding information.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not repeat nearly every sentence from the original. Do not give only small details while missing the main idea. Do not add what you think should have happened when the task is to summarise what the text says.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Choose an Oral Summary

This minor detail leaves out the main clean-up effort and result.","The pupils should have punished anyone who dropped litter because that would keep the field clean forever."]

This minor detail leaves out the main clean-up effort and result.":{"errorPattern":"omits_main_idea_and_lists_minor_details","diagnosticState":"misconception","diagnosticConfidence":0.8},"The pupils should have punished anyone who dropped litter because that would keep the field clean forever.":{"errorPattern":"adds_personal_opinion_not_supported_by_text","diagnosticState":"misconception","diagnosticConfidence":0.8}}

title: Résumer oralement un texte
body: Un résumé oral présente les idées les plus importantes d'un texte avec tes propres mots. Il est plus court que le texte original. Pour une histoire, identifie les personnages principaux, le cadre, le problème ou l'événement central et le résultat important. Pour un texte informatif, identifie l'idée principale et les détails essentiels qui l'expliquent. Laisse de côté les petits détails et les opinions personnelles.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Texte : "A storm damaged the roof of the community library. Residents contributed materials, and local carpenters repaired the roof over two days. The library reopened on Monday." Résumé oral : "After a storm damaged the community library roof, residents and carpenters worked together to repair it, allowing the library to reopen."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Lis ou écoute pour trouver l'idée principale. Étape 2 : identifie les personnages, événements ou faits les plus importants. Étape 3 : enlève les répétitions et les détails secondaires. Étape 4 : place les idées essentielles dans un ordre logique. Étape 5 : reformule-les brièvement avec tes propres mots sans ajouter d'informations.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne répète pas presque toutes les phrases du texte original. Ne donne pas seulement de petits détails en oubliant l'idée principale. N'ajoute pas ce qui, selon toi, aurait dû se passer lorsque la tâche consiste à résumer ce que dit le texte.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Write a Short Summary
body: A written summary presents the main idea and the most important supporting points in a shorter form. Read the whole passage first. Decide what the passage is mainly about, select only the key details, put them in a logical order, and write them in your own words. A summary must stay faithful to the original text.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Text: "The school garden became dry during the harmattan. Pupils collected water left after washing their lunch bowls and used it on the vegetable beds. Within two weeks, the plants looked healthier." Short summary: "Pupils reused water to keep the school garden healthy during the harmattan."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Read the complete passage. Step 2: state the main idea in a few words. Step 3: choose the details needed to explain that idea. Step 4: leave out examples and small details unless they are essential. Step 5: write one or more clear sentences in your own words. Step 6: compare the summary with the passage to check accuracy.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not copy several original sentences and call them a summary. Do not focus on small details while missing the main idea. Do not add facts, explanations or opinions that the passage does not contain.

title: Écrire un court résumé
body: Un résumé écrit présente l'idée principale et les points essentiels sous une forme plus courte. Lis d'abord tout le passage. Détermine son sujet principal, choisis seulement les détails importants, place-les dans un ordre logique et écris-les avec tes propres mots. Un résumé doit rester fidèle au texte original.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Texte : "The school garden became dry during the harmattan. Pupils collected water left after washing their lunch bowls and used it on the vegetable beds. Within two weeks, the plants looked healthier." Court résumé : "Pupils reused water to keep the school garden healthy during the harmattan."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Lis tout le passage. Étape 2 : exprime l'idée principale en quelques mots. Étape 3 : choisis les détails nécessaires pour expliquer cette idée. Étape 4 : laisse de côté les exemples et les petits détails sauf s'ils sont essentiels. Étape 5 : écris une ou plusieurs phrases claires avec tes propres mots. Étape 6 : compare le résumé au passage pour vérifier son exactitude.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne copie pas plusieurs phrases du texte original en les appelant un résumé. Ne te concentre pas sur de petits détails en oubliant l'idée principale. N'ajoute pas de faits, d'explications ou d'opinions absents du passage.

title: Use Noun Phrases for Quantities and Units
body: We often use noun phrases to show a quantity or unit. Expressions such as "a piece of paper", "a bowl of rice", "two litres of water" and "a pair of trousers" tell us how much, how many or what unit is meant. The quantity expression must fit the noun and the situation.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: In "Please give me a piece of paper", the phrase "a piece of paper" refers to one portion of the material called paper. In "I bought two litres of milk", "litres" is the unit used to state the amount of milk.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Identify the thing being measured or counted. Step 2: decide whether it can be counted directly. Step 3: if needed, choose a suitable quantity or unit noun such as piece, bowl, loaf, pair, kilogram or litre. Step 4: form the complete noun phrase. Step 5: use it naturally in the sentence.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not place a number directly before a mass noun when a quantity expression is needed. Do not treat words such as rice or water as separate countable objects in these contexts. Do not choose a unit that cannot sensibly measure the item.

title: Utiliser des groupes nominaux pour les quantités et les unités
body: Nous utilisons souvent des groupes nominaux pour indiquer une quantité ou une unité. Des expressions comme "a piece of paper", "a bowl of rice", "two litres of water" et "a pair of trousers" indiquent combien, quelle quantité ou quelle unité est visée. L'expression de quantité doit convenir au nom et à la situation.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Dans "Please give me a piece of paper", le groupe "a piece of paper" désigne une portion de la matière appelée paper. Dans "I bought two litres of milk", "litres" est l'unité utilisée pour indiquer la quantité de lait.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Identifie ce qui est mesuré ou compté. Étape 2 : décide si cela peut être compté directement. Étape 3 : si nécessaire, choisis un nom de quantité ou d'unité convenable comme piece, bowl, loaf, pair, kilogram ou litre. Étape 4 : forme le groupe nominal complet. Étape 5 : utilise-le naturellement dans la phrase.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne place pas directement un nombre devant un nom massif lorsqu'une expression de quantité est nécessaire. Ne traite pas des mots comme rice ou water comme des objets séparés que l'on peut compter dans ces contextes. Ne choisis pas une unité qui ne peut pas mesurer l'élément de façon logique.

title: Use Different Types of Nouns
body: Nouns can work in different ways. Proper nouns name particular people, places, festivals or events and begin with capital letters, as in "Homowo". Count nouns can be counted directly, such as "chair" and "chairs". Non-count nouns, such as "water" and "rice", are usually measured with quantity expressions. Plural count nouns may be regular, irregular, or have no extra plural marker.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Compare: "The people of Ga celebrate Homowo." "Homowo" is the proper name of a festival. "Three chairs" uses a regular plural. "Two children" uses the irregular plural of "child". In "The sheep are grazing", "sheep" has the same form in singular and plural. We say "some rice" or "a bowl of rice", not "three rices" when referring to the food generally.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Decide whether the noun names a particular person, place, festival or event. Step 2: decide whether it can be counted directly. Step 3: if it is countable, check whether the plural takes s or es, changes form, or stays unchanged. Step 4: use the correct noun form in a complete sentence.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Utiliser différents types de noms
body: Les noms peuvent fonctionner de différentes façons. Les noms propres désignent des personnes, des lieux, des fêtes ou des événements particuliers et commencent par une majuscule, comme "Homowo". Les noms comptables peuvent être comptés directement, comme "chair" et "chairs". Les noms non comptables, comme "water" et "rice", sont généralement mesurés avec des expressions de quantité. Les noms comptables au pluriel peuvent être réguliers, irréguliers ou ne pas porter de marque supplémentaire du pluriel.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Compare : "The people of Ga celebrate Homowo." "Homowo" est le nom propre d'une fête. "Three chairs" utilise un pluriel régulier. "Two children" utilise le pluriel irrégulier de "child". Dans "The sheep are grazing", "sheep" garde la même forme au singulier et au pluriel. On dit "some rice" ou "a bowl of rice", et non "three rices" lorsqu'on parle du riz comme aliment en général.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas

Étape 3 : s'il est comptable, vérifie si le pluriel prend s ou es, change de forme ou reste inchangé. Étape 4 : utilise la bonne forme du nom dans une phrase complète.

title: Use Collective Nouns
body: A collective noun names a group of people, animals or objects as one group. Examples include "audience" for people watching or listening, "congregation" for people gathered for worship, "a flock of sheep", "a troop of monkeys" and "a bunch of keys". Choose a collective noun that matches the group being described.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: In "A flock of sheep crossed the road", "flock" is the collective noun and "sheep" tells us which animals form the group. In "The audience listened quietly", "audience" refers to the people together as one group.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Identify the people, animals or objects in the group. Step 2: choose the collective noun normally used for that kind of group. Step 3: form the expression correctly, such as "a flock of sheep". Step 4: use the collective noun naturally in a complete sentence.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not use the name of one member when you mean the whole group. Do not combine a collective noun with a group it does not normally describe. Do not replace a collective expression with a loose list of separate members when the task asks for the group name.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Utiliser les noms collectifs
body: Un nom collectif désigne un groupe de personnes, d'animaux ou d'objets considéré comme un ensemble. Les exemples comprennent "audience" pour des personnes qui regardent ou écoutent, "congregation" pour des personnes réunies pour le culte, "a flock of sheep", "a troop of monkeys" et "a bunch of keys". Choisis un nom collectif qui correspond au groupe décrit.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Dans "A flock of sheep crossed the road", "flock" est le nom collectif et "sheep" indique quels animaux forment le groupe. Dans "The audience listened quietly", "audience" désigne les personnes réunies comme un seul groupe.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Identifie les personnes, les animaux ou les objets du groupe. Étape 2 : choisis le nom collectif normalement utilisé pour ce type de groupe. Étape 3 : forme correctement l'expression, par exemple "a flock of sheep". Étape 4 : utilise naturellement le nom collectif dans une phrase complète.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: N'utilise pas le nom d'un seul membre lorsque tu veux désigner tout le groupe. N'associe pas un nom collectif à un groupe qu'il ne désigne pas normalement. Ne remplace pas une expression collective par une simple liste de membres séparés lorsque la tâche demande le nom du groupe.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Use Abstract Nouns
body: An abstract noun names an idea, quality, state or concept rather than an ordinary physical object. Words such as "beauty", "peace", "honesty", "kindness" and "freedom" name things we understand through ideas, feelings or qualities. Concrete nouns such as "book", "chair" and "mango" name physical things.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: In "Ama showed kindness to the new pupil", "kindness" is an abstract noun because it names a quality. In "Ama gave the pupil a pencil", "pencil" is a concrete noun because it names a physical object.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Find the noun. Step 2: ask what it names. Step 3: if it names an idea, quality, state or concept, identify it as abstract. Step 4: if it names a physical person, animal, place or object, treat it as concrete. Step 5: use the abstract noun naturally to express the intended idea.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not call a physical object abstract simply because it appears in an important sentence. Do not treat a quality such as honesty as though it were an object that can be picked up. Do not decide that a word is abstract only because of where it appears in the sentence.

title: Utiliser les noms abstraits
body: Un nom abstrait désigne une idée, une qualité, un état ou un concept plutôt qu'un objet physique ordinaire. Des mots comme "beauty", "peace", "honesty", "kindness" et "freedom" désignent des réalités que nous comprenons comme des idées, des sentiments ou des qualités. Les noms concrets comme "book", "chair" et "mango" désignent des choses physiques.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Dans "Ama showed kindness to the new pupil", "kindness" est un nom abstrait parce qu'il désigne une qualité. Dans "Ama gave the pupil a pencil", "pencil" est un nom concret parce qu'il désigne un objet physique.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Trouve le nom. Étape 2 : demande-toi ce qu'il désigne. Étape 3 : s'il désigne une idée, une qualité, un état ou un concept, identifie-le comme abstrait. Étape 4 : s'il désigne une personne, un animal, un lieu ou un objet physique, considère-le comme concret. Étape 5 : utilise naturellement le nom abstrait pour exprimer l'idée voulue.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne considère pas un objet physique comme abstrait simplement parce qu'il apparaît dans une phrase importante. Ne traite pas une qualité comme "honesty" comme s'il s'agissait d'un objet que l'on peut prendre. Ne décide pas qu'un mot est abstrait uniquement à cause de sa place dans la phrase.

title: Use Articles in Sentences
body: Articles help us show whether a noun is general, one of many, or already specific. Use "a" before a singular count noun beginning with a consonant sound, as in "a teacher". Use "an" before a singular count noun beginning with a vowel sound, as in "an orange". Use "the" when the listener can identify the particular person, animal, event, time or object. Some general non-count nouns can appear without an article, as in "I enjoy music."

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Decide whether the noun is singular and countable. Step 2: if introducing one non-specific item, listen to the first sound and choose "a" or "an". Step 3: if the noun is already known or clearly specific, use "the". Step 4: check whether a general non-count noun needs no article.

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not choose "a" or "an" only by looking at a letter without considering the beginning sound. Do not use an indefinite article when the noun is already specific in the context. Do not automatically place an article before a general non-count noun.

title: Utiliser les articles dans les phrases
body: Les articles nous aident à montrer si un nom est général, représente un élément parmi plusieurs ou désigne quelque chose de précis. Utilise "a" devant un nom comptable singulier qui commence par un son consonantique, comme dans "a teacher". Utilise "an" devant un nom comptable singulier qui commence par un son vocalique, comme dans "an orange". Utilise "the" lorsque l'interlocuteur peut identifier la personne, l'animal, l'événement, le moment ou l'objet précis. Certains noms non comptables employés de façon générale peuvent apparaître sans article, comme dans "I enjoy music."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Compare : "Kofi saw a dog near the gate. The dog followed him." La première mention introduit un chien parmi d'autres. La deuxième utilise "the" parce que le chien est maintenant précis. Dans "Abena ate an orange", "an" correspond au son vocalique au début de "orange".

title: Pas à pas

Étape 3 : si le nom est déjà connu ou clairement précis, utilise "the". Étape 4 : vérifie si un nom non comptable employé de façon générale ne demande aucun article.

title: Use Quantifiers Correctly
body: Quantifiers give information about number, amount or order. Ordinals such as "first" and "second" show position. Use "a few" and "fewer" with count nouns such as books. Use "a little" and "less" with non-count nouns such as water. "Both" refers to two together. "Each" considers members separately, while "every" includes all members of a group. "Another" means one more or a different single item, while "other" can refer to additional items.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Compare: "We have a few oranges" but "We have a little juice." Say "fewer pupils" but "less noise." In "Both girls finished", exactly two girls are included. In "Each pupil received a book", the pupils are considered one by one.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Decide whether you are showing order, number or amount. Step 2: identify whether the noun is countable or non-countable. Step 3: choose the quantifier that fits the meaning. Step 4: check whether you mean two together, members individually, all members, one more item or a comparison in quantity.

title: Utiliser correctement les quantificateurs
body: Les quantificateurs donnent des informations sur le nombre, la quantité ou l'ordre. Les ordinaux comme "first" et "second" indiquent une position. Utilise "a few" et "fewer" avec des noms comptables comme books. Utilise "a little" et "less" avec des noms non comptables comme water. "Both" désigne deux éléments ensemble. "Each" considère les membres séparément, tandis que "every" inclut tous les membres d'un groupe. "Another" signifie un élément supplémentaire ou différent au singulier, tandis que "other" peut désigner des éléments supplémentaires.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Compare : "We have a few oranges" mais "We have a little juice." On dit "fewer pupils" mais "less noise." Dans "Both girls finished", exactement deux filles sont incluses. Dans "Each pupil received a book", les élèves sont considérés un par un.

title: Pas à pas

Étape 4 : vérifie si tu veux parler de deux éléments ensemble, des membres individuellement, de tous les membres, d'un élément supplémentaire ou d'une comparaison de quantité.

title: Use Possessive Pronouns
body: Possessive pronouns show who owns something without repeating the noun. They include "mine", "yours", "his", "hers", "ours" and "theirs". A possessive pronoun can stand alone: "This book is mine." Words such as "my", "your", "her", "our" and "their" normally come before a noun: "This is my book."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Compare "That bag is hers" with "That is her bag." In the first sentence, "hers" stands alone as a possessive pronoun. In the second, "her" comes before the noun "bag". Possessive pronouns do not take an apostrophe: write "yours", not "your's".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Identify the owner. Step 2: decide whether the ownership word stands alone or comes before a noun. Step 3: if it stands alone, choose the correct possessive pronoun. Step 4: match it to the owner. Step 5: check that you have not added an apostrophe.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not use "my", "your", "her", "our" or "their" alone when a possessive pronoun is required. Do not write forms such as "your's" or "her's". Do not choose a pronoun that refers to a different owner.

title: Utiliser les pronoms possessifs
body: Les pronoms possessifs indiquent à qui appartient quelque chose sans répéter le nom. Ils comprennent "mine", "yours", "his", "hers", "ours" et "theirs". Un pronom possessif peut être employé seul : "This book is mine." Des mots comme "my", "your", "her", "our" et "their" se placent normalement devant un nom : "This is my book."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Compare "That bag is hers" et "That is her bag." Dans la première phrase, "hers" est employé seul comme pronom possessif. Dans la deuxième, "her" précède le nom "bag". Les pronoms possessifs ne prennent pas d'apostrophe : on écrit "yours", et non "your's".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Identifie le propriétaire. Étape 2 : décide si le mot qui exprime la possession est employé seul ou devant un nom. Étape 3 : s'il est employé seul, choisis le bon pronom possessif. Étape 4 : fais-le correspondre au propriétaire. Étape 5 : vérifie que tu n'as pas ajouté d'apostrophe.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: N'utilise pas "my", "your", "her", "our" ou "their" seuls lorsqu'un pronom possessif est nécessaire. N'écris pas des formes comme "your's" ou "her's". Ne choisis pas un pronom qui renvoie à un autre propriétaire.

title: Use Demonstratives
body: Demonstratives point to particular people or things. Use "this" for one person or thing that is near, and "that" for one that is farther away. Use "these" for more than one person or thing that is near, and "those" for more than one that is farther away.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: If a pupil is holding one book, the pupil can say, "This book is mine." If one book is across the room, the pupil can say, "That book is yours." For several nearby books, say "these books". For several distant books, say "those books".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Decide whether the noun is singular or plural. Step 2: decide whether the person or thing is near or farther away. Step 3: choose this, that, these or those. Step 4: check that the demonstrative agrees with the noun in number.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not choose a demonstrative from singular or plural information alone while ignoring distance. Do not use "this" or "that" with an ordinary plural noun. Do not use "these" or "those" with an ordinary singular noun.

title: Utiliser les démonstratifs
body: Les démonstratifs servent à désigner des personnes ou des choses précises. Utilise "this" pour une seule personne ou chose proche, et "that" pour une seule personne ou chose plus éloignée. Utilise "these" pour plusieurs personnes ou choses proches, et "those" pour plusieurs personnes ou choses plus éloignées.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Si un élève tient un livre, il peut dire : "This book is mine." Si un livre se trouve de l'autre côté de la salle, il peut dire : "That book is yours." Pour plusieurs livres proches, dis "these books". Pour plusieurs livres éloignés, dis "those books".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Décide si le nom est au singulier ou au pluriel. Étape 2 : décide si la personne ou la chose est proche ou plus éloignée. Étape 3 : choisis this, that, these ou those. Étape 4 : vérifie que le démonstratif s'accorde avec le nom en nombre.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne choisis pas un démonstratif uniquement à partir du singulier ou du pluriel en ignorant la distance. N'utilise pas "this" ou "that" avec un nom ordinaire au pluriel. N'utilise pas "these" ou "those" avec un nom ordinaire au singulier.

title: Use Which and Whose
body: Interrogative determiners help us ask questions about nouns. Use "which" before a noun when choosing from a known or limited set, as in "Which book do you want?" Use "whose" before a noun when asking about ownership, as in "Whose bag is this?"

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: At the classroom shelf, a teacher may ask, "Which dictionary do you need, the English one or the French one?" If a pencil is found on the floor, the teacher may ask, "Whose pencil is this?" The first question asks for a choice. The second asks about ownership.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Decide what information the question needs. Step 2: if the question asks someone to choose a particular noun from a known set, use "which". Step 3: if it asks who owns the noun, use "whose". Step 4: place the interrogative determiner before the noun.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not use "which" when the real question is about ownership. Do not confuse "whose" with "who's", which means "who is" or "who has". When "which" or "whose" functions as a determiner, keep the noun it determines.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Utiliser Which et Whose
body: Les déterminants interrogatifs servent à poser des questions à propos des noms. Utilise "which" devant un nom lorsqu'il faut choisir parmi un ensemble connu ou limité, comme dans "Which book do you want?" Utilise "whose" devant un nom lorsqu'on demande à qui quelque chose appartient, comme dans "Whose bag is this?"

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Près de l'étagère de la classe, un enseignant peut demander : "Which dictionary do you need, the English one or the French one?" Si un crayon est trouvé par terre, il peut demander : "Whose pencil is this?" La première question demande un choix. La deuxième demande à qui appartient l'objet.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Détermine l'information recherchée par la question. Étape 2 : si la question demande de choisir un nom précis parmi un ensemble connu, utilise "which". Étape 3 : si elle demande à qui appartient le nom, utilise "whose". Étape 4 : place le déterminant interrogatif devant le nom.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: N'utilise pas "which" lorsque la vraie question porte sur la possession. Ne confonds pas "whose" avec "who's", qui signifie "who is" ou "who has". Lorsque "which" ou "whose" fonctionne comme déterminant, garde le nom qu'il détermine.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Use Indefinite and Possessive Pronouns
body: Indefinite pronouns refer to people or things without naming a particular one. Examples include "someone", "anyone", "everyone", "something", "anything" and "everything". Possessive pronouns such as "mine", "yours", "his", "hers", "ours" and "theirs" show ownership and can stand without a following noun.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: In "Someone knocked at the door", the speaker does not identify the person. In "Everything is ready", the pronoun refers to all the things involved. Compare "This pencil is mine" with "This is my pencil": "mine" stands alone, while "my" comes before a noun.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Decide whether the sentence refers to a specific named person or to an unspecified person or thing. Step 2: choose an indefinite pronoun whose meaning fits. Step 3: when showing ownership without repeating the noun, choose the possessive pronoun that matches the owner.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not replace a clearly named person with an indefinite pronoun when the identity matters. Do not use a pronoun for a thing when the sentence requires an unspecified person, or the reverse. Do not use "my", "your", "her", "our" or "their" alone where "mine", "yours", "hers", "ours" or "theirs" is required.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Utiliser les pronoms indéfinis et possessifs
body: Les pronoms indéfinis désignent des personnes ou des choses sans nommer une personne ou une chose précise. Les exemples comprennent "someone", "anyone", "everyone", "something", "anything" et "everything". Les pronoms possessifs comme "mine", "yours", "his", "hers", "ours" et "theirs" indiquent la possession et peuvent être employés sans nom après eux.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Dans "Someone knocked at the door", le locuteur n'identifie pas la personne. Dans "Everything is ready", le pronom désigne toutes les choses concernées. Compare "This pencil is mine" et "This is my pencil" : "mine" est employé seul, tandis que "my" se place devant un nom.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Décide si la phrase désigne une personne précise et nommée ou une personne ou une chose non précisée. Étape 2 : choisis un pronom indéfini dont le sens convient. Étape 3 : pour exprimer la possession sans répéter le nom, choisis le pronom possessif qui correspond au propriétaire.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body: Ne remplace pas une personne clairement nommée par un pronom indéfini lorsque son identité est importante. N'utilise pas un pronom désignant une chose lorsque la phrase demande une personne non précisée, ni l'inverse. N'utilise pas "my", "your", "her", "our" ou "their" seuls lorsque "mine", "yours", "hers", "ours" ou "theirs" est nécessaire.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Make Comparisons with Adjectives
body: Comparative adjectives compare two people, things or qualities. Many short regular adjectives form the comparative with "-er": "short" becomes "shorter" and "tall" becomes "taller". Some adjectives are irregular: "good" becomes "better" and "bad" becomes "worse". We often use "than" after a comparative.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Compare: "Ama is taller than Esi." The adjective "tall" changes to "taller" because two people are compared. In "This story is better than the first one", "good" changes irregularly to "better".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Identify the two people, things or qualities being compared. Step 2: find the adjective. Step 3: decide whether its comparative is regular or irregular. Step 4: use the comparative form, often followed by "than".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not leave the adjective in its base form when a comparison requires a comparative. Do not invent forms such as "gooder" or "badder" for irregular adjectives. Do not use a superlative such as "tallest" when only two things are being compared.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Faire des comparaisons avec les adjectifs
body: Les adjectifs comparatifs servent à comparer deux personnes, choses ou qualités. Beaucoup d'adjectifs courts et réguliers forment le comparatif avec "-er" : "short" devient "shorter" et "tall" devient "taller". Certains adjectifs sont irréguliers : "good" devient "better" et "bad" devient "worse". On utilise souvent "than" après un comparatif.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Compare : "Ama is taller than Esi." L'adjectif "tall" devient "taller" parce que deux personnes sont comparées. Dans "This story is better than the first one", "good" prend la forme irrégulière "better".

title: Pas à pas

title: Use Main and Helping Verbs
body: A main verb carries the central action or state in a clause. A helping verb, also called an auxiliary, works with the main verb. Primary auxiliaries include forms of "be", "have" and "do". Modal auxiliaries include "can", "may", "must", "will" and "should". In "Ama is reading", "is" helps the main verb "reading". In "Kojo can swim", "can" is a modal and "swim" is the main verb.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Consider "The boy has bought a new football." The main verb is "bought" and "has" is the helping verb. In "Esi will visit Tamale tomorrow", "visit" gives the action and "will" helps to express future time.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Find the action or state at the centre of the clause. Step 2: identify any verb that helps that main verb express time, possibility, ability, obligation or another meaning. Step 3: read the whole verb phrase to check that no necessary helper is missing.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not label the helping verb as the main action just because it appears first. Do not remove a necessary auxiliary from a verb phrase. Do not replace one modal with another if that changes the intended meaning.

title: Utiliser les verbes principaux et auxiliaires
body: Un verbe principal porte l'action ou l'état essentiel d'une proposition. Un verbe auxiliaire accompagne le verbe principal. Les auxiliaires primaires comprennent les formes de "be", "have" et "do". Les auxiliaires modaux comprennent "can", "may", "must", "will" et "should". Dans "Ama is reading", "is" accompagne le verbe principal "reading". Dans "Kojo can swim", "can" est un modal et "swim" est le verbe principal.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Observe : "The boy has bought a new football." Le verbe principal est "bought" et "has" est l'auxiliaire. Dans "Esi will visit Tamale tomorrow", "visit" exprime l'action et "will" aide à exprimer le futur.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Trouve l'action ou l'état au centre de la proposition. Étape 2 : identifie tout verbe qui accompagne le verbe principal pour exprimer le temps, la possibilité, la capacité, l'obligation ou un autre sens. Étape 3 : lis tout le groupe verbal pour vérifier qu'aucun auxiliaire nécessaire ne manque.

title: Use Subject-Verb Agreement
body: A verb must agree with its subject. In the simple present, a third-person singular subject usually takes a verb ending in "-s" or "-es": "Ama walks to school." A plural subject usually takes the base form: "Ama and Esi walk to school." Forms of "be" also change: "The boy is ready" but "The boys are ready."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: In "The basket of oranges is heavy", the subject is "basket", not "oranges". The nearby plural noun must not control the verb. In "My friends play football", the plural subject "friends" agrees with "play".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Find the subject. Step 2: decide whether it is singular or plural. Step 3: choose the verb form that agrees with that subject. Step 4: ignore other nouns between the subject and the verb. Step 5: reread the complete sentence.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not choose a verb without checking whether the subject is singular or plural. Do not let a noun close to the verb replace the real subject in your thinking. Do not use the base verb after a third-person singular subject when the simple present requires "-s" or "-es".

title: Utiliser l'accord sujet-verbe
body: Le verbe doit s'accorder avec son sujet. Au présent simple, un sujet à la troisième personne du singulier prend généralement un verbe terminé par "-s" ou "-es" : "Ama walks to school." Un sujet pluriel prend généralement la forme de base : "Ama and Esi walk to school." Les formes de "be" changent aussi : "The boy is ready" mais "The boys are ready."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body: Dans "The basket of oranges is heavy", le sujet est "basket", et non "oranges". Le nom pluriel proche ne doit pas commander le verbe. Dans "My friends play football", le sujet pluriel "friends" s'accorde avec "play".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body: Étape 1 : Trouve le sujet. Étape 2 : décide s'il est singulier ou pluriel. Étape 3 : choisis la forme verbale qui s'accorde avec ce sujet. Étape 4 : ignore les autres noms placés entre le sujet et le verbe. Étape 5 : relis la phrase complète.

title: Use the Simple Present for Needs, Preferences, Thoughts and Ideas
body: Use the simple present to express needs, preferences, thoughts and ideas. Examples include "I need a ruler", "I prefer rice to yam", "I think the answer is correct" and "She likes reading stories". With he, she or it, the verb usually takes "-s" or "-es".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: A pupil can say, "I want more time" to express a need, or "I like football more than volleyball" to express a preference. "Kojo thinks the plan will work" expresses a thought. Notice the "-s" in "thinks" because Kojo is one person.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Decide whether the sentence expresses a need, preference, thought or idea. Step 2: choose the simple present verb. Step 3: check the subject. Step 4: add the correct third-person singular ending when the subject is he, she, it or one named person.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not automatically use the present continuous for a state, preference or opinion such as "need", "like" or "think" in these meanings. Do not omit the third-person singular ending. Do not confuse a lasting preference with a temporary action happening at this moment.

body: Utilise le présent simple pour exprimer les besoins, les préférences, les pensées et les idées. Par exemple : "I need a ruler", "I prefer rice to yam", "I think the answer is correct" et "She likes reading stories". Avec he, she ou it, le verbe prend généralement "-s" ou "-es".

title: Exemple résolu
body: Un élève peut dire "I want more time" pour exprimer un besoin, ou "I like football more than volleyball" pour exprimer une préférence. "Kojo thinks the plan will work" exprime une pensée. Remarque le "-s" dans "thinks" parce que Kojo est une seule personne.

title: Use the Simple Past for Past Needs, Interests and Feelings
body: Use the simple past to express needs, interests and feelings that belonged to an earlier time. For example: "Yesterday, I needed some money." "I felt sad when my friend left." "Last year, I was interested in the school competition." Time expressions such as "yesterday", "last week" and "last year" often signal a past context.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Compare "I need a ruler today" with "I needed a ruler yesterday." The first describes a present need. The second describes a past need. In "Ama felt happy after the match", "felt" tells us about a feeling at a completed time in the past.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: Find the time of the situation. Step 2: decide whether the need, interest or feeling belongs to the past. Step 3: choose the correct simple past form. Step 4: reread the sentence to make sure the verb agrees with the past-time expression.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Do not use the simple present when the need or feeling is clearly located in the past. Do not invent past forms such as "needded". Do not use a continuous form merely because the situation lasted for some time when the task asks for a completed past need, interest or feeling.
