title: Identifier et utiliser différentes sortes de noms
body:
Les noms propres d'organisations et d'événements prennent une majuscule à chaque mot important :
  the Ghana Police Service, the National Health Insurance Authority, the Hogbetsotso Festival, Republic Day

Les noms comptables peuvent se compter et ont un pluriel : one mango, two mangoes.
Les noms non comptables ne se comptent pas et ne prennent PAS de -s : rice, water, money, furniture, equipment, luggage, information, advice, knowledge.
  On dit "some furniture", "a piece of advice", et non "furnitures" ou "advices".

Les pluriels réguliers ajoutent -s ou -es : book -> books, box -> boxes.
Les pluriels irréguliers changent de forme : child -> children, man -> men, woman -> women, tooth -> teeth, mouse -> mice, foot -> feet.
Certains pluriels ne changent pas : one sheep, ten sheep ; one fish, many fish ; one deer, two deer.

Attention : en anglais, "furniture", "information" et "advice" sont toujours au singulier, contrairement au français "des informations" ou "des conseils".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Kojo écrit : "the ghana police service gave the mans some advices about road safety."

1. Nom d'organisation : Ghana Police Service prend des majuscules, et la phrase a besoin d'un T majuscule.
2. Pluriel irrégulier : man -> men, et non "mans".
3. Nom non comptable : advice ne prend pas de -s.

Phrase corrigée : "The Ghana Police Service gave the men some advice about road safety."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère tout nom d'organisation ou d'événement. Mets une majuscule à chaque mot important.
Étape 2 : Pour chaque autre nom, demande-toi : "Puis-je le compter ? (one, two, three)"
Étape 3 : Si NON (rice, furniture, advice) : n'ajoute jamais de -s. Utilise "some" ou "a piece of".
Étape 4 : Si OUI : le pluriel est-il irrégulier (children, men, teeth) ou invariable (sheep, fish) ?
Étape 5 : Sinon, ajoute -s ou -es.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase et vérifie chaque nom.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Un -s sur des noms non comptables ou invariables : "luggages", "knowledges", "sheeps". Ces noms ne prennent jamais de -s.
2. Un -s sur des pluriels irréguliers : "foots", "tooths", "mouses". Utilise feet, teeth, mice.
3. Des minuscules pour les noms : "the hogbetsotso festival", "the ghana police service". Les noms d'organisations et d'événements prennent des majuscules.

title: Use -ing Nouns and Noun Phrases for Activities
body:
An -ing noun names an activity: singing, swimming, jogging, shopping.
  I enjoy singing.   I like swimming.

An -ing noun can grow into a noun phrase:
  Reading storybooks is fun.   Early morning jogging keeps Uncle Fiifi fit.   We listened to the singing of the choir.

Where do -ing nouns go?
1. As the subject: Dancing makes me happy.
2. After verbs such as enjoy, finish, avoid, keep, mind, miss, practise: She practises writing every day.
3. After prepositions such as at, in, of, for, before, after, without: He is interested in drawing.

Spelling the -ing form:
- Most verbs just add -ing: read -> reading, play -> playing.
- Drop the silent e: write -> writing, dance -> dancing.
- Double the last consonant after one short vowel: swim -> swimming, run -> running, shop -> shopping.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Ama writes: "I enjoy to dance, and I am good at write stories. Swiming is my other hobby."

1. After enjoy, use an -ing noun: enjoy dancing, not "enjoy to dance".
2. After the preposition at, use an -ing noun: good at writing, not "good at write".
3. Spelling: swim has one short vowel before m, so double it: swimming.

Corrected: "I enjoy dancing, and I am good at writing stories. Swimming is my other hobby."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the word that names the activity.
Step 2: Look at the word just before it. Is it a verb such as enjoy, finish, avoid or keep? Is it a preposition such as at, of, for or before? Or is the activity the subject?
Step 3: If yes, use the -ing noun, not the base verb and not "to" + verb.
Step 4: Spell it: drop a silent e, double one final consonant after one short vowel, otherwise just add -ing.
Step 5: Read the whole sentence again.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. The base verb in place of the activity noun: "We enjoy play football." Write: We enjoy playing football.
2. "To" + verb after enjoy, finish or a preposition: "He finished to wash the plates." Write: He finished washing the plates.
3. Spelling errors: "makeing", "hopeing", "runing", "siting". Write: making, hoping, running, sitting.

title: Utiliser des noms en -ing et des groupes nominaux pour désigner des activités
body:
Un nom en -ing désigne une activité : singing, swimming, jogging, shopping.
  I enjoy singing.   I like swimming.

Un nom en -ing peut devenir un groupe nominal :
  Reading storybooks is fun.   Early morning jogging keeps Uncle Fiifi fit.   We listened to the singing of the choir.

Où place-t-on les noms en -ing ?
1. Comme sujet : Dancing makes me happy.
2. Après des verbes comme enjoy, finish, avoid, keep, mind, miss, practise : She practises writing every day.
3. Après des prépositions comme at, in, of, for, before, after, without : He is interested in drawing.

Orthographe de la forme en -ing :
- La plupart des verbes ajoutent simplement -ing : read -> reading, play -> playing.
- On supprime le e muet : write -> writing, dance -> dancing.
- On double la dernière consonne après une seule voyelle courte : swim -> swimming, run -> running, shop -> shopping.

Attention : en français on dit "j'aime nager" avec l'infinitif, mais en anglais on dit "I enjoy swimming", jamais "I enjoy to swim".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Ama écrit : "I enjoy to dance, and I am good at write stories. Swiming is my other hobby."

1. Après enjoy, on utilise un nom en -ing : enjoy dancing, et non "enjoy to dance".
2. Après la préposition at, on utilise un nom en -ing : good at writing, et non "good at write".
3. Orthographe : swim a une seule voyelle courte avant le m, on double donc le m : swimming.

Phrase corrigée : "I enjoy dancing, and I am good at writing stories. Swimming is my other hobby."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère le mot qui désigne l'activité.
Étape 2 : Regarde le mot juste avant. Est-ce un verbe comme enjoy, finish, avoid ou keep ? Une préposition comme at, of, for ou before ? Ou bien l'activité est-elle le sujet ?
Étape 3 : Si oui, utilise le nom en -ing, ni le verbe de base, ni "to" + verbe.
Étape 4 : Écris-le correctement : supprime le e muet, double la consonne finale après une seule voyelle courte, sinon ajoute simplement -ing.
Étape 5 : Relis toute la phrase.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Le verbe de base à la place du nom d'activité : "We enjoy play football." Écris : We enjoy playing football.
2. "To" + verbe après enjoy, finish ou une préposition : "He finished to wash the plates." Écris : He finished washing the plates.
3. Des fautes d'orthographe : "makeing", "hopeing", "runing", "siting". Écris : making, hoping, running, sitting.

title: Identify and Use Abstract Nouns for Concepts and Ideas
body:
An abstract noun names something you cannot see or touch: a quality, a feeling, a concept or an idea.
  intelligence, knowledge, idea, patience
  I admire Ama because of her patience.

Many abstract nouns are made from adjectives or verbs by adding a suffix:
  -ence / -ance: intelligent -> intelligence, important -> importance
  -ness: sad -> sadness, lazy -> laziness
  -dom: wise -> wisdom, bored -> boredom
  -th: warm -> warmth, true -> truth
  -ion: decide -> decision, educate -> education
  -ment: agree -> agreement, punish -> punishment
  -ship: friend -> friendship, leader -> leadership

An abstract noun sits where a noun goes: after his, her, their, the, of, because of, or as the subject.
  Her intelligence surprised everyone.   The importance of education is clear.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Yaw writes: "Everyone admires Efua for her intelligent. Her decide to help the old woman showed great wiseness."

1. After her, we need a noun, not the adjective intelligent: her intelligence.
2. After her, we need a noun, not the verb decide: her decision.
3. Wise takes the suffix -dom, not -ness: wisdom.

Corrected: "Everyone admires Efua for her intelligence. Her decision to help the old woman showed great wisdom."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the place in the sentence where an idea or quality is named.
Step 2: Look at the word before it. After his, her, their, the, of or because of, you need a noun.
Step 3: Is the word there an adjective (describes) or a verb (an action)? Change it into its noun.
Step 4: Choose the right suffix for that word (-ence, -ness, -dom, -th, -ion, -ment, -ship). Check a dictionary if you are not sure.
Step 5: Read the sentence again. Does it name the idea clearly?

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. An adjective in a noun position: "We felt the warm of the fire." Write: We felt the warmth of the fire.
2. A verb in a noun position: "Their agree ended the quarrel." Write: Their agreement ended the quarrel.
3. The wrong suffix: "boredness", "friendment", "trueness". Write: boredom, friendship, truth.

title: Identifier et utiliser des noms abstraits pour des concepts et des idées
body:
Un nom abstrait désigne quelque chose qu'on ne peut ni voir ni toucher : une qualité, un sentiment, un concept ou une idée.
  intelligence, knowledge, idea, patience
  I admire Ama because of her patience.

Beaucoup de noms abstraits viennent d'adjectifs ou de verbes auxquels on ajoute un suffixe :
  -ence / -ance : intelligent -> intelligence, important -> importance
  -ness : sad -> sadness, lazy -> laziness
  -dom : wise -> wisdom, bored -> boredom
  -th : warm -> warmth, true -> truth
  -ion : decide -> decision, educate -> education
  -ment : agree -> agreement, punish -> punishment
  -ship : friend -> friendship, leader -> leadership

Un nom abstrait se place là où va un nom : après his, her, their, the, of, because of, ou comme sujet.
  Her intelligence surprised everyone.   The importance of education is clear.

Attention : chaque mot a son propre suffixe. On ne peut pas en choisir un au hasard ; vérifie dans le dictionnaire en cas de doute.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Yaw écrit : "Everyone admires Efua for her intelligent. Her decide to help the old woman showed great wiseness."

1. Après her, il faut un nom, pas l'adjectif intelligent : her intelligence.
2. Après her, il faut un nom, pas le verbe decide : her decision.
3. Wise prend le suffixe -dom, pas -ness : wisdom.

Phrase corrigée : "Everyone admires Efua for her intelligence. Her decision to help the old woman showed great wisdom."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère l'endroit de la phrase où une idée ou une qualité est nommée.
Étape 2 : Regarde le mot qui précède. Après his, her, their, the, of ou because of, il faut un nom.
Étape 3 : Le mot placé là est-il un adjectif (il décrit) ou un verbe (une action) ? Transforme-le en nom.
Étape 4 : Choisis le bon suffixe pour ce mot (-ence, -ness, -dom, -th, -ion, -ment, -ship). Vérifie dans un dictionnaire si tu n'es pas sûr.
Étape 5 : Relis la phrase. Nomme-t-elle clairement l'idée ?

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Un adjectif à la place d'un nom : "We felt the warm of the fire." Écris : We felt the warmth of the fire.
2. Un verbe à la place d'un nom : "Their agree ended the quarrel." Écris : Their agreement ended the quarrel.
3. Le mauvais suffixe : "boredness", "friendment", "trueness". Écris : boredom, friendship, truth.

title: Identify and Use Definite and Indefinite Articles
body:
Articles are small words that come before nouns.
  Indefinite articles: a, an. They mean "one" or "any one", for something not yet known.
  Definite article: the. It points to something known or specific.

Use a or an with ONE thing you can count (a singular count noun):
  a teacher, an umbrella, a cup
A singular count noun never stands alone. It needs a, an, the or another determiner (my, this...).

Do NOT use a or an with:
  plural nouns: chairs, mangoes, pupils
  non-count nouns: sugar, water, sand, milk
Use them with no article when you speak in general, or with the or some when you mean a particular amount.
  Children need sleep.   Please pass the sugar.

Use the when:
  the noun was mentioned before or both speakers know which one: I saw a dog. The dog was hungry.
  there is only one of it: the sun, the moon, the sky, the earth
  the noun follows a superlative or an ordinal: the tallest boy, the first lesson

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Mawuli writes: "Kwesi is pupil at a best school in town. Every morning he buys a bread and watches a sun rise."

1. Pupil is one countable person, so it needs an article: a pupil.
2. Best is a superlative, so it takes the: the best school.
3. Bread is a non-count noun, so it does not take a: he buys bread.
4. There is only one sun, so it takes the: the sun.

Corrected: "Kwesi is a pupil at the best school in town. Every morning he buys bread and watches the sun rise."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Underline each noun in the sentence.
Step 2: Ask: is it one countable thing, many things, or something you cannot count?
Step 3: One countable thing: it must have a, an, the or another determiner in front of it.
Step 4: Many things or something uncountable: do not use a or an.
Step 5: Is the thing the only one, or does it come after a word like tallest, best, first or last? Use the.
Step 6: Read the sentence aloud and check each article again.

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. No article before one countable thing: "My father is farmer." Write: My father is a farmer.
2. A or an before a plural or non-count noun: "a sugar", "a shoes". Write: some sugar, shoes, a pair of shoes.
3. A or an before something unique or after a superlative: "a moon", "a longest river". Write: the moon, the longest river.

title: Identifier et utiliser les articles définis et indéfinis
body:
Les articles sont de petits mots placés devant les noms.
  Articles indéfinis : a, an. Ils veulent dire "un" ou "n'importe lequel", pour une chose pas encore connue.
  Article défini : the. Il désigne une chose connue ou précise.

On utilise a ou an avec UNE chose qu'on peut compter (un nom comptable au singulier) :
  a teacher, an umbrella, a cup
Un nom comptable au singulier ne reste jamais seul. Il lui faut a, an, the ou un autre déterminant (my, this...).

On n'utilise PAS a ou an avec :
  les noms au pluriel : chairs, mangoes, pupils
  les noms non comptables : sugar, water, sand, milk
On les emploie sans article quand on parle en général, ou avec the ou some quand on pense à une quantité précise.
  Children need sleep.   Please pass the sugar.

On utilise the quand :
  le nom a déjà été mentionné ou que tout le monde sait de quoi on parle : I saw a dog. The dog was hungry.
  la chose est unique : the sun, the moon, the sky, the earth
  le nom suit un superlatif ou un ordinal : the tallest boy, the first lesson

Attention : en français on dit "le sucre" pour parler du sucre en général, mais en anglais on dit simplement sugar, sans article.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Mawuli écrit : "Kwesi is pupil at a best school in town. Every morning he buys a bread and watches a sun rise."

1. Pupil désigne une personne qu'on peut compter, il faut donc un article : a pupil.
2. Best est un superlatif, il prend donc the : the best school.
3. Bread est un nom non comptable, il ne prend donc pas a : he buys bread.
4. Il n'y a qu'un seul soleil, il prend donc the : the sun.

Phrase corrigée : "Kwesi is a pupil at the best school in town. Every morning he buys bread and watches the sun rise."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Souligne chaque nom de la phrase.
Étape 2 : Demande-toi : est-ce une seule chose comptable, plusieurs choses, ou quelque chose qu'on ne peut pas compter ?
Étape 3 : Une seule chose comptable : elle doit avoir a, an, the ou un autre déterminant devant elle.
Étape 4 : Plusieurs choses ou quelque chose qu'on ne compte pas : n'utilise pas a ou an.
Étape 5 : La chose est-elle unique, ou vient-elle après un mot comme tallest, best, first ou last ? Utilise the.
Étape 6 : Lis la phrase à voix haute et vérifie encore chaque article.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Pas d'article devant une seule chose comptable : "My father is farmer." Écris : My father is a farmer.
2. A ou an devant un nom au pluriel ou non comptable : "a sugar", "a shoes". Écris : some sugar, shoes, a pair of shoes.
3. A ou an devant une chose unique ou après un superlatif : "a moon", "a longest river". Écris : the moon, the longest river.

Attention : en français on dit "il est fermier" sans article, mais en anglais il faut dire "he is a farmer".

title: Identify and Use Quantifiers
body:
A quantifier comes before a noun and tells how many, how much, or which one in order.

Ordinals show ORDER: first, second, third, fourth, fifth, ninth, twelfth, twentieth.
Cardinals show HOW MANY: one, two, three, four.
  the second lesson (its place in order)   two lessons (how many)

Each quantifier goes with a certain kind of noun:
  singular count noun: each, every, another, one     each desk, every house, another day
  plural count noun: both, several, many, few, fewer, other     both hands, several cars, other pupils
  non-count noun: little, less, much     little time, less salt
  plural or non-count noun: some, all, no     some eggs, all the oil, no money

Another means "one more" or "a different one", so it is followed by ONE thing: another orange.
For more than one, use other: other oranges.

Remember from Basic 5: few and fewer go with count nouns; little and less go with non-count nouns.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Dzifa writes: "Every dancers in our group wore another beads for the five show of the festival."

1. Every goes with a singular noun: every dancer.
2. Another means one more thing, so it cannot go before the plural beads. Use other: other beads.
3. The show has a place in order, so we need an ordinal: the fifth show.

Corrected: "Every dancer in our group wore other beads for the fifth show of the festival."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find each quantifier in the sentence (each, every, both, several, another, some...).
Step 2: Look at the noun that follows it. Is it singular, plural or non-count?
Step 3: Check that the noun matches: each, every and another need one thing; both, several and other need more than one.
Step 4: Find any number. Does it tell how many, or a place in order?
Step 5: If it tells a place in order (day, turn, visit, lesson), use an ordinal: first, second, third...
Step 6: Read the sentence again to make sure each quantifier fits its noun.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Another before a plural noun: "another chairs". Write: another chair, or other chairs.
2. The wrong noun number after a quantifier: "each learners", "both cup". Write: each learner, both cups.
3. A counting number where order is meant: "the two lesson". Write: the second lesson.

title: Identifier et utiliser les quantifieurs
body:
Un quantifieur se place devant un nom et indique combien, quelle quantité, ou quel rang.

Les ordinaux indiquent le RANG : first, second, third, fourth, fifth, ninth, twelfth, twentieth.
Les cardinaux indiquent COMBIEN : one, two, three, four.
  the second lesson (sa place dans l'ordre)   two lessons (combien)

Chaque quantifieur va avec un certain type de nom :
  nom comptable au singulier : each, every, another, one     each desk, every house, another day
  nom comptable au pluriel : both, several, many, few, fewer, other     both hands, several cars, other pupils
  nom non comptable : little, less, much     little time, less salt
  nom au pluriel ou non comptable : some, all, no     some eggs, all the oil, no money

Another veut dire "un de plus" ou "un autre", il est donc suivi d'UNE seule chose : another orange.
Pour plusieurs, on utilise other : other oranges.

Rappel de Basic 5 : few et fewer vont avec les noms comptables ; little et less vont avec les noms non comptables.

Attention : en français "chaque" et "tous les" se ressemblent par le sens, mais en anglais each et every sont toujours suivis d'un nom au singulier.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Dzifa écrit : "Every dancers in our group wore another beads for the five show of the festival."

1. Every va avec un nom au singulier : every dancer.
2. Another veut dire une chose de plus, il ne peut donc pas se placer devant le pluriel beads. On utilise other : other beads.
3. Le spectacle a une place dans l'ordre, il faut donc un ordinal : the fifth show.

Phrase corrigée : "Every dancer in our group wore other beads for the fifth show of the festival."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère chaque quantifieur de la phrase (each, every, both, several, another, some...).
Étape 2 : Regarde le nom qui le suit. Est-il au singulier, au pluriel ou non comptable ?
Étape 3 : Vérifie que le nom convient : each, every et another veulent une seule chose ; both, several et other en veulent plusieurs.
Étape 4 : Repère chaque nombre. Indique-t-il combien, ou une place dans l'ordre ?
Étape 5 : S'il indique une place dans l'ordre (jour, tour, visite, leçon), utilise un ordinal : first, second, third...
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase pour t'assurer que chaque quantifieur va avec son nom.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Another devant un nom au pluriel : "another chairs". Écris : another chair, ou other chairs.
2. Le mauvais nombre après un quantifieur : "each learners", "both cup". Écris : each learner, both cups.
3. Un nombre cardinal là où il faut un rang : "the two lesson". Écris : the second lesson.

title: Identify and Use Possessive Pronouns to Show Possession
body:
Possessive words show who owns something.

Before a noun: my, your, his, her, its, our, their
  I gave my book to Mary. She sold her phone. The goat fed its kid.
Standing alone: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs
  This seat is mine. The red bicycle is theirs.

Possessive words NEVER take an apostrophe.
  its = belonging to it: The bird built its nest.
  it's = it is: It's raining.
  their = belonging to them: The pupils opened their books.
  there = a place: Put the box there.
  they're = they are: They're late today.

To say that someone belongs to a group of your friends, relatives or classmates, use of + a possessive pronoun:
  a friend of mine, a cousin of yours, an aunt of his, a teacher of hers, a neighbour of theirs
Do not use me, you, him, her, us or them after of to show possession.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Efua writes: "The twins' cat hurt it's paw, so there uncle, a neighbour of us, took it to the vet."

1. The paw belongs to the cat, so we need the possessive its, with no apostrophe: its paw.
2. The uncle belongs to the twins, so we need the possessive their, not the place word there: their uncle.
3. After of, we need a possessive pronoun, not us: a neighbour of ours.

Corrected: "The twins' cat hurt its paw, so their uncle, a neighbour of ours, took it to the vet."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find each word that shows who owns something.
Step 2: Ask: who is the owner? One thing (it), several people (they), or me, you, him, her, us?
Step 3: For an owner that is a thing or an animal, write its with no apostrophe. Test: if "it is" does not fit, do not write it's.
Step 4: For several owners, write their. Test: if "they are" fits, it is they're; if it is a place, it is there.
Step 5: After of, use mine, yours, his, hers, ours or theirs.
Step 6: Read the sentence again and check every possessive word.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. It's for belonging: "The tree lost it's leaves." Write: The tree lost its leaves.
2. There or they're for belonging: "The boys left they're shoes outside." Write: The boys left their shoes outside.
3. An object pronoun after of: "Kweku is a teammate of me." Write: Kweku is a teammate of mine.

title: Identifier et utiliser les pronoms possessifs pour exprimer la possession
body:
Les mots possessifs indiquent à qui appartient une chose.

Devant un nom : my, your, his, her, its, our, their
  I gave my book to Mary. She sold her phone. The goat fed its kid.
Seuls, sans nom : mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs
  This seat is mine. The red bicycle is theirs.

Les mots possessifs ne prennent JAMAIS d'apostrophe.
  its = qui appartient à cela : The bird built its nest.
  it's = it is : It's raining.
  their = qui leur appartient : The pupils opened their books.
  there = un lieu : Put the box there.
  they're = they are : They're late today.

Pour dire qu'une personne fait partie de tes amis, de ta famille ou de tes camarades, on utilise of + un pronom possessif :
  a friend of mine, a cousin of yours, an aunt of his, a teacher of hers, a neighbour of theirs
On n'utilise pas me, you, him, her, us ou them après of pour exprimer la possession.

Attention : en français on dit "un ami à moi", mais en anglais on dit "a friend of mine", et non "a friend of me".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Efua écrit : "The twins' cat hurt it's paw, so there uncle, a neighbour of us, took it to the vet."

1. La patte appartient au chat, il faut donc le possessif its, sans apostrophe : its paw.
2. L'oncle est celui des jumeaux, il faut donc le possessif their, et non le mot de lieu there : their uncle.
3. Après of, il faut un pronom possessif, et non us : a neighbour of ours.

Phrase corrigée : "The twins' cat hurt its paw, so their uncle, a neighbour of ours, took it to the vet."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère chaque mot qui indique à qui appartient une chose.
Étape 2 : Demande-toi : qui est le propriétaire ? Une chose (it), plusieurs personnes (they), ou me, you, him, her, us ?
Étape 3 : Si le propriétaire est une chose ou un animal, écris its sans apostrophe. Test : si "it is" ne convient pas, n'écris pas it's.
Étape 4 : S'il y a plusieurs propriétaires, écris their. Test : si "they are" convient, c'est they're ; si c'est un lieu, c'est there.
Étape 5 : Après of, utilise mine, yours, his, hers, ours ou theirs.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase et vérifie chaque mot possessif.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. It's pour la possession : "The tree lost it's leaves." Écris : The tree lost its leaves.
2. There ou they're pour la possession : "The boys left they're shoes outside." Écris : The boys left their shoes outside.
3. Un pronom complément après of : "Kweku is a teammate of me." Écris : Kweku is a teammate of mine.

title: Identify and Use Demonstratives for Things, Times and Ideas
body:
Demonstratives point to something: this, that, these, those.
In Basic 5 you used them for things that are near or far, and for one thing or many.
In Basic 6 we use them in three more ways.

1. Before a noun, use those, never them.
  Pass me those plates. (not: them plates)
  Them is a pronoun. It stands alone: I washed them.

2. With kind, sort and type, the demonstrative agrees with kind, sort or type.
  this kind of mango / these kinds of mangoes
  that sort of game / those sorts of games
  Do not write "these kind of" or "those sort of".

3. Demonstratives can point to times and ideas.
  Now or very recent: this week, these days.
  The past: that year, at that time, in those days.
  An idea someone has just said: That is a good plan.
  An idea you are about to say: This is my plan: we start at six.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Yaw writes: "In these days, my grandmother carried them big pots to the stream, and she cooked these sort of soup every Sunday."

1. The grandmother's childhood is in the past, so we need those: In those days.
2. The word pots is a noun, so we need those, not them: those big pots.
3. The demonstrative agrees with sort, which is singular: this sort of soup.

Corrected: "In those days, my grandmother carried those big pots to the stream, and she cooked this sort of soup every Sunday."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find each demonstrative and each place where them comes before a noun.
Step 2: If a noun follows, write those, not them.
Step 3: If kind, sort or type follows, look at that word: kind needs this or that; kinds needs these or those.
Step 4: Ask: is the time now or in the past? Now: this or these. Past: that or those.
Step 5: For an idea that was just said, use that. For an idea you are about to say, use this.
Step 6: Read the sentence again and check every demonstrative.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Them before a noun: "Can you lift them chairs?" Write: Can you lift those chairs?
2. Agreement with the noun after kind: "I like these type of shoes." Write: I like this type of shoe, or: I like these types of shoes.
3. This or these for the past: "In 1957, Ghana became independent. At this time, my uncle was a teacher." Write: At that time, my uncle was a teacher.

title: Identifier et utiliser les démonstratifs pour les choses, les moments et les idées
body:
Les démonstratifs montrent quelque chose : this, that, these, those.
En Basic 5, tu les as utilisés pour des choses proches ou éloignées, au singulier ou au pluriel.
En Basic 6, on les utilise de trois autres façons.

1. Devant un nom, on utilise those, jamais them.
  Pass me those plates. (et non : them plates)
  Them est un pronom. Il s'emploie seul : I washed them.

2. Avec kind, sort et type, le démonstratif s'accorde avec kind, sort ou type.
  this kind of mango / these kinds of mangoes
  that sort of game / those sorts of games
  N'écris pas "these kind of" ni "those sort of".

3. Les démonstratifs peuvent désigner des moments et des idées.
  Maintenant ou très récent : this week, these days.
  Le passé : that year, at that time, in those days.
  Une idée que quelqu'un vient de dire : That is a good plan.
  Une idée que tu vas annoncer : This is my plan: we start at six.

Attention : en français on dit "ces jours-là" pour le passé ; en anglais on dit "in those days", et non "in these days".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Yaw écrit : "In these days, my grandmother carried them big pots to the stream, and she cooked these sort of soup every Sunday."

1. L'enfance de la grand-mère appartient au passé, il faut donc those : In those days.
2. Le mot pots est un nom, il faut donc those, et non them : those big pots.
3. Le démonstratif s'accorde avec sort, qui est au singulier : this sort of soup.

Phrase corrigée : "In those days, my grandmother carried those big pots to the stream, and she cooked this sort of soup every Sunday."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère chaque démonstratif et chaque endroit où them est placé devant un nom.
Étape 2 : Si un nom suit, écris those, et non them.
Étape 3 : Si kind, sort ou type suit, regarde ce mot : kind demande this ou that ; kinds demande these ou those.
Étape 4 : Demande-toi : le moment est-il maintenant ou dans le passé ? Maintenant : this ou these. Passé : that ou those.
Étape 5 : Pour une idée qui vient d'être dite, utilise that. Pour une idée que tu vas annoncer, utilise this.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase et vérifie chaque démonstratif.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Them devant un nom : "Can you lift them chairs?" Écris : Can you lift those chairs?
2. Accord avec le nom placé après kind : "I like these type of shoes." Écris : I like this type of shoe, ou : I like these types of shoes.
3. This ou these pour le passé : "In 1957, Ghana became independent. At this time, my uncle was a teacher." Écris : At that time, my uncle was a teacher.

title: Identify and Use Reflexive, Relative and Reciprocal Pronouns
body:
1. Reflexive pronouns show that the object of a verb is the same person as the subject.
  myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves
  Kwame cut himself. The girls taught themselves to sew.
  Singular ends in -self; plural ends in -selves.
  himself and themselves are built on him and them, not on his and their.

2. Relative pronouns link ideas and add information to a noun.
  who for people: The nurse who helped us was kind.
  which for things and animals: The bus which broke down is old.
  whose for belonging: The boy whose bag tore cried.
  where for places: This is the farm where we work.

3. Reciprocal pronouns show that two or more people do the same action to one another.
  each other, one another
  Esi and Aba hugged each other. (Esi hugged Aba, and Aba hugged Esi.)
  The players greeted one another.
  Compare: The players warmed themselves by the fire. (each player warmed his own body)

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Akua writes: "The two brothers, which live near the river, waved at themselves and then made breakfast by theirselves."

1. Brothers are people, so the relative pronoun is who: who live near the river.
2. Each brother waved at the other one, so the pronoun is reciprocal: waved at each other.
3. The plural reflexive is built on them: by themselves.

Corrected: "The two brothers, who live near the river, waved at each other and then made breakfast by themselves."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the pronouns that end in -self or -selves, the words who, which, whose and where, and the phrases each other and one another.
Step 2: For a reflexive pronoun, check the spelling: himself, themselves, ourselves (plural ends in -selves).
Step 3: For a relative pronoun, look at the noun before it: a person needs who, a thing or an animal needs which.
Step 4: Ask: does each person do the action to the other person? If yes, use each other or one another.
Step 5: If each person does the action to his or her own body, use the reflexive pronoun.
Step 6: Read the sentence again and check every pronoun.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. A wrong reflexive form: "He dressed hisself." Write: He dressed himself. "We blamed ourself." Write: We blamed ourselves.
2. Which for a person or who for a thing: "The driver which stopped was polite." Write: The driver who stopped was polite.
3. A reflexive pronoun for a shared action: "The cousins phoned themselves every night." Write: The cousins phoned each other every night.

title: Identifier et utiliser les pronoms réfléchis, relatifs et réciproques
body:
1. Les pronoms réfléchis montrent que le complément du verbe est la même personne que le sujet.
  myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves
  Kwame cut himself. The girls taught themselves to sew.
  Au singulier, ils se terminent par -self ; au pluriel, par -selves.
  himself et themselves sont formés sur him et them, et non sur his et their.

2. Les pronoms relatifs relient des idées et ajoutent une information à un nom.
  who pour les personnes : The nurse who helped us was kind.
  which pour les choses et les animaux : The bus which broke down is old.
  whose pour l'appartenance : The boy whose bag tore cried.
  where pour les lieux : This is the farm where we work.

3. Les pronoms réciproques montrent que deux personnes ou plus font la même action l'une envers l'autre.
  each other, one another
  Esi and Aba hugged each other. (Esi a serré Aba dans ses bras, et Aba a serré Esi.)
  The players greeted one another.
  Compare : The players warmed themselves by the fire. (chaque joueur s'est réchauffé lui-même)

Attention : en français, "ils se sont salués" peut vouloir dire "l'un l'autre". En anglais, il faut dire "they greeted each other", et non "they greeted themselves".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Akua écrit : "The two brothers, which live near the river, waved at themselves and then made breakfast by theirselves."

1. Les frères sont des personnes, le pronom relatif est donc who : who live near the river.
2. Chaque frère a fait signe à l'autre, le pronom est donc réciproque : waved at each other.
3. Le pronom réfléchi pluriel est formé sur them : by themselves.

Phrase corrigée : "The two brothers, who live near the river, waved at each other and then made breakfast by themselves."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère les pronoms qui se terminent par -self ou -selves, les mots who, which, whose et where, et les expressions each other et one another.
Étape 2 : Pour un pronom réfléchi, vérifie l'orthographe : himself, themselves, ourselves (le pluriel se termine par -selves).
Étape 3 : Pour un pronom relatif, regarde le nom placé avant : une personne demande who, une chose ou un animal demande which.
Étape 4 : Demande-toi : chaque personne fait-elle l'action à l'autre ? Si oui, utilise each other ou one another.
Étape 5 : Si chaque personne fait l'action à elle-même, utilise le pronom réfléchi.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase et vérifie chaque pronom.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Une forme réfléchie incorrecte : "He dressed hisself." Écris : He dressed himself. "We blamed ourself." Écris : We blamed ourselves.
2. Which pour une personne ou who pour une chose : "The driver which stopped was polite." Écris : The driver who stopped was polite.
3. Un pronom réfléchi pour une action partagée : "The cousins phoned themselves every night." Écris : The cousins phoned each other every night.

title: Use Comparative Forms of Regular and Irregular Adjectives to Make Comparisons
body:
We use a comparative adjective to compare two people, things or places.
  Musah is taller than Safianu.

1. Short adjectives (one syllable) add -er: tall, taller; cold, colder.
2. Long adjectives (most with two syllables and all with three or more) use more:
  careful, more careful; intelligent, more intelligent; important, more important.
  Adjectives that end in -y are the exception: they add -er.
3. Watch the spelling when you add -er:
  one vowel + one consonant: double the consonant: sad, sadder; red, redder; slim, slimmer.
  consonant + y: change y to i: happy, happier; lazy, lazier; noisy, noisier.
  ends in e: add only -r: nice, nicer; safe, safer.
4. Irregular adjectives change their form:
  good, better; bad, worse; far, farther; much or many, more; little, less.
5. After a comparative, write than (not then).
  than compares: Accra is larger than Cape Coast.
  then tells time: We ate, then we slept.

To compare three or more, use the superlative: Ali is the tallest; this is the most intelligent answer.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Adwoa writes: "My new shoes are comfortabler then my old ones, and the soles are thiner too."

1. Comfortable is a long adjective, so we use more: more comfortable.
2. To compare, we write than, not then: more comfortable than my old ones.
3. Thin has one vowel and one consonant, so we double the n: thinner.

Corrected: "My new shoes are more comfortable than my old ones, and the soles are thinner too."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find each adjective that compares two things.
Step 2: Count its syllables. One syllable: add -er. Two syllables ending in -y: add -er. Other long adjectives: use more.
Step 3: Check whether the adjective is irregular (good, bad, far, much, many, little) and use its special form.
Step 4: Before adding -er, check the spelling: double a final consonant after one vowel, change y to i, or add only -r after e.
Step 5: After the comparative, write than and then the second thing being compared.
Step 6: Read the sentence again and check every comparison.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. -er on a long adjective: "This puzzle is difficulter." Write: This puzzle is more difficult.
2. Spelling ignored: "The path is wetter and bumpyer today." Write: The path is wetter and bumpier today. "My dog is fater now." Write: My dog is fatter now.
3. Then for than: "Lemons are sourer then oranges." Write: Lemons are sourer than oranges.

title: Utiliser les comparatifs des adjectifs réguliers et irréguliers pour comparer
body:
On utilise un adjectif au comparatif pour comparer deux personnes, deux choses ou deux lieux.
  Musah is taller than Safianu.

1. Les adjectifs courts (une syllabe) prennent -er : tall, taller ; cold, colder.
2. Les adjectifs longs (la plupart des adjectifs de deux syllabes et tous ceux de trois syllabes ou plus) prennent more :
  careful, more careful ; intelligent, more intelligent ; important, more important.
  Les adjectifs en -y font exception : ils prennent -er.
3. Attention à l'orthographe quand tu ajoutes -er :
  une voyelle + une consonne : on double la consonne : sad, sadder ; red, redder ; slim, slimmer.
  consonne + y : le y devient i : happy, happier ; lazy, lazier ; noisy, noisier.
  terminaison en e : on ajoute seulement -r : nice, nicer ; safe, safer.
4. Les adjectifs irréguliers changent de forme :
  good, better ; bad, worse ; far, farther ; much ou many, more ; little, less.
5. Après un comparatif, on écrit than (et non then).
  than compare : Accra is larger than Cape Coast.
  then indique le temps : We ate, then we slept.

Pour comparer trois éléments ou plus, on utilise le superlatif : Ali is the tallest ; this is the most intelligent answer.

Attention : en français on dit "plus grand que" ; en anglais, que se dit than, jamais then.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Adwoa écrit : "My new shoes are comfortabler then my old ones, and the soles are thiner too."

1. Comfortable est un adjectif long, on utilise donc more : more comfortable.
2. Pour comparer, on écrit than, et non then : more comfortable than my old ones.
3. Thin a une voyelle et une consonne, on double donc le n : thinner.

Phrase corrigée : "My new shoes are more comfortable than my old ones, and the soles are thinner too."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère chaque adjectif qui compare deux choses.
Étape 2 : Compte ses syllabes. Une syllabe : ajoute -er. Deux syllabes terminées par -y : ajoute -er. Autres adjectifs longs : utilise more.
Étape 3 : Vérifie si l'adjectif est irrégulier (good, bad, far, much, many, little) et utilise sa forme particulière.
Étape 4 : Avant d'ajouter -er, vérifie l'orthographe : double la consonne finale après une seule voyelle, change y en i, ou ajoute seulement -r après e.
Étape 5 : Après le comparatif, écris than puis le deuxième élément comparé.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase et vérifie chaque comparaison.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. -er sur un adjectif long : "This puzzle is difficulter." Écris : This puzzle is more difficult.
2. Orthographe oubliée : "The path is wetter and bumpyer today." Écris : The path is wetter and bumpier today. "My dog is fater now." Écris : My dog is fatter now.
3. Then au lieu de than : "Lemons are sourer then oranges." Écris : Lemons are sourer than oranges.

title: Use Main Verbs and Helping Verbs (Primary and Modal Auxiliaries)
body:
A main verb carries the meaning of the action: run, cook, write, think.
A helping verb (auxiliary) stands before the main verb and helps it.

1. Primary auxiliaries: be, have, do.
  be (am, is, are, was, were): She is singing.
  have (has, had): They have finished.
  do (does, did): Do you know him? I did not see it.
  These three can also be main verbs: I have a pen. He does his homework.

2. Modal auxiliaries: can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should, must, ought to.
  They show ability, permission, possibility, duty or advice.

Three rules for the main verb after a helping verb:
  After a modal, use the base verb with no to: You must wash. We can stay.
  Only ought keeps to: You ought to rest.
  After a modal, the main verb never takes -s or a past form: He can swim. (not: can swims) She could hear. (not: could heard)
  After do, does or did, use the base verb too: Does he cook? We did not travel. (not: did not travelled)
  The helping verb carries the -s or the past, so the main verb stays plain.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Esi writes: "My brother must to feed the hens, but he can runs fast, so he did not missed the bus."

1. Must is a modal, so no to follows it: must feed.
2. After can, the main verb stays plain: can run.
3. Did already shows the past, so the main verb stays plain: did not miss.

Corrected: "My brother must feed the hens, but he can run fast, so he did not miss the bus."
Helping verbs: must, can, did. Main verbs: feed, run, miss.

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Underline every verb in the sentence.
Step 2: Mark the helping verbs (be, have, do and the modals) and the main verb that follows each one.
Step 3: After a modal, remove any to (except in ought to).
Step 4: After a modal, remove any -s or past ending from the main verb.
Step 5: After do, does or did, check that the main verb is the base form.
Step 6: Read the sentence again and check every verb pair.

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. To after a modal: "We should to plant trees." Write: We should plant trees.
2. An -s or a past form after a modal: "The baby might cried." Write: The baby might cry.
3. A changed verb after do, does or did: "Does your uncle sells bread?" Write: Does your uncle sell bread?

title: Utiliser les verbes principaux et les verbes auxiliaires (auxiliaires primaires et modaux)
body:
Un verbe principal porte le sens de l'action : run, cook, write, think.
Un verbe auxiliaire se place devant le verbe principal et l'aide.

1. Les auxiliaires primaires : be, have, do.
  be (am, is, are, was, were) : She is singing.
  have (has, had) : They have finished.
  do (does, did) : Do you know him? I did not see it.
  Ces trois verbes peuvent aussi être des verbes principaux : I have a pen. He does his homework.

2. Les auxiliaires modaux : can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should, must, ought to.
  Ils expriment la capacité, la permission, la possibilité, l'obligation ou le conseil.

Trois règles pour le verbe principal placé après un auxiliaire :
  Après un modal, on utilise la base verbale sans to : You must wash. We can stay.
  Seul ought garde to : You ought to rest.
  Après un modal, le verbe principal ne prend jamais -s ni une forme du passé : He can swim. (et non : can swims) She could hear. (et non : could heard)
  Après do, does ou did, on utilise aussi la base verbale : Does he cook? We did not travel. (et non : did not travelled)
  C'est l'auxiliaire qui porte le -s ou le passé ; le verbe principal reste à la base.

Attention : en français on dit "il doit partir" sans préposition ; en anglais on dit aussi "he must go", et non "he must to go".

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Esi écrit : "My brother must to feed the hens, but he can runs fast, so he did not missed the bus."

1. Must est un modal, il n'est donc pas suivi de to : must feed.
2. Après can, le verbe principal reste à la base : can run.
3. Did indique déjà le passé, le verbe principal reste donc à la base : did not miss.

Phrase corrigée : "My brother must feed the hens, but he can run fast, so he did not miss the bus."
Verbes auxiliaires : must, can, did. Verbes principaux : feed, run, miss.

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Souligne chaque verbe de la phrase.
Étape 2 : Repère les auxiliaires (be, have, do et les modaux) et le verbe principal qui suit chacun d'eux.
Étape 3 : Après un modal, supprime to (sauf dans ought to).
Étape 4 : Après un modal, supprime tout -s ou toute terminaison du passé du verbe principal.
Étape 5 : Après do, does ou did, vérifie que le verbe principal est à la base verbale.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase et vérifie chaque paire de verbes.

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. To après un modal : "We should to plant trees." Écris : We should plant trees.
2. Un -s ou une forme du passé après un modal : "The baby might cried." Écris : The baby might cry.
3. Un verbe modifié après do, does ou did : "Does your uncle sells bread?" Écris : Does your uncle sell bread?

title: Use Subject-Verb Agreement with Indefinite Pronouns, Singular and Plural Subjects and Collective Nouns
body:
A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb.
  The girl sings. The girls sing.

1. Some indefinite pronouns are always singular:
  everyone, everybody, everything, someone, somebody, anyone, nobody, nothing, each, either, neither
  Everybody likes rice. Each of the drums is new. Nobody was late.
  Even when a plural noun follows (each of the drums), the verb agrees with each.

2. Some indefinite pronouns are always plural:
  both, few, many, several, others
  Both are ready. Many of the mangoes are ripe. Few were absent.

3. A collective noun names a group: team, class, family, choir, committee, crowd, herd.
  When the group acts as one unit, use a singular verb and its:
    The committee meets on Mondays. The herd has left its kraal.
  When the members act separately, use a plural verb and their:
    The family were arguing about their plans.
  Do not mix them: a singular verb goes with its; a plural verb goes with their.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Kwabena writes: "Everyone in our street are proud because several of the boys has won prizes and the band have opened its new hall."

1. Everyone is singular: Everyone in our street is proud.
2. Several is plural: several of the boys have won prizes.
3. The band acts as one unit and the sentence uses its, so the verb is singular: the band has opened its new hall.

Corrected: "Everyone in our street is proud because several of the boys have won prizes and the band has opened its new hall."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the subject of each verb. Ignore the words after of.
Step 2: If the subject is everyone, somebody, nobody, each, either or neither, use a singular verb (is, was, has, likes).
Step 3: If the subject is both, few, many or several, use a plural verb (are, were, have, like).
Step 4: If the subject is a collective noun, ask: does the group act as one unit? If yes, use a singular verb and its.
Step 5: Check that the verb and any its or their that follows agree with each other.
Step 6: Read the sentence again and check every subject and verb.

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. A plural verb after a singular indefinite pronoun: "Somebody have taken my ruler." Write: Somebody has taken my ruler.
2. A singular verb after a plural indefinite pronoun: "Few of the pupils knows the answer." Write: Few of the pupils know the answer.
3. A plural verb for a group acting as one: "The crowd are moving towards its seats." Write: The crowd is moving towards its seats.

title: Utiliser l'accord sujet-verbe avec les pronoms indéfinis, les sujets singuliers et pluriels et les noms collectifs
body:
Un sujet singulier prend un verbe au singulier ; un sujet pluriel prend un verbe au pluriel.
  The girl sings. The girls sing.

1. Certains pronoms indéfinis sont toujours au singulier :
  everyone, everybody, everything, someone, somebody, anyone, nobody, nothing, each, either, neither
  Everybody likes rice. Each of the drums is new. Nobody was late.
  Même si un nom pluriel suit (each of the drums), le verbe s'accorde avec each.

2. Certains pronoms indéfinis sont toujours au pluriel :
  both, few, many, several, others
  Both are ready. Many of the mangoes are ripe. Few were absent.

3. Un nom collectif désigne un groupe : team, class, family, choir, committee, crowd, herd.
  Quand le groupe agit comme un tout, on utilise un verbe au singulier et its :
    The committee meets on Mondays. The herd has left its kraal.
  Quand les membres agissent séparément, on utilise un verbe au pluriel et their :
    The family were arguing about their plans.
  Ne les mélange pas : un verbe au singulier va avec its ; un verbe au pluriel va avec their.

Attention : en français on dit "tout le monde est là" au singulier ; en anglais aussi : "everyone is here", et non "everyone are here".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Kwabena écrit : "Everyone in our street are proud because several of the boys has won prizes and the band have opened its new hall."

1. Everyone est au singulier : Everyone in our street is proud.
2. Several est au pluriel : several of the boys have won prizes.
3. La fanfare agit comme un tout et la phrase utilise its, le verbe est donc au singulier : the band has opened its new hall.

Phrase corrigée : "Everyone in our street is proud because several of the boys have won prizes and the band has opened its new hall."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Trouve le sujet de chaque verbe. Ne tiens pas compte des mots placés après of.
Étape 2 : Si le sujet est everyone, somebody, nobody, each, either ou neither, utilise un verbe au singulier (is, was, has, likes).
Étape 3 : Si le sujet est both, few, many ou several, utilise un verbe au pluriel (are, were, have, like).
Étape 4 : Si le sujet est un nom collectif, demande-toi : le groupe agit-il comme un tout ? Si oui, utilise un verbe au singulier et its.
Étape 5 : Vérifie que le verbe et le its ou le their qui suit s'accordent.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase et vérifie chaque sujet et chaque verbe.

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Un verbe au pluriel après un pronom indéfini singulier : "Somebody have taken my ruler." Écris : Somebody has taken my ruler.
2. Un verbe au singulier après un pronom indéfini pluriel : "Few of the pupils knows the answer." Écris : Few of the pupils know the answer.
3. Un verbe au pluriel pour un groupe qui agit comme un tout : "The crowd are moving towards its seats." Écris : The crowd is moving towards its seats.

title: Use Irregular Verb Forms and the Infinitive to Talk About Personal Activities
body:
When we talk about our own activities, we often use two verb forms together.

1. The to-infinitive is to + the base verb: to read, to swim, to visit.
  It follows verbs such as want, hope, plan, decide, learn, try, need, agree, promise, forget:
    I want to learn the drums. We decided to walk.
  It also follows ask, tell, help-type patterns with a person in between:
    I asked my friend to read the story. Father told us to wait.
  Do not leave out to, and do not use -ing here: (not: I want learn, not: we decided walking)

2. After to, the verb is ALWAYS the base form, even in a past sentence:
  Yesterday I tried to fix my kite. (not: tried to fixed)
  The past is shown by the first verb (tried), not by the infinitive.

3. Irregular verbs have their own past forms. Some look alike, so check the meaning:
  buy, bought (paid for) / bring, brought (carried here)
  think, thought (had an idea) / teach, taught (gave a lesson)
  fall, fell (went down) / feel, felt (sensed)
  send, sent (posted) / spend, spent (used time or money)

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Akosua writes: "On Saturday I brought a new pen at the market, and I hoped writing neatly, so I asked my sister to helped me."

1. The pen was paid for, so the past of buy is needed: I bought a new pen.
2. Hope is followed by to + base verb: I hoped to write neatly.
3. After to, the verb stays in the base form: to help me.

Corrected: "On Saturday I bought a new pen at the market, and I hoped to write neatly, so I asked my sister to help me."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find each verb such as want, plan, decide, ask or tell that leads to a second action.
Step 2: Check that the second action has to in front of it.
Step 3: Check that the verb after to is the base form, with no -ed, -s or past spelling.
Step 4: Find each irregular past verb and ask what it means: paid for or carried? had an idea or gave a lesson?
Step 5: Choose the past form that matches the meaning.
Step 6: Read the sentence again and check every verb.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. To left out or -ing used: "I need finish my homework." Write: I need to finish my homework.
2. A past form after to: "She agreed to came early." Write: She agreed to come early.
3. A look-alike irregular past: "Our coach thought us a new game." Write: Our coach taught us a new game.

title: Utiliser les formes irrégulières des verbes et l'infinitif pour parler de ses activités personnelles
body:
Quand nous parlons de nos propres activités, nous utilisons souvent deux formes verbales ensemble.

1. L'infinitif avec to est formé de to + la base verbale : to read, to swim, to visit.
  Il suit des verbes comme want, hope, plan, decide, learn, try, need, agree, promise, forget :
    I want to learn the drums. We decided to walk.
  Il suit aussi ask, tell et des verbes semblables, avec une personne au milieu :
    I asked my friend to read the story. Father told us to wait.
  N'oublie pas to et n'utilise pas la forme en -ing ici : (et non : I want learn, ni : we decided walking)

2. Après to, le verbe est TOUJOURS à la base verbale, même dans une phrase au passé :
  Yesterday I tried to fix my kite. (et non : tried to fixed)
  Le passé est indiqué par le premier verbe (tried), et non par l'infinitif.

3. Les verbes irréguliers ont leurs propres formes du passé. Certaines se ressemblent, vérifie donc le sens :
  buy, bought (payer) / bring, brought (apporter)
  think, thought (penser) / teach, taught (enseigner)
  fall, fell (tomber) / feel, felt (ressentir)
  send, sent (envoyer) / spend, spent (passer du temps, dépenser)

Attention : en français on dit "j'ai décidé de marcher" ; en anglais on dit "I decided to walk", et non "I decided walking".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Akosua écrit : "On Saturday I brought a new pen at the market, and I hoped writing neatly, so I asked my sister to helped me."

1. Le stylo a été payé, il faut donc le passé de buy : I bought a new pen.
2. Hope est suivi de to + la base verbale : I hoped to write neatly.
3. Après to, le verbe reste à la base verbale : to help me.

Phrase corrigée : "On Saturday I bought a new pen at the market, and I hoped to write neatly, so I asked my sister to help me."

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère chaque verbe comme want, plan, decide, ask ou tell qui mène à une deuxième action.
Étape 2 : Vérifie que la deuxième action est précédée de to.
Étape 3 : Vérifie que le verbe placé après to est à la base verbale, sans -ed, sans -s et sans forme du passé.
Étape 4 : Repère chaque verbe irrégulier au passé et demande-toi ce qu'il signifie : payé ou apporté ? pensé ou enseigné ?
Étape 5 : Choisis la forme du passé qui correspond au sens.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase et vérifie chaque verbe.

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. To oublié ou forme en -ing : "I need finish my homework." Écris : I need to finish my homework.
2. Une forme du passé après to : "She agreed to came early." Écris : She agreed to come early.
3. Un passé irrégulier qui ressemble à un autre : "Our coach thought us a new game." Écris : Our coach taught us a new game.

title: Use the Simple Present for Scheduled Future Actions and Future Possibilities or Plans
body:
The simple present can talk about the future in three ways.

1. Timetables and fixed schedules:
  The train leaves at seven tomorrow. The shop opens at eight on Monday.

2. After if, for something that may happen:
  If he doesn't come early, we shall go without him.
  If the price drops, Mother will buy a fridge.
  Use the present (comes, drops), not will come and not a past form (came, dropped).

3. After when, before, after, until and as soon as, for a plan:
  I will phone you when I reach Accra.
  We will wait until the music ends.
  Use the present (reach, ends), not will reach or will end.

The other part of the sentence can use will, shall, may or can.
Only the if-part or the time-part stays in the simple present.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Kwesi writes: "If my cousin arrived tomorrow, we will cook fufu as soon as she will come in."

1. Tomorrow is a future possibility after if, so we use the present: If my cousin arrives tomorrow.
2. After as soon as, we use the present for the plan: as soon as she comes in.
3. The main part keeps will: we will cook fufu.

Corrected: "If my cousin arrives tomorrow, we will cook fufu as soon as she comes in."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Check that the sentence is about the future (tomorrow, next week, on Friday).
Step 2: Find the part that begins with if, when, before, after, until or as soon as.
Step 3: In that part, remove will and write the simple present (arrives, finish, stops).
Step 4: In that part, do not use a past form for a future possibility.
Step 5: For a timetable (bus, train, school, film), you can use the simple present on its own: The film starts at six tomorrow.
Step 6: Read the sentence again and check both parts.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Will after if: "If you will practise, you will improve." Write: If you practise, you will improve.
2. Will after a time word: "Call me when you will be ready." Write: Call me when you are ready.
3. A past form after if for the future: "If the price fell next week, I will buy it." Write: If the price falls next week, I will buy it.

title: Utiliser le présent simple pour des actions futures programmées et des possibilités ou projets futurs
body:
Le présent simple peut exprimer le futur de trois façons.

1. Les horaires et les programmes fixes :
  The train leaves at seven tomorrow. The shop opens at eight on Monday.

2. Après if, pour une chose qui peut arriver :
  If he doesn't come early, we shall go without him.
  If the price drops, Mother will buy a fridge.
  On utilise le présent (comes, drops), et non will come ni une forme du passé (came, dropped).

3. Après when, before, after, until et as soon as, pour un projet :
  I will phone you when I reach Accra.
  We will wait until the music ends.
  On utilise le présent (reach, ends), et non will reach ni will end.

L'autre partie de la phrase peut utiliser will, shall, may ou can.
Seule la partie avec if ou avec le mot de temps reste au présent simple.

Attention : en français on dit "quand j'arriverai" au futur ; en anglais on dit "when I arrive", et non "when I will arrive".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Kwesi écrit : "If my cousin arrived tomorrow, we will cook fufu as soon as she will come in."

1. Tomorrow est une possibilité future après if, on utilise donc le présent : If my cousin arrives tomorrow.
2. Après as soon as, on utilise le présent pour le projet : as soon as she comes in.
3. La partie principale garde will : we will cook fufu.

Phrase corrigée : "If my cousin arrives tomorrow, we will cook fufu as soon as she comes in."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Vérifie que la phrase parle du futur (tomorrow, next week, on Friday).
Étape 2 : Repère la partie qui commence par if, when, before, after, until ou as soon as.
Étape 3 : Dans cette partie, supprime will et écris le présent simple (arrives, finish, stops).
Étape 4 : Dans cette partie, n'utilise pas de forme du passé pour une possibilité future.
Étape 5 : Pour un horaire (bus, train, école, film), tu peux utiliser le présent simple seul : The film starts at six tomorrow.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase et vérifie les deux parties.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Will après if : "If you will practise, you will improve." Écris : If you practise, you will improve.
2. Will après un mot de temps : "Call me when you will be ready." Écris : Call me when you are ready.
3. Une forme du passé après if pour le futur : "If the price fell next week, I will buy it." Écris : If the price falls next week, I will buy it.

title: Use the Past Continuous for an Action Going On When a Second One Took Place
body:
The past continuous shows an action that was going on in the past.
A second, short action in the simple past interrupts it.
  We were playing football when the fire broke out.

1. Was or were:
  I was, he was, she was, it was (and one person or thing: Ama was, the dog was)
  we were, you were, they were (and more than one: the boys were)

2. Spelling of the -ing form:
  Most verbs: add -ing: read, reading; play, playing.
  Short verbs with one vowel + one consonant: double the consonant: shop, shopping; plan, planning.
  Verbs ending in e: drop the e: ride, riding; smile, smiling.
  Verbs ending in ie: change ie to y: die, dying.

3. When and while:
  while goes with the long action that was going on:
    While Dad was shaving, the phone rang.
  when usually goes with the short action that interrupted it:
    Dad was shaving when the phone rang.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Kweku writes: "While the visitors knocked, my sisters was cleaning and I was dusting and moping the floor."

1. Sisters is plural, so we need were: my sisters were cleaning.
2. Mop has one vowel and one consonant, so we double the p: mopping.
3. While goes with the long actions, not with the short knock: While my sisters were cleaning..., the visitors knocked.

Corrected: "While my sisters were cleaning and I was dusting and mopping the floor, the visitors knocked."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the long action that was going on and the short action that happened suddenly.
Step 2: Put the long action in the past continuous: was or were + verb-ing.
Step 3: Choose was for I, he, she, it or one person; choose were for we, you, they or more than one.
Step 4: Check the -ing spelling: double, drop e, or change ie to y when needed.
Step 5: Put while before the long action, and the short action in the simple past.
Step 6: Read the sentence again and check both actions.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Was or were with the wrong subject: "They was clapping when the lights failed." Write: They were clapping when the lights failed.
2. A misspelled -ing form: "She was hopeing for a prize." Write: She was hoping for a prize.
3. While with the sudden action: "While the bell rang, we were singing." Write: While we were singing, the bell rang.

title: Utiliser le passé progressif pour une action en cours quand une deuxième action s'est produite
body:
Le passé progressif montre une action qui était en cours dans le passé.
Une deuxième action, courte, au prétérit, l'interrompt.
  We were playing football when the fire broke out.

1. Was ou were :
  I was, he was, she was, it was (et une seule personne ou chose : Ama was, the dog was)
  we were, you were, they were (et plusieurs : the boys were)

2. Orthographe de la forme en -ing :
  La plupart des verbes : on ajoute -ing : read, reading ; play, playing.
  Verbes courts avec une voyelle + une consonne : on double la consonne : shop, shopping ; plan, planning.
  Verbes terminés par e : on supprime le e : ride, riding ; smile, smiling.
  Verbes terminés par ie : ie devient y : die, dying.

3. When et while :
  while accompagne l'action longue qui était en cours :
    While Dad was shaving, the phone rang.
  when accompagne en général l'action courte qui l'a interrompue :
    Dad was shaving when the phone rang.

Attention : en français on dit "je mangeais quand il est arrivé" à l'imparfait ; en anglais on dit "I was eating when he arrived".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Kweku écrit : "While the visitors knocked, my sisters was cleaning and I was dusting and moping the floor."

1. Sisters est au pluriel, il faut donc were : my sisters were cleaning.
2. Mop a une voyelle et une consonne, on double donc le p : mopping.
3. While accompagne les actions longues, et non le coup bref frappé à la porte : While my sisters were cleaning..., the visitors knocked.

Phrase corrigée : "While my sisters were cleaning and I was dusting and mopping the floor, the visitors knocked."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère l'action longue qui était en cours et l'action courte qui s'est produite soudainement.
Étape 2 : Mets l'action longue au passé progressif : was ou were + verbe en -ing.
Étape 3 : Choisis was pour I, he, she, it ou une seule personne ; choisis were pour we, you, they ou plusieurs.
Étape 4 : Vérifie l'orthographe en -ing : double la consonne, supprime le e ou change ie en y si nécessaire.
Étape 5 : Place while devant l'action longue, et mets l'action courte au prétérit.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase et vérifie les deux actions.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Was ou were avec le mauvais sujet : "They was clapping when the lights failed." Écris : They were clapping when the lights failed.
2. Une forme en -ing mal écrite : "She was hopeing for a prize." Écris : She was hoping for a prize.
3. While avec l'action soudaine : "While the bell rang, we were singing." Écris : While we were singing, the bell rang.

title: Use the Imperative to Give Warnings and Express Prohibitions
body:
The imperative uses the base verb with no subject. We can use it to warn and to forbid.

1. A prohibition says what must not be done. Use Do not or Don't + base verb, or Never + base verb:
  Do not climb the wall. Don't shout in the ward. Never play with fire.
  Notices may use No + -ing: No smoking. No parking.
  Do not write "Not climb" or "No climb".

2. A warning shows what will happen. There are two patterns:
  Imperative + and + result: if you DO it, the result follows.
    Break the glass, and you will pay for it.
  Imperative + or + result: if you do NOT obey, the result follows.
    Hurry, or you will be late. Don't lean out, or you may fall.
  After Don't ..., the warning almost always needs or.

3. One negative is enough. After Don't or Never, use any, anything, anyone, anywhere:
  Don't tell anyone. Never leave anything here.
  Do not write "Don't tell no one" or "Never leave nothing".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Mansa writes on a sign: "Not feed no animals at the zoo, and they may bite you."

1. A prohibition needs Do not: Do not feed.
2. One negative is enough, so no becomes any: any animals.
3. The bite happens if you disobey, so we use or: or they may bite you.

Corrected: "Do not feed any animals at the zoo, or they may bite you."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Decide whether you are forbidding something or warning about a result.
Step 2: For a prohibition, start with Do not, Don't or Never + the base verb.
Step 3: After Don't or Never, change no, nothing, nobody, no one or nowhere to any, anything, anybody, anyone or anywhere.
Step 4: Ask: does the result happen if the person obeys or if the person disobeys?
Step 5: If the result comes from disobeying, join it with or. If it comes from doing the action, join it with and.
Step 6: Read the warning aloud and check that it makes sense.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. No Do not: "No shout in the library." Write: Do not shout in the library.
2. And instead of or: "Don't be late, and you will miss the bus." Write: Don't be late, or you will miss the bus.
3. Two negatives: "Don't say nothing to the stranger." Write: Don't say anything to the stranger.
