title: Utiliser l'impératif pour donner des avertissements et exprimer des interdictions
body:
L'impératif utilise la base verbale sans sujet. On peut l'employer pour avertir et pour interdire.

1. Une interdiction dit ce qu'il ne faut pas faire. On utilise Do not ou Don't + base verbale, ou Never + base verbale :
  Do not climb the wall. Don't shout in the ward. Never play with fire.
  Les panneaux peuvent utiliser No + -ing : No smoking. No parking.
  N'écris pas "Not climb" ni "No climb".

2. Un avertissement montre ce qui va arriver. Il existe deux modèles :
  Impératif + and + résultat : si tu LE fais, le résultat suit.
    Break the glass, and you will pay for it.
  Impératif + or + résultat : si tu N'obéis PAS, le résultat suit.
    Hurry, or you will be late. Don't lean out, or you may fall.
  Après Don't ..., l'avertissement demande presque toujours or.

3. Une seule négation suffit. Après Don't ou Never, on utilise any, anything, anyone, anywhere :
  Don't tell anyone. Never leave anything here.
  N'écris pas "Don't tell no one" ni "Never leave nothing".

Attention : en français on dit "ne dis rien à personne" avec deux mots négatifs ; en anglais on dit "don't tell anyone anything", avec une seule négation.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Mansa écrit sur un panneau : "Not feed no animals at the zoo, and they may bite you."

1. Une interdiction demande Do not : Do not feed.
2. Une seule négation suffit, no devient donc any : any animals.
3. La morsure arrive si on désobéit, on utilise donc or : or they may bite you.

Phrase corrigée : "Do not feed any animals at the zoo, or they may bite you."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Décide si tu interdis quelque chose ou si tu avertis d'un résultat.
Étape 2 : Pour une interdiction, commence par Do not, Don't ou Never + la base verbale.
Étape 3 : Après Don't ou Never, remplace no, nothing, nobody, no one ou nowhere par any, anything, anybody, anyone ou anywhere.
Étape 4 : Demande-toi : le résultat arrive-t-il si la personne obéit ou si elle désobéit ?
Étape 5 : Si le résultat vient de la désobéissance, relie-le avec or. S'il vient du fait de faire l'action, relie-le avec and.
Étape 6 : Lis l'avertissement à voix haute et vérifie qu'il a du sens.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Do not oublié : "No shout in the library." Écris : Do not shout in the library.
2. And au lieu de or : "Don't be late, and you will miss the bus." Écris : Don't be late, or you will miss the bus.
3. Deux négations : "Don't say nothing to the stranger." Écris : Don't say anything to the stranger.

title: Use Adverbs to Express Degree and Reason
body:
Adverbs of degree tell how much or how strongly. Adverbs and phrases of reason tell why.

1. Very and too both make a word stronger, but they do not mean the same.
  Very means a lot. It can be good news: The mangoes are very sweet.
  Too means more than is wanted, so there is a problem: The tea is too hot to drink.
  Too often comes with to + verb or for + someone: too heavy to lift, too small for me.
  Do not write "The party was too nice" when you mean it was very nice.

2. Enough means as much as is needed. It comes AFTER an adjective or adverb:
  tall enough, warm enough, fast enough.
  Do not write "enough tall" or "enough fast".
  (Before a noun, enough comes first: enough chairs, enough water.)

3. Because and because of both give a reason.
  Because + a clause (subject + verb): We stayed inside because it was raining.
  Because of + a noun or noun phrase: We stayed inside because of the rain.
  Do not write "because the rain" or "because of it was raining".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Yaw writes: "I could not wear my brother's shoes because of they were too long. The laces were not enough strong either, but the colour was too lovely."

1. "They were too long" is a clause, so we use because, not because of: because they were too long.
2. Enough comes after the adjective: strong enough.
3. A lovely colour is good news, not a problem, so we use very: very lovely.

Corrected: "I could not wear my brother's shoes because they were too long. The laces were not strong enough either, but the colour was very lovely."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the word that shows degree (very, too, enough) and the words that give a reason.
Step 2: Ask: is the strong quality good news, or does it cause a problem? Use very for good news and too for a problem.
Step 3: If you used too, check that the problem is clear, for example with to + verb or for + someone.
Step 4: Check that enough comes after the adjective or adverb.
Step 5: Look at what follows the reason word. A subject and verb need because. A noun or noun phrase needs because of.
Step 6: Read the sentence aloud and check that it makes sense.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Too for good news: "The music was too nice, so we danced." Write: The music was very nice, so we danced.
2. Enough in front: "Is the rope enough long?" Write: Is the rope long enough?
3. Because before a noun: "The match stopped because the thunder." Write: The match stopped because of the thunder.

title: Utiliser les adverbes pour exprimer le degré et la raison
body:
Les adverbes de degré indiquent combien ou à quel point. Les adverbes et expressions de raison indiquent pourquoi.

1. Very et too renforcent tous les deux un mot, mais ils n'ont pas le même sens.
  Very veut dire beaucoup. Cela peut être une bonne nouvelle : The mangoes are very sweet.
  Too veut dire plus que ce qu'on souhaite, il y a donc un problème : The tea is too hot to drink.
  Too s'emploie souvent avec to + verbe ou for + quelqu'un : too heavy to lift, too small for me.
  N'écris pas "The party was too nice" si tu veux dire que la fête était très bien.

2. Enough veut dire autant qu'il le faut. Il se place APRÈS un adjectif ou un adverbe :
  tall enough, warm enough, fast enough.
  N'écris pas "enough tall" ni "enough fast".
  (Devant un nom, enough se place avant : enough chairs, enough water.)

3. Because et because of donnent tous les deux une raison.
  Because + une proposition (sujet + verbe) : We stayed inside because it was raining.
  Because of + un nom ou un groupe nominal : We stayed inside because of the rain.
  N'écris pas "because the rain" ni "because of it was raining".

Attention : very correspond à « très » et too à « trop ». Enough se place après l'adjectif, alors que « assez » se place avant : « assez grand » se dit tall enough. Because correspond à « parce que » et because of à « à cause de ».

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Yaw écrit : "I could not wear my brother's shoes because of they were too long. The laces were not enough strong either, but the colour was too lovely."

1. "They were too long" est une proposition, on utilise donc because et non because of : because they were too long.
2. Enough se place après l'adjectif : strong enough.
3. Une jolie couleur est une bonne nouvelle, pas un problème, on utilise donc very : very lovely.

Phrase corrigée : "I could not wear my brother's shoes because they were too long. The laces were not strong enough either, but the colour was very lovely."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère le mot qui montre le degré (very, too, enough) et les mots qui donnent une raison.
Étape 2 : Demande-toi : la qualité forte est-elle une bonne nouvelle ou cause-t-elle un problème ? Utilise very pour une bonne nouvelle et too pour un problème.
Étape 3 : Si tu as utilisé too, vérifie que le problème est clair, par exemple avec to + verbe ou for + quelqu'un.
Étape 4 : Vérifie que enough se place après l'adjectif ou l'adverbe.
Étape 5 : Regarde ce qui suit le mot de raison. Un sujet et un verbe demandent because. Un nom ou un groupe nominal demande because of.
Étape 6 : Lis la phrase à voix haute et vérifie qu'elle a du sens.

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Too pour une bonne nouvelle : "The music was too nice, so we danced." Écris : The music was very nice, so we danced.
2. Enough placé devant : "Is the rope enough long?" Écris : Is the rope long enough?
3. Because devant un nom : "The match stopped because the thunder." Écris : The match stopped because of the thunder.

title: Identify, Explain and Use Idiomatic Expressions
body:
An idiom is a group of words with a special meaning that the single words do not show. Every idiom has fixed words and its own meaning.

1. Idioms that share a word can mean very different things. Learn each one on its own.
  look up to someone: respect and admire them
  look down on someone: think they are less important than you
  make up: become friends again after a quarrel
  make up for something: do something good to repair a wrong

2. The small words in an idiom are fixed too. Do not add, drop or change a, an or the, and do not change singular to plural.
  in hot water (in trouble), not "in a hot water"
  all ears (listening carefully), not "all ear"
  by heart (from memory), not "by the heart"

3. Do not mix two idioms into one, even when they mean nearly the same.
  I know this road like the back of my hand. I learnt the poem by heart.
  Do not write "I know this road by the back of my hand".

Use the situation to decide which idiom fits, and check its exact words in a dictionary.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Afia writes: "I look down on my aunt, who is a nurse, and I want to be like her. When she tells stories, I am all ear, and I feel on top of the moon."

1. Afia admires her aunt, so the idiom is look up to, not look down on.
2. The idiom is all ears, with a plural: I am all ears.
3. "On top of the moon" mixes on top of the world and over the moon. Choose one: on top of the world.

Corrected: "I look up to my aunt, who is a nurse, and I want to be like her. When she tells stories, I am all ears, and I feel on top of the world."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the group of words that does not mean what the single words say.
Step 2: Read the situation and say in your own words what the speaker means.
Step 3: If another idiom shares a word with it, check that you chose the one whose meaning fits the situation.
Step 4: Check the small words: a, an, the, and singular or plural must be exactly as in the idiom.
Step 5: Check that you used one whole idiom and did not join parts of two idioms.
Step 6: Read the sentence aloud and check that it makes sense.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. A look-alike idiom: "After the fight, the two friends made up for." Write: After the fight, the two friends made up.
2. A changed small word: "Kofi learnt the song by the heart." Write: Kofi learnt the song by heart.
3. Two idioms mixed: "It is raining cats and buckets." Write: It is raining cats and dogs.

title: Identifier, expliquer et utiliser les expressions idiomatiques
body:
Une expression idiomatique est un groupe de mots qui a un sens spécial que les mots pris seuls ne montrent pas. Chaque expression a des mots fixes et un sens qui lui est propre.

1. Des expressions qui partagent un mot peuvent avoir des sens très différents. Apprends chacune séparément.
  look up to someone : respecter et admirer quelqu'un
  look down on someone : penser que quelqu'un est moins important que toi
  make up : se réconcilier après une dispute
  make up for something : faire quelque chose de bien pour réparer un tort

2. Les petits mots d'une expression sont fixes eux aussi. N'ajoute pas, n'enlève pas et ne change pas a, an ou the, et ne mets pas un singulier au pluriel.
  in hot water (avoir des ennuis), et non "in a hot water"
  all ears (écouter très attentivement), et non "all ear"
  by heart (par cœur), et non "by the heart"

3. Ne mélange pas deux expressions en une seule, même quand elles ont presque le même sens.
  I know this road like the back of my hand. I learnt the poem by heart.
  N'écris pas "I know this road by the back of my hand".

Utilise la situation pour décider quelle expression convient, et vérifie ses mots exacts dans un dictionnaire.

Attention : c'est pareil en français. On dit « il pleut des cordes » et non « il pleut une corde » : les mots d'une expression figée ne changent pas.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Afia écrit : "I look down on my aunt, who is a nurse, and I want to be like her. When she tells stories, I am all ear, and I feel on top of the moon."

1. Afia admire sa tante, l'expression est donc look up to et non look down on.
2. L'expression est all ears, au pluriel : I am all ears.
3. "On top of the moon" mélange on top of the world et over the moon. Choisis-en une : on top of the world.

Phrase corrigée : "I look up to my aunt, who is a nurse, and I want to be like her. When she tells stories, I am all ears, and I feel on top of the world."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère le groupe de mots qui ne veut pas dire ce que disent les mots pris seuls.
Étape 2 : Lis la situation et dis avec tes propres mots ce que la personne veut dire.
Étape 3 : Si une autre expression partage un mot avec elle, vérifie que tu as choisi celle dont le sens convient à la situation.
Étape 4 : Vérifie les petits mots : a, an, the, et le singulier ou le pluriel doivent être exactement comme dans l'expression.
Étape 5 : Vérifie que tu as utilisé une seule expression entière et que tu n'as pas réuni des morceaux de deux expressions.
Étape 6 : Lis la phrase à voix haute et vérifie qu'elle a du sens.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Une expression qui se ressemble : "After the fight, the two friends made up for." Écris : After the fight, the two friends made up.
2. Un petit mot changé : "Kofi learnt the song by the heart." Écris : Kofi learnt the song by heart.
3. Deux expressions mélangées : "It is raining cats and buckets." Écris : It is raining cats and dogs.

title: Use So That, When, While and If
body:
Conjunctions join two parts of a sentence. Some of them show purpose, time or condition.

1. Purpose: so that tells the aim of an action.
  After so that, write a full clause: subject + verb (often with can, could, will or would).
  Water the seedlings so that they can grow. She spoke loudly so that everyone could hear.
  Do not write "so that to grow". If you want to use to + verb, drop so that: Water them to help them grow.

2. Time or condition: when or if?
  Use when for something you are sure will happen: When the sun sets, we will go home.
  Use if for something that may or may not happen: If I find my lost pen, I will lend it to you.
  Do not write "If the sun sets", because the sun always sets.
  Do not write "When I find my lost pen" if you are not sure you will find it.

3. Time: while shows two actions happening at the same time. While is followed by a clause (subject + verb).
  While Grandpa was resting, we played quietly.
  During is followed by a noun only: during the break, during the night.
  Do not write "During Grandpa was resting".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Kwabena writes: "During Mum was at work, I tidied the room so that to surprise her. If Mum comes home this evening, she will be happy."

1. "Mum was at work" has a subject and a verb, so we use while, not during: While Mum was at work.
2. So that needs a subject and verb: so that she would have a nice surprise.
3. Mum comes home every evening, so it is certain. We use when: When Mum comes home this evening.

Corrected: "While Mum was at work, I tidied the room so that she would have a nice surprise. When Mum comes home this evening, she will be happy."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the conjunctions in the sentence and decide what each one shows: purpose, time or condition.
Step 2: After so that, check that there is a subject and a verb, not to + verb.
Step 3: For when or if, ask: is this event sure to happen? If yes, use when. If it may not happen, use if.
Step 4: For two actions at the same time, look at what follows. A subject and verb need while. A noun alone needs during.
Step 5: Read the sentence aloud and check that it makes sense.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. To after so that: "Close the window so that to keep the dust out." Write: Close the window so that the dust stays out.
2. If for a certain event: "If the school year ends, we will have a party." Write: When the school year ends, we will have a party.
3. During before a clause: "During the teacher was talking, Kojo fell asleep." Write: While the teacher was talking, Kojo fell asleep.

title: Utiliser So That, When, While et If
body:
Les conjonctions relient deux parties d'une phrase. Certaines montrent le but, le temps ou la condition.

1. Le but : so that indique le but d'une action.
  Après so that, on écrit une proposition complète : sujet + verbe (souvent avec can, could, will ou would).
  Water the seedlings so that they can grow. She spoke loudly so that everyone could hear.
  N'écris pas "so that to grow". Si tu veux utiliser to + verbe, enlève so that : Water them to help them grow.

2. Le temps ou la condition : when ou if ?
  Utilise when pour quelque chose dont tu es sûr qu'il va arriver : When the sun sets, we will go home.
  Utilise if pour quelque chose qui peut arriver ou ne pas arriver : If I find my lost pen, I will lend it to you.
  N'écris pas "If the sun sets", car le soleil se couche toujours.
  N'écris pas "When I find my lost pen" si tu n'es pas sûr de le retrouver.

3. Le temps : while montre deux actions qui se passent en même temps. While est suivi d'une proposition (sujet + verbe).
  While Grandpa was resting, we played quietly.
  During est suivi seulement d'un nom : during the break, during the night.
  N'écris pas "During Grandpa was resting".

Attention : so that correspond à « pour que » + proposition, et to + verbe à « pour » + verbe. Le français « pendant » sert dans les deux cas, mais en anglais on dit during devant un nom (« pendant la nuit ») et while devant une proposition (« pendant que grand-père dormait »).

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Kwabena écrit : "During Mum was at work, I tidied the room so that to surprise her. If Mum comes home this evening, she will be happy."

1. "Mum was at work" a un sujet et un verbe, on utilise donc while et non during : While Mum was at work.
2. So that demande un sujet et un verbe : so that she would have a nice surprise.
3. Maman rentre tous les soirs, c'est donc certain. On utilise when : When Mum comes home this evening.

Phrase corrigée : "While Mum was at work, I tidied the room so that she would have a nice surprise. When Mum comes home this evening, she will be happy."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère les conjonctions de la phrase et décide ce que chacune montre : le but, le temps ou la condition.
Étape 2 : Après so that, vérifie qu'il y a un sujet et un verbe, et non to + verbe.
Étape 3 : Pour when ou if, demande-toi : cet événement va-t-il sûrement arriver ? Si oui, utilise when. S'il peut ne pas arriver, utilise if.
Étape 4 : Pour deux actions en même temps, regarde ce qui suit. Un sujet et un verbe demandent while. Un nom seul demande during.
Étape 5 : Lis la phrase à voix haute et vérifie qu'elle a du sens.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. To après so that : "Close the window so that to keep the dust out." Écris : Close the window so that the dust stays out.
2. If pour un événement certain : "If the school year ends, we will have a party." Écris : When the school year ends, we will have a party.
3. During devant une proposition : "During the teacher was talking, Kojo fell asleep." Écris : While the teacher was talking, Kojo fell asleep.

title: Use Modals to Express a Variety of Meanings
body:
Modals add meaning to a verb. They can show ability, permission, possibility, obligation, advice or politeness.
  can: ability now          could: ability in the past, or a polite request
  may: permission, possibility          might: possibility
  must / have to / need to: obligation          should / ought to: advice
  will / shall: prediction, intention          would: politeness
  used to: a past habit

1. Mustn't and don't have to are NOT the same.
  mustn't = it is forbidden: You mustn't cross the road when the light is red.
  don't have to = it is not necessary, you may choose: It is Saturday, so you don't have to wear your uniform.

2. Used to is only for the past: something that happened again and again but has stopped.
  I used to cry at night when I was a baby.
  For a habit now, use the present simple, often with usually: I usually help my mother on Saturdays.
  Do not write "I use to help my mother now".

3. Can is for ability now. For ability in the past, use could.
  Now I can ride a bicycle. When I was four, I could already count to fifty.
  Do not write "When I was four, I can count to fifty".

4. For polite requests, could and would sound kinder than can and will:
  Could you pass the salt, please? Would you open the door for me?

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Esi writes: "When I was in Class 2, I can't read long books. Now I use to read one book every week. My teacher says we don't have to write in library books, because it spoils them."

1. Class 2 is in the past, so the ability needs could: I couldn't read long books.
2. Reading one book a week is a habit now, so we use the present simple: Now I usually read one book every week.
3. Writing in library books spoils them, so it is forbidden. We use mustn't: we mustn't write in library books.

Corrected: "When I was in Class 2, I couldn't read long books. Now I usually read one book every week. My teacher says we mustn't write in library books, because it spoils them."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find each modal and ask what meaning it should show: ability, permission, possibility, obligation, advice or politeness.
Step 2: For a rule, ask: is the action forbidden, or simply not necessary? Forbidden needs mustn't. Not necessary needs don't have to.
Step 3: For a habit, ask: has it stopped? If yes, use used to. If it still happens, use the present simple, often with usually.
Step 4: For ability, ask: now or in the past? Use can for now and could for the past.
Step 5: Read the sentence aloud and check that the meaning fits the situation.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Don't have to for a rule: "You don't have to touch the hot iron!" Write: You mustn't touch the hot iron!
2. Use to for a habit now: "These days my brother use to cook supper." Write: These days my brother usually cooks supper.
3. Can for the past: "Last year Kofi can't swim, but now he can." Write: Last year Kofi couldn't swim, but now he can.

title: Utiliser les modaux pour exprimer des sens variés
body:
Les modaux ajoutent un sens au verbe. Ils peuvent exprimer la capacité, la permission, la possibilité, l'obligation, le conseil ou la politesse.
  can : capacité maintenant          could : capacité dans le passé, ou demande polie
  may : permission, possibilité          might : possibilité
  must / have to / need to : obligation          should / ought to : conseil
  will / shall : prédiction, intention          would : politesse
  used to : une habitude passée

1. Mustn't et don't have to ne veulent PAS dire la même chose.
  mustn't = c'est interdit : You mustn't cross the road when the light is red.
  don't have to = ce n'est pas nécessaire, on peut choisir : It is Saturday, so you don't have to wear your uniform.

2. Used to sert seulement pour le passé : une chose qui se répétait mais qui s'est arrêtée.
  I used to cry at night when I was a baby.
  Pour une habitude actuelle, on utilise le présent simple, souvent avec usually : I usually help my mother on Saturdays.
  N'écris pas "I use to help my mother now".

3. Can exprime une capacité maintenant. Pour une capacité dans le passé, on utilise could.
  Now I can ride a bicycle. When I was four, I could already count to fifty.
  N'écris pas "When I was four, I can count to fifty".

4. Pour une demande polie, could et would sont plus aimables que can et will :
  Could you pass the salt, please? Would you open the door for me?

Attention : « il ne faut pas » se dit mustn't, et « tu n'es pas obligé » se dit don't have to. Don't have to n'est donc pas une interdiction. « J'avais l'habitude de » se dit used to ; pour une habitude actuelle, on dit « d'habitude », usually.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Esi écrit : "When I was in Class 2, I can't read long books. Now I use to read one book every week. My teacher says we don't have to write in library books, because it spoils them."

1. La Class 2, c'est dans le passé, la capacité demande donc could : I couldn't read long books.
2. Lire un livre par semaine est une habitude actuelle, on utilise donc le présent simple : Now I usually read one book every week.
3. Écrire dans les livres de la bibliothèque les abîme, c'est donc interdit. On utilise mustn't : we mustn't write in library books.

Phrase corrigée : "When I was in Class 2, I couldn't read long books. Now I usually read one book every week. My teacher says we mustn't write in library books, because it spoils them."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère chaque modal et demande-toi quel sens il doit exprimer : capacité, permission, possibilité, obligation, conseil ou politesse.
Étape 2 : Pour une règle, demande-toi : l'action est-elle interdite, ou simplement pas nécessaire ? Interdite demande mustn't. Pas nécessaire demande don't have to.
Étape 3 : Pour une habitude, demande-toi : s'est-elle arrêtée ? Si oui, utilise used to. Si elle continue, utilise le présent simple, souvent avec usually.
Étape 4 : Pour une capacité, demande-toi : maintenant ou dans le passé ? Utilise can pour maintenant et could pour le passé.
Étape 5 : Lis la phrase à voix haute et vérifie que le sens convient à la situation.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Don't have to pour une règle : "You don't have to touch the hot iron!" Écris : You mustn't touch the hot iron!
2. Use to pour une habitude actuelle : "These days my brother use to cook supper." Écris : These days my brother usually cooks supper.
3. Can pour le passé : "Last year Kofi can't swim, but now he can." Écris : Last year Kofi couldn't swim, but now he can.

title: Use Prepositions to Convey a Variety of Meanings
body:
Prepositions link a noun or pronoun to the rest of the sentence. They can show time, purpose, possession, comparison, and support or opposition.

1. Time: at, on, in.
  at + a clock time or a point in the day: at 7 o'clock, at noon, at night
  on + a day or a date: on Monday, on 6th March, on Independence Day
  in + a month, year, season or part of the day: in June, in 2019, in the dry season, in the morning
  When a day is named, use on: on Monday morning.

2. Purpose: why someone does something.
  to + base verb: She went to the farm to harvest cassava.
  for + noun: She went to the farm for cassava.
  Do not write "for harvest cassava" or "for to harvest cassava".

3. Possession: what someone has.
  with shows something a person has, wears or carries: the boy with a limp, the woman with the yellow umbrella.
  of shows that something belongs to a thing or a group: the roof of the house, the captain of the team.
  Do not write "the woman of the yellow umbrella".

4. Comparison, support and opposition.
  Use than after a comparative: Kumasi is bigger than Ho.
  for shows support and against shows opposition: Ten pupils voted for the plan and two voted against it.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Kojo writes: "In Friday, the girl of the long braids came to our class for read a story."

1. Friday is a day, so we use on: On Friday.
2. The braids are something the girl has, so we use with: the girl with the long braids.
3. Read is a verb showing purpose, so we use to: to read a story.

Corrected: "On Friday, the girl with the long braids came to our class to read a story."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find each preposition and decide what it shows: time, purpose, possession, comparison, support or opposition.
Step 2: For time, look at the word after it. A clock time needs at, a day or date needs on, and a month, year, season or part of the day needs in.
Step 3: For purpose, look at what follows. A verb needs to. A noun can take for.
Step 4: For possession, ask: is it something a person has, wears or carries? Use with. Is it part of a thing or group? Use of.
Step 5: Read the sentence aloud and check that it makes sense.

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Wrong time word: "The party starts on 4 o'clock." Write: The party starts at 4 o'clock.
2. For + verb: "We saved money for buy a football." Write: We saved money to buy a football.
3. Of for what a person has: "Call the man of the big beard." Write: Call the man with the big beard.

title: Utiliser les prépositions pour exprimer des sens variés
body:
Les prépositions relient un nom ou un pronom au reste de la phrase. Elles peuvent exprimer le temps, le but, la possession, la comparaison, le soutien ou l'opposition.

1. Le temps : at, on, in.
  at + une heure ou un moment de la journée : at 7 o'clock, at noon, at night
  on + un jour ou une date : on Monday, on 6th March, on Independence Day
  in + un mois, une année, une saison ou une partie de la journée : in June, in 2019, in the dry season, in the morning
  Quand un jour est nommé, on utilise on : on Monday morning.

2. Le but : pourquoi quelqu'un fait quelque chose.
  to + base verbale : She went to the farm to harvest cassava.
  for + nom : She went to the farm for cassava.
  N'écris pas "for harvest cassava" ni "for to harvest cassava".

3. La possession : ce que quelqu'un a.
  with montre ce qu'une personne a, porte ou tient : the boy with a limp, the woman with the yellow umbrella.
  of montre qu'une chose appartient à un objet ou à un groupe : the roof of the house, the captain of the team.
  N'écris pas "the woman of the yellow umbrella".

4. La comparaison, le soutien et l'opposition.
  On utilise than après un comparatif : Kumasi is bigger than Ho.
  for montre le soutien et against l'opposition : Ten pupils voted for the plan and two voted against it.

Attention : « pour » + verbe se dit to + verbe, et non for + verbe : « Il est venu pour aider » se dit He came to help. « La femme au parapluie jaune » se dit the woman with the yellow umbrella. Pour le temps : « lundi » se dit on Monday, « en juin » in June, « à 7 heures » at 7 o'clock.

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Kojo écrit : "In Friday, the girl of the long braids came to our class for read a story."

1. Friday est un jour, on utilise donc on : On Friday.
2. Les tresses sont quelque chose que la fille a, on utilise donc with : the girl with the long braids.
3. Read est un verbe qui montre le but, on utilise donc to : to read a story.

Phrase corrigée : "On Friday, the girl with the long braids came to our class to read a story."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère chaque préposition et décide ce qu'elle exprime : le temps, le but, la possession, la comparaison, le soutien ou l'opposition.
Étape 2 : Pour le temps, regarde le mot qui suit. Une heure demande at, un jour ou une date demande on, et un mois, une année, une saison ou une partie de la journée demande in.
Étape 3 : Pour le but, regarde ce qui suit. Un verbe demande to. Un nom peut prendre for.
Étape 4 : Pour la possession, demande-toi : est-ce quelque chose qu'une personne a, porte ou tient ? Utilise with. Est-ce une partie d'un objet ou d'un groupe ? Utilise of.
Étape 5 : Lis la phrase à voix haute et vérifie qu'elle a du sens.

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Mauvais mot de temps : "The party starts on 4 o'clock." Écris : The party starts at 4 o'clock.
2. For + verbe : "We saved money for buy a football." Écris : We saved money to buy a football.
3. Of pour ce qu'une personne a : "Call the man of the big beard." Écris : Call the man with the big beard.

title: Form and Use Adjective Phrases Correctly
body:
An adjective phrase is a group of words built around an adjective, which is the head. It describes a noun.
  One adjective: a beautiful house.
  An adjective with a word before it: a very beautiful flower, an extremely hot day.
  Two or more adjectives: a strong African oven.
  An adjective with a phrase after it: full of water, afraid of snakes.

1. When two or more adjectives come before a noun, use this order:
  opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material + noun
  a lovely big old house, a small round yellow ball, a strong African clay oven.

2. English adjectives never take -s, even before or after a plural noun.
  one tall tree, three tall trees (not "talls trees")
  The mangoes are ripe (not "ripes").

3. Many adjectives are followed by a fixed preposition. Learn the adjective and its preposition together:
  afraid of, proud of, full of, fond of, good at, kind to, responsible for, different from, similar to.
  Do not write "proud on" or "fond with".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Nana writes: "Grandma keeps two black big goats. They are fond with ripe mangoes, and their kids are very playfuls."

1. Size comes before colour: two big black goats.
2. Fond is followed by of: fond of ripe mangoes.
3. Adjectives never take -s: very playful.

Corrected: "Grandma keeps two big black goats. They are fond of ripe mangoes, and their kids are very playful."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find each adjective phrase and its head adjective.
Step 2: If two or more adjectives come before a noun, put them in order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material.
Step 3: Check that no adjective ends in a plural -s, even when the noun is plural.
Step 4: If the adjective is followed by a preposition, check that it is the fixed one, for example afraid of or kind to.
Step 5: Read the sentence aloud and check that it sounds natural.

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Wrong order: "I bought a wooden beautiful box." Write: I bought a beautiful wooden box.
2. Plural -s on an adjective: "The bananas are greens." Write: The bananas are green.
3. Wrong preposition: "Esi is proud on her brother." Write: Esi is proud of her brother.

title: Former et utiliser correctement les groupes adjectivaux
body:
Un groupe adjectival est un groupe de mots construit autour d'un adjectif, qui en est le noyau. Il décrit un nom.
  Un seul adjectif : a beautiful house.
  Un adjectif précédé d'un mot : a very beautiful flower, an extremely hot day.
  Deux adjectifs ou plus : a strong African oven.
  Un adjectif suivi d'un groupe de mots : full of water, afraid of snakes.

1. Quand deux adjectifs ou plus se placent devant un nom, on suit cet ordre :
  opinion, taille, âge, forme, couleur, origine, matière + nom
  a lovely big old house, a small round yellow ball, a strong African clay oven.

2. Les adjectifs anglais ne prennent jamais de -s, même devant ou après un nom au pluriel.
  one tall tree, three tall trees (et non "talls trees")
  The mangoes are ripe (et non "ripes").

3. Beaucoup d'adjectifs sont suivis d'une préposition fixe. Apprends l'adjectif et sa préposition ensemble :
  afraid of, proud of, full of, fond of, good at, kind to, responsible for, different from, similar to.
  N'écris pas "proud on" ni "fond with".

Attention : en français, l'adjectif s'accorde (« des arbres grands »), mais en anglais l'adjectif ne prend jamais de -s. Les prépositions changent aussi : « fier de » se dit proud of, « gentil avec » se dit kind to, « responsable de » se dit responsible for, « différent de » se dit different from.

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Nana écrit : "Grandma keeps two black big goats. They are fond with ripe mangoes, and their kids are very playfuls."

1. La taille vient avant la couleur : two big black goats.
2. Fond est suivi de of : fond of ripe mangoes.
3. Les adjectifs ne prennent jamais de -s : very playful.

Phrase corrigée : "Grandma keeps two big black goats. They are fond of ripe mangoes, and their kids are very playful."

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère chaque groupe adjectival et son adjectif noyau.
Étape 2 : Si deux adjectifs ou plus se placent devant un nom, mets-les dans l'ordre : opinion, taille, âge, forme, couleur, origine, matière.
Étape 3 : Vérifie qu'aucun adjectif ne se termine par un -s du pluriel, même quand le nom est au pluriel.
Étape 4 : Si l'adjectif est suivi d'une préposition, vérifie que c'est la préposition fixe, par exemple afraid of ou kind to.
Étape 5 : Lis la phrase à voix haute et vérifie qu'elle sonne naturellement.

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Mauvais ordre : "I bought a wooden beautiful box." Écris : I bought a beautiful wooden box.
2. -s du pluriel sur un adjectif : "The bananas are greens." Écris : The bananas are green.
3. Mauvaise préposition : "Esi is proud on her brother." Écris : Esi is proud of her brother.

title: Form and Use Adverb Phrases Correctly
body:
An adverb phrase is a word or group of words that does the work of an adverb. It modifies a verb and tells how, where, when or how often an action happens.
  how: very carefully, with great care
  where: at the market, under the table
  when: last night, next week, this morning
  how often: every day, twice a week
  He comes to the house every day.

1. Every day (two words) is an adverb phrase. It tells how often.
  Everyday (one word) is an adjective meaning ordinary. It comes before a noun: my everyday clothes.
  I brush my teeth every day. Do not write "I brush my teeth everyday".

2. Do not put an adverb phrase between a verb and its object. Keep the verb and its object together, then add the phrase.
  She speaks English very well. (not "She speaks very well English")
  We read the newspaper every evening. (not "We read every evening the newspaper")

3. With last, next, this and every, do not add in, on or at.
  last week, next Monday, this morning, every Friday
  Do not write "on next Monday" or "in last week".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Adwoa writes: "Everyday my father drinks slowly his tea, and on last Sunday he drank three cups."

1. The phrase tells how often, so it is two words: Every day.
2. Drinks and his tea belong together, so the adverb comes after the object: drinks his tea slowly.
3. Last Sunday needs no preposition: last Sunday.

Corrected: "Every day my father drinks his tea slowly, and last Sunday he drank three cups."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the verb and ask how, where, when or how often the action happens. The words that answer are the adverb phrase.
Step 2: If the phrase tells how often, check that every day is written as two words.
Step 3: If the verb has an object, keep the verb and the object together and put the adverb phrase after them.
Step 4: If the phrase begins with last, next, this or every, check that there is no in, on or at in front of it.
Step 5: Read the sentence aloud and check that it sounds natural.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. One word for how often: "We pray everyday." Write: We pray every day.
2. Phrase between verb and object: "Kofi kicked hard the ball." Write: Kofi kicked the ball hard.
3. Extra preposition: "The exam starts on next Tuesday." Write: The exam starts next Tuesday.

title: Former et utiliser correctement les groupes adverbiaux
body:
Un groupe adverbial est un mot ou un groupe de mots qui joue le rôle d'un adverbe. Il modifie un verbe et indique comment, où, quand ou à quelle fréquence une action se passe.
  comment : very carefully, with great care
  où : at the market, under the table
  quand : last night, next week, this morning
  à quelle fréquence : every day, twice a week
  He comes to the house every day.

1. Every day (deux mots) est un groupe adverbial. Il indique la fréquence.
  Everyday (un seul mot) est un adjectif qui veut dire ordinaire. Il se place devant un nom : my everyday clothes.
  I brush my teeth every day. N'écris pas "I brush my teeth everyday".

2. Ne place pas un groupe adverbial entre un verbe et son complément d'objet. Garde le verbe et son complément ensemble, puis ajoute le groupe.
  She speaks English very well. (et non "She speaks very well English")
  We read the newspaper every evening. (et non "We read every evening the newspaper")

3. Avec last, next, this et every, on n'ajoute pas in, on ou at.
  last week, next Monday, this morning, every Friday
  N'écris pas "on next Monday" ni "in last week".

Attention : « tous les jours » se dit every day, en deux mots ; everyday veut dire « ordinaire, de tous les jours ». En français on peut dire « je lis tous les soirs le journal », mais en anglais le verbe et son complément restent ensemble : I read the newspaper every evening. « Lundi prochain » se dit next Monday, sans préposition.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Adwoa écrit : "Everyday my father drinks slowly his tea, and on last Sunday he drank three cups."

1. Le groupe indique la fréquence, il s'écrit donc en deux mots : Every day.
2. Drinks et his tea vont ensemble, l'adverbe se place donc après le complément : drinks his tea slowly.
3. Last Sunday n'a pas besoin de préposition : last Sunday.

Phrase corrigée : "Every day my father drinks his tea slowly, and last Sunday he drank three cups."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère le verbe et demande-toi comment, où, quand ou à quelle fréquence l'action se passe. Les mots qui répondent forment le groupe adverbial.
Étape 2 : Si le groupe indique la fréquence, vérifie que every day est écrit en deux mots.
Étape 3 : Si le verbe a un complément d'objet, garde le verbe et le complément ensemble et place le groupe adverbial après eux.
Étape 4 : Si le groupe commence par last, next, this ou every, vérifie qu'il n'y a pas in, on ou at devant.
Étape 5 : Lis la phrase à voix haute et vérifie qu'elle sonne naturellement.

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:

2. Groupe placé entre le verbe et le complément : "Kofi kicked hard the ball." Écris : Kofi kicked the ball hard.
3. Préposition en trop : "The exam starts on next Tuesday." Écris : The exam starts next Tuesday.

title: Form and Use Reported Speech Appropriately
body:
Direct speech gives a speaker's exact words inside quotation marks:
  "We saw an eagle," said Aba.
Reported speech tells what someone said without using the exact words:
  Aba said that they had seen an eagle.

To change direct speech into reported speech:

1. Start with a reporting clause: Aba said that ...

2. Remove the quotation marks and the comma that goes with them. No quotation marks come after that.

3. When the reporting verb is said, move the verb one step back in time:
  is / am becomes was, are becomes were: "Esi is tired," said Mum. Mum said that Esi was tired.
  has / have becomes had: "Joe has become rich," said Atongo. Atongo said that Joe had become rich.
  saw becomes had seen, will becomes would, can becomes could.

4. Change the pronouns to fit the person who is reporting:
  I becomes he or she, we becomes they, my becomes his or her, our becomes their.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Yaa says: "Our team has won the cup."
A pupil writes: Yaa said that, "our team has won the cup."

1. Reported speech has no quotation marks and no comma after that: Yaa said that ...
2. Our belongs to Yaa, so it becomes their: their team.
3. Has won moves one step back: had won.

Corrected: Yaa said that their team had won the cup.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the speaker and the exact words inside the quotation marks.
Step 2: Write the reporting clause: [speaker] said that.
Step 3: Copy the words without the quotation marks and without a comma after that.
Step 4: Move the verb one step back in time: is to was, are to were, has to had, will to would, can to could.
Step 5: Change I, we, my, our and you so that they fit the person reporting.
Step 6: Read the sentence aloud and check that it tells what the speaker meant.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Tense not changed: Mary said, "I am sick." Not: Mary said that she is sick. Write: Mary said that she was sick.
2. Pronoun not changed: Ama said, "I like rice." Not: Ama said that I liked rice. Write: Ama said that she liked rice.
3. Quotation marks kept: Ben said, "I am late." Not: Ben said that "he was late." Write: Ben said that he was late.

title: Former et utiliser correctement le discours rapporté
body:
Le discours direct donne les mots exacts d'une personne entre guillemets :
  "We saw an eagle," said Aba.
Le discours rapporté dit ce que quelqu'un a dit sans reprendre ses mots exacts :
  Aba said that they had seen an eagle.

Pour passer du discours direct au discours rapporté :

1. Commence par une proposition introductive : Aba said that ...

2. Enlève les guillemets et la virgule qui les accompagne. Après that, il n'y a pas de guillemets.

3. Quand le verbe introducteur est said, recule le verbe d'un temps dans le passé :
  is / am devient was, are devient were : "Esi is tired," said Mum. Mum said that Esi was tired.
  has / have devient had : "Joe has become rich," said Atongo. Atongo said that Joe had become rich.
  saw devient had seen, will devient would, can devient could.

4. Change les pronoms pour qu'ils conviennent à la personne qui rapporte :
  I devient he ou she, we devient they, my devient his ou her, our devient their.

Attention : le français fait la même chose (« Je suis fatiguée », dit Esi. Esi a dit qu'elle était fatiguée). Mais en anglais, les guillemets s'écrivent " " et non « ».

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Yaa dit : "Our team has won the cup."
Un élève écrit : Yaa said that, "our team has won the cup."

1. Le discours rapporté n'a pas de guillemets ni de virgule après that : Yaa said that ...
2. Our renvoie à Yaa, il devient donc their : their team.
3. Has won recule d'un temps : had won.

Phrase corrigée : Yaa said that their team had won the cup.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Repère la personne qui parle et les mots exacts entre guillemets.
Étape 2 : Écris la proposition introductive : [personne] said that.
Étape 3 : Recopie les mots sans les guillemets et sans virgule après that.
Étape 4 : Recule le verbe d'un temps : is devient was, are devient were, has devient had, will devient would, can devient could.
Étape 5 : Change I, we, my, our et you pour qu'ils conviennent à la personne qui rapporte.
Étape 6 : Lis la phrase à voix haute et vérifie qu'elle dit ce que la personne voulait dire.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Temps non changé : Mary said, "I am sick." Pas : Mary said that she is sick. Écris : Mary said that she was sick.
2. Pronom non changé : Ama said, "I like rice." Pas : Ama said that I liked rice. Écris : Ama said that she liked rice.
3. Guillemets gardés : Ben said, "I am late." Pas : Ben said that "he was late." Écris : Ben said that he was late.

title: Write with a Legible, Fluent and Personal Handwriting Style
body:
Good handwriting is:
  legible: easy for anyone to read;
  fluent: smooth and steady, with letters joined in a flowing joint script;
  personal: it has your own small touches, but every letter is still clear.

1. Keep it even.
  Small letters (a, c, e, m, n, o, r, s, u) are all the same height.
  Tall letters (b, d, f, h, k, l, t) reach higher than the small letters.
  Tail letters (g, j, p, q, y) hang below the line.
  All letters sit on the line and lean the same way.

2. Finish every letter.
  Close the round part of a, d, g, o and q. Cross t and f. Dot i and j.
  An unfinished letter can change a word: an open a can make "bat" look like "but", and a t without its cross can make "tin" look like "lin".

3. Make it yours, but keep it readable.
  A personal style can come from a slight slant, rounder or narrower letters, or the way you join them.
  Do not add bubbles, hearts, stars or long curls that hide the shapes of the letters.

4. Practise fluency.
  Copy sentences from your reader in joint script at a steady pace. Then ask a partner to read them back. If your partner stops at a word, look closely at the letters in that word.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Kweku copies this sentence from his reader: The old fisherman mended his net.
His partner reads it aloud as: The old fisherman mended nis nel.

1. The h in his was as short as an n, so it looked like nis. Tall letters must reach higher: his.
2. The t in net had no cross, so it looked like nel. Cross every t: net.
3. Kweku had also drawn a big star over the i in fisherman. A star hides the dot, so he uses a small dot instead.

Kweku rewrites the sentence with tall letters taller than small ones, every t crossed and every i dotted. His partner now reads it without stopping.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Choose a sentence from your reader and read it carefully.
Step 2: Write it in joint script at a steady pace, keeping every letter on the line.
Step 3: Check the heights: small letters the same size, tall letters higher, tail letters below the line.
Step 4: Check the slant: all letters lean the same way.
Step 5: Check that every letter is finished: round parts closed, t and f crossed, i and j dotted.
Step 6: Check your personal touches: they must not hide any letter shape.
Step 7: Give it to a partner to read aloud. Fix any letter that made your partner stop.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Uneven letters: if l is as short as e, "led" can look like "eed". Make tall letters reach higher, and keep every letter leaning the same way.
2. Decoration in place of style: curls and bubbles can make an o look like an a. Keep your personal touches small.
3. Unfinished letters: an open o can look like a u, so "hop" becomes "hup". Close every round letter.

title: Écrire avec une écriture lisible, fluide et personnelle
body:
Une bonne écriture est :
  lisible : facile à lire pour tout le monde ;
  fluide : régulière et souple, avec des lettres reliées dans une écriture liée continue ;
  personnelle : elle a tes petites touches à toi, mais chaque lettre reste claire.

1. Garde une écriture régulière.
  Les petites lettres (a, c, e, m, n, o, r, s, u) ont toutes la même hauteur.
  Les grandes lettres (b, d, f, h, k, l, t) montent plus haut que les petites lettres.
  Les lettres à queue (g, j, p, q, y) descendent sous la ligne.
  Toutes les lettres reposent sur la ligne et penchent dans le même sens.

2. Termine chaque lettre.
  Ferme la partie ronde de a, d, g, o et q. Barre t et f. Mets le point sur i et j.
  Une lettre inachevée peut changer un mot : un a ouvert peut faire ressembler "bat" à "but", et un t non barré peut faire ressembler "tin" à "lin".

3. Rends-la personnelle, mais lisible.
  Un style personnel peut venir d'une légère inclinaison, de lettres plus rondes ou plus étroites, ou de ta façon de les relier.
  N'ajoute pas de bulles, de cœurs, d'étoiles ni de longues boucles qui cachent la forme des lettres.

4. Entraîne-toi à la fluidité.
  Recopie des phrases de ton livre de lecture en écriture liée, à un rythme régulier. Puis demande à un camarade de les relire. Si ton camarade s'arrête sur un mot, regarde de près les lettres de ce mot.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Kweku recopie cette phrase de son livre de lecture : The old fisherman mended his net.
Son camarade la lit à voix haute ainsi : The old fisherman mended nis nel.

1. Le h de his était aussi petit qu'un n, il ressemblait donc à nis. Les grandes lettres doivent monter plus haut : his.
2. Le t de net n'était pas barré, il ressemblait donc à nel. Barre chaque t : net.
3. Kweku avait aussi dessiné une grosse étoile sur le i de fisherman. Une étoile cache le point, il met donc un petit point à la place.

Kweku réécrit la phrase avec des grandes lettres plus hautes que les petites, chaque t barré et chaque i pointé. Son camarade la lit maintenant sans s'arrêter.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Choisis une phrase de ton livre de lecture et lis-la attentivement.
Étape 2 : Écris-la en écriture liée, à un rythme régulier, en gardant chaque lettre sur la ligne.
Étape 3 : Vérifie les hauteurs : les petites lettres de même taille, les grandes lettres plus hautes, les lettres à queue sous la ligne.
Étape 4 : Vérifie l'inclinaison : toutes les lettres penchent dans le même sens.
Étape 5 : Vérifie que chaque lettre est terminée : parties rondes fermées, t et f barrés, i et j pointés.
Étape 6 : Vérifie tes touches personnelles : elles ne doivent cacher la forme d'aucune lettre.
Étape 7 : Donne ta phrase à un camarade pour qu'il la lise à voix haute. Corrige chaque lettre qui l'a fait s'arrêter.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Lettres irrégulières : si l est aussi petit que e, "led" peut ressembler à "eed". Fais monter les grandes lettres plus haut et garde toutes les lettres penchées dans le même sens.
2. Décoration au lieu de style : des boucles et des bulles peuvent faire ressembler un o à un a. Garde tes touches personnelles discrètes.
3. Lettres inachevées : un o ouvert peut ressembler à un u, et "hop" devient "hup". Ferme chaque lettre ronde.

title: Write Complex Sentences Clearly and Correctly
body:
A simple sentence has one clause: We will go.
A complex sentence has a main clause and at least one subordinate clause. The subordinate clause cannot stand alone.
  You will come. We will go.  becomes  When you come, we will go.
  The girl won the prize. She sits beside me.  becomes  The girl who sits beside me won the prize.

Subordinate clauses often begin with when, because, although, if, before, after, until (time, reason, contrast, condition)
or with who, which, that (relative clauses that describe a noun).

1. A subordinate clause must be joined to a main clause in the same sentence.
  Not: Because the road was flooded. We stayed at home.
  Write: Because the road was flooded, we stayed at home.

2. One link needs only one linking word.
  Not: Although it was late, but we kept working.   Not: Because he was sick, so he stayed home.
  Write: Although it was late, we kept working.   Because he was sick, he stayed home.

3. After a relative clause, do not repeat the subject with a pronoun.
  Not: The man who sells bread he lives near us.
  Write: The man who sells bread lives near us.

When a subordinate clause comes first, put a comma after it.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Two simple sentences: The boy found a wallet. He returned it to the owner. The boy lives next door.
Esi writes: "The boy who lives next door he found a wallet. Although it had money inside. But he returned it to the owner."

1. After the relative clause who lives next door, the pronoun he repeats the subject. Remove it.
2. "Although it had money inside" cannot stand alone. Join it to the main clause.
3. Although already shows the contrast, so but is not needed.

Corrected: "The boy who lives next door found a wallet. Although it had money inside, he returned it to the owner."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Read the simple sentences and decide how they are linked: time, reason, contrast, condition, or a description of a noun.
Step 2: Choose one linking word: when, because, although, if, before, after, until, or who, which, that.
Step 3: Join the subordinate clause to the main clause in one sentence. If the subordinate clause comes first, add a comma after it.
Step 4: Check that there is no second linking word such as but, so or then in the main clause.
Step 5: After a who, which or that clause, check that the subject is not repeated with he, she, it or they.
Step 6: Read the sentence aloud and check that it is clear.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. A clause standing alone: "After we ate supper. We washed the plates." Write: After we ate supper, we washed the plates.
2. Two linking words: "Because the shop was closed, so we went home." Write: Because the shop was closed, we went home.
3. A repeated subject: "The pupils who won the quiz they received books." Write: The pupils who won the quiz received books.

title: Écrire des phrases complexes de façon claire et correcte
body:
Une phrase simple a une seule proposition : We will go.
Une phrase complexe a une proposition principale et au moins une proposition subordonnée. La subordonnée ne peut pas être seule.
  You will come. We will go.  devient  When you come, we will go.
  The girl won the prize. She sits beside me.  devient  The girl who sits beside me won the prize.

Les subordonnées commencent souvent par when, because, although, if, before, after, until (temps, cause, opposition, condition)
ou par who, which, that (propositions relatives qui décrivent un nom).

1. Une subordonnée doit être rattachée à une principale dans la même phrase.
  Pas : Because the road was flooded. We stayed at home.
  Écris : Because the road was flooded, we stayed at home.

2. Un seul lien demande un seul mot de liaison.
  Pas : Although it was late, but we kept working.   Pas : Because he was sick, so he stayed home.
  Écris : Although it was late, we kept working.   Because he was sick, he stayed home.

3. Après une relative, ne répète pas le sujet avec un pronom.
  Pas : The man who sells bread he lives near us.
  Écris : The man who sells bread lives near us.

Quand la subordonnée vient en premier, mets une virgule après elle.

Attention : en français, on dit « Bien qu'il soit tard, nous avons continué », sans « mais ». En anglais non plus, on ne met pas but après although.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Trois phrases simples : The boy found a wallet. He returned it to the owner. The boy lives next door.
Esi écrit : "The boy who lives next door he found a wallet. Although it had money inside. But he returned it to the owner."

1. Après la relative who lives next door, le pronom he répète le sujet. Enlève-le.
2. "Although it had money inside" ne peut pas être seule. Rattache-la à la principale.
3. Although montre déjà l'opposition, donc but n'est pas nécessaire.

Phrase corrigée : "The boy who lives next door found a wallet. Although it had money inside, he returned it to the owner."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Lis les phrases simples et décide quel est le lien : temps, cause, opposition, condition, ou description d'un nom.
Étape 2 : Choisis un seul mot de liaison : when, because, although, if, before, after, until, ou who, which, that.
Étape 3 : Rattache la subordonnée à la principale dans une seule phrase. Si la subordonnée vient en premier, ajoute une virgule après elle.
Étape 4 : Vérifie qu'il n'y a pas un deuxième mot de liaison comme but, so ou then dans la principale.
Étape 5 : Après une proposition en who, which ou that, vérifie que le sujet n'est pas répété avec he, she, it ou they.
Étape 6 : Lis la phrase à voix haute et vérifie qu'elle est claire.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Une subordonnée seule : "After we ate supper. We washed the plates." Écris : After we ate supper, we washed the plates.
2. Deux mots de liaison : "Because the shop was closed, so we went home." Écris : Because the shop was closed, we went home.
3. Un sujet répété : "The pupils who won the quiz they received books." Écris : The pupils who won the quiz received books.

title: Choose Appropriate Modes of Writing
body:
Each mode of writing has its own purpose, audience and way of organising ideas.

  Process: explains how to do or make something. Lists materials, then numbered steps in order, often with command verbs (Cut, Mix, Pour).
  Narrative: tells a story of events that happened to characters, usually in time order, with a beginning, middle and end.
  Descriptive: paints a picture of one person, place or thing using the senses: what you see, hear, smell, taste and feel.
  Persuasive: tries to make the reader think or act in a certain way. Uses strong reasons and feelings and ends with a call to act.
  Argumentative: looks at both sides of an issue, gives reasons and evidence for each, then reaches a conclusion.
  Letter: written to a particular reader, with an address or greeting, a body and a closing (Dear ... Yours sincerely / Your friend).

Be careful: most texts contain describing words, some opinions and some time-order words. These single clues do not decide the mode.
  A recipe may say "golden" and "tastes best", but it is still process writing because its purpose is to show the steps.
Ask: What is the writer trying to do? Who is the reader? How are the ideas organised?

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Read: "Our village well is deep and cool. First, I want you to know that the water is dirty. Then think about the children who fall sick. Please give money at the durbar so that we can build a borehole!"

1. Describing words (deep, cool) do not make it descriptive: the text does not paint a picture of the well.
2. Time-order words (first, then) do not make it a narrative or a process: there is no story and no steps to follow.
3. The writer wants readers to give money, uses feelings (children who fall sick) and ends with a call to act.

The mode is persuasive writing.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Read the whole text or task, not just a few words.
Step 2: Ask what the writer wants to do: explain steps, tell a story, paint a picture, make the reader act, weigh both sides, or write to a particular person.
Step 3: Ask who the reader is.
Step 4: Look at how the ideas are organised: numbered steps, events in a story, details for the senses, reasons with a call to act, both sides and a conclusion, or a greeting and a closing.
Step 5: Do not decide from single clues such as describing words, opinion words or time-order words.
Step 6: Name the mode and give the reason.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Deciding from describing words: a story about a "tall, dark forest" is still a narrative if it tells events that happened to characters.
2. Deciding from opinion words: a recipe that says "this soup is the best" is still process writing.
3. Deciding from time-order words: a speech that says "first" and "finally" is not a narrative if it is trying to make listeners act.

title: Choisir le mode d'écriture qui convient
body:
Chaque mode d'écriture a son propre but, son public et sa façon d'organiser les idées.

  Process (texte procédural) : explique comment faire ou fabriquer quelque chose. Liste le matériel, puis des étapes numérotées dans l'ordre, souvent avec des verbes à l'impératif (Cut, Mix, Pour).
  Narrative (récit) : raconte une histoire d'événements arrivés à des personnages, en général dans l'ordre chronologique, avec un début, un milieu et une fin.
  Descriptive (description) : fait le portrait d'une personne, d'un lieu ou d'une chose en utilisant les sens : ce qu'on voit, entend, sent, goûte et touche.
  Persuasive (texte persuasif) : cherche à faire penser ou agir le lecteur d'une certaine façon. Utilise des raisons fortes et des sentiments et se termine par un appel à agir.
  Argumentative (texte argumentatif) : examine les deux côtés d'une question, donne des raisons et des preuves pour chacun, puis arrive à une conclusion.
  Letter (lettre) : écrite à un lecteur précis, avec une adresse ou une formule d'appel, un corps et une formule de fin (Dear ... Yours sincerely / Your friend).

Attention : la plupart des textes contiennent des mots qui décrivent, quelques opinions et quelques mots de temps. Ces indices isolés ne décident pas du mode.
  Une recette peut dire "golden" et "tastes best", mais c'est quand même un texte procédural, car son but est de montrer les étapes.
Demande-toi : que cherche à faire l'auteur ? Qui est le lecteur ? Comment les idées sont-elles organisées ?

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Lis : "Our village well is deep and cool. First, I want you to know that the water is dirty. Then think about the children who fall sick. Please give money at the durbar so that we can build a borehole!"

1. Les mots qui décrivent (deep, cool) ne rendent pas le texte descriptif : il ne fait pas le portrait du puits.
2. Les mots de temps (first, then) n'en font ni un récit ni un texte procédural : il n'y a pas d'histoire ni d'étapes à suivre.
3. L'auteur veut que les lecteurs donnent de l'argent, fait appel aux sentiments (children who fall sick) et termine par un appel à agir.

Le mode est le texte persuasif.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Lis tout le texte ou toute la consigne, pas seulement quelques mots.
Étape 2 : Demande-toi ce que veut faire l'auteur : expliquer des étapes, raconter une histoire, faire un portrait, faire agir le lecteur, peser les deux côtés, ou écrire à une personne précise.
Étape 3 : Demande-toi qui est le lecteur.
Étape 4 : Regarde comment les idées sont organisées : étapes numérotées, événements d'une histoire, détails pour les sens, raisons avec un appel à agir, deux côtés et une conclusion, ou une formule d'appel et une formule de fin.
Étape 5 : Ne décide pas à partir d'indices isolés comme les mots qui décrivent, les mots d'opinion ou les mots de temps.
Étape 6 : Nomme le mode et donne la raison.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Décider à partir des mots qui décrivent : une histoire sur une "tall, dark forest" reste un récit si elle raconte des événements arrivés à des personnages.
2. Décider à partir des mots d'opinion : une recette qui dit "this soup is the best" reste un texte procédural.
3. Décider à partir des mots de temps : un discours qui dit "first" et "finally" n'est pas un récit s'il cherche à faire agir les auditeurs.

title: Use Key Words to Introduce the Main Idea of a Paragraph
body:
The sentence that introduces the main idea of a paragraph is called the topic sentence. It is usually the first sentence. The other sentences support it.

A good topic sentence has two parts:
  the topic: what the paragraph is about (my school, rainy days, our chief);
  the key words that tell what you will say about it (is a busy place, causes many problems, helps us in three ways).
  Example: Rainy days cause many problems in our town.

Key words, phrases or clauses that often introduce a main idea:
  There are several reasons why ... / ... in three ways / One important ... is ...
  ... is the most ... / When ..., ... (a clause that sets the scene)

Three checks:
1. Do not just announce the topic. "In this paragraph I will talk about rain" does not say anything about rain.
2. Not too narrow. The topic sentence must cover ALL the supporting sentences, not just one of them.
3. Not too broad. "Water is important everywhere in the world" is too big for a paragraph about rain in your town.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Supporting sentences: "The gutters overflow and flood the road. Taxis refuse to drive to our area. Many pupils arrive at school with wet uniforms."

Three possible topic sentences:
  "I am going to write about rain." This only announces the topic.
  "The gutters overflow when it rains." This covers only the first sentence.
  "Weather changes all over the world." This is far too big.

Best: "Heavy rain causes many problems in our area." The key words "causes many problems" cover all three supporting sentences.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Read all the supporting sentences and ask what they have in common.
Step 2: Name the topic in a few words.
Step 3: Add key words that say what all the sentences show about the topic, for example "in three ways", "many problems", "a wonderful place".
Step 4: Check that your sentence does not just announce the topic.
Step 5: Check that it covers every supporting sentence, not just one.
Step 6: Check that it is not so big that it covers things the paragraph never talks about.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Announcing: "This paragraph is about my uncle." Say something about him: My uncle is the funniest person in our family.
2. Too narrow: "My uncle tells jokes at dinner." That is one detail; it cannot introduce the whole paragraph.
3. Too broad: "Families are found in every country." That is far bigger than a paragraph about one uncle.

title: Utiliser des mots clés pour introduire l'idée principale d'un paragraphe
body:
La phrase qui introduit l'idée principale d'un paragraphe s'appelle la phrase d'introduction (topic sentence). C'est en général la première phrase. Les autres phrases la soutiennent.

Une bonne phrase d'introduction a deux parties :
  le sujet : ce dont parle le paragraphe (my school, rainy days, our chief) ;
  les mots clés qui disent ce que tu vas en dire (is a busy place, causes many problems, helps us in three ways).
  Exemple : Rainy days cause many problems in our town.

Mots, groupes de mots ou propositions clés qui introduisent souvent une idée principale :
  There are several reasons why ... / ... in three ways / One important ... is ...
  ... is the most ... / When ..., ... (une proposition qui plante le décor)

Trois vérifications :
1. N'annonce pas seulement le sujet. "In this paragraph I will talk about rain" ne dit rien sur la pluie.
2. Pas trop étroite. La phrase d'introduction doit couvrir TOUTES les phrases de soutien, pas une seule.
3. Pas trop large. "Water is important everywhere in the world" est trop vaste pour un paragraphe sur la pluie dans ta ville.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Phrases de soutien : "The gutters overflow and flood the road. Taxis refuse to drive to our area. Many pupils arrive at school with wet uniforms."

Trois phrases d'introduction possibles :
  "I am going to write about rain." Elle annonce seulement le sujet.
  "The gutters overflow when it rains." Elle ne couvre que la première phrase.
  "Weather changes all over the world." Elle est beaucoup trop vaste.

La meilleure : "Heavy rain causes many problems in our area." Les mots clés "causes many problems" couvrent les trois phrases de soutien.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Lis toutes les phrases de soutien et demande-toi ce qu'elles ont en commun.
Étape 2 : Nomme le sujet en quelques mots.
Étape 3 : Ajoute des mots clés qui disent ce que toutes les phrases montrent sur le sujet, par exemple "in three ways", "many problems", "a wonderful place".
Étape 4 : Vérifie que ta phrase n'annonce pas seulement le sujet.
Étape 5 : Vérifie qu'elle couvre toutes les phrases de soutien, pas une seule.
Étape 6 : Vérifie qu'elle n'est pas si vaste qu'elle couvre des choses dont le paragraphe ne parle jamais.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Annoncer : "This paragraph is about my uncle." Dis quelque chose sur lui : My uncle is the funniest person in our family.
2. Trop étroite : "My uncle tells jokes at dinner." C'est un seul détail ; elle ne peut pas introduire tout le paragraphe.
3. Trop large : "Families are found in every country." C'est bien plus vaste qu'un paragraphe sur un seul oncle.
