title: Use Words, Phrases and Clauses to Link Claims and Reasons
body:
In an argument, the reader must see clearly which part is the claim and which part is the reason.

Claim first, then the reason: use because, since or as before the REASON.
  Claim, because + reason: "We should save electricity, because power cuts hurt small businesses."

Reason first, then the claim: use so, therefore, for this reason or this shows that before the CLAIM.
  Reason. For this reason, + claim: "Power cuts hurt small businesses. For this reason, we should save electricity."

The word "and" only adds. It does not show that one idea supports the other, so it hides the link.

Adjectives in their forms help you argue:
  Comparative: cheaper than, more useful than, better than.
  Superlative: the cheapest of all, the most useful of the three.
  A comparison must say what is being compared: "cheaper than candles", not just "cheaper".
  Clauses such as "which means that" can also make the link clear: "LED bulbs use less power, which means that families pay less."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Ama's claim: our class should keep a class garden.
Her reason: looking after plants teaches us more about science than reading about them.

Claim first: "Our class should keep a garden, because looking after plants teaches us more about science than reading about them."
Reason first: "Looking after plants teaches us more about science than reading about them. Therefore, our class should keep a garden."

In both, the reason word sits in the right place, the link is clear, and the comparison says what it is compared with ("than reading about them").

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Write your claim and your reason separately.
Step 2: Decide which comes first.
Step 3: If the claim comes first, put because, since or as before the reason.
Step 4: If the reason comes first, put so, therefore or for this reason before the claim.
Step 5: Do not join them with "and" alone.
Step 6: If you used a comparative (cheaper, safer, more useful), check that "than ..." tells the reader what it is compared with.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes. The claim here is that families should use mosquito nets.

1. The reason word on the wrong part: "Nets are cheaper than malaria medicine, because families should use them" makes the claim look like the reason. Write: "Families should use nets, because nets are cheaper than malaria medicine."
2. Only "and": "Families should use nets, and nets are cheaper than malaria medicine" puts two ideas side by side without showing that one supports the other.
3. A half comparison: "Families should use nets, because nets are cheaper" leaves the reader asking: cheaper than what?

title: Utiliser des mots, des groupes de mots et des propositions pour relier thèse et raisons
body:
Dans une argumentation, le lecteur doit voir clairement quelle partie est la thèse et quelle partie est la raison.

La thèse d'abord, puis la raison : utilise because, since ou as devant la RAISON.
  Thèse, because + raison : "We should save electricity, because power cuts hurt small businesses."

La raison d'abord, puis la thèse : utilise so, therefore, for this reason ou this shows that devant la THÈSE.
  Raison. For this reason, + thèse : "Power cuts hurt small businesses. For this reason, we should save electricity."

Le mot "and" ne fait qu'ajouter. Il ne montre pas qu'une idée appuie l'autre, donc il cache le lien.

Les formes de l'adjectif aident à argumenter :
  Comparatif : cheaper than, more useful than, better than.
  Superlatif : the cheapest of all, the most useful of the three.
  Une comparaison doit dire avec quoi on compare : "cheaper than candles", pas seulement "cheaper".
  Des propositions comme "which means that" peuvent aussi rendre le lien clair : "LED bulbs use less power, which means that families pay less."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
La thèse d'Ama : notre classe devrait avoir un jardin.
Sa raison : s'occuper des plantes nous apprend plus en sciences que de lire sur elles.

La thèse d'abord : "Our class should keep a garden, because looking after plants teaches us more about science than reading about them."
La raison d'abord : "Looking after plants teaches us more about science than reading about them. Therefore, our class should keep a garden."

Dans les deux cas, le mot de raison est à la bonne place, le lien est clair, et la comparaison dit avec quoi on compare ("than reading about them").

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Écris ta thèse et ta raison séparément.
Étape 2 : Décide laquelle vient en premier.
Étape 3 : Si la thèse vient en premier, mets because, since ou as devant la raison.
Étape 4 : Si la raison vient en premier, mets so, therefore ou for this reason devant la thèse.
Étape 5 : Ne les relie pas seulement avec "and".
Étape 6 : Si tu as utilisé un comparatif (cheaper, safer, more useful), vérifie que "than ..." dit au lecteur avec quoi on compare.

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes. La thèse ici est que les familles devraient utiliser des moustiquaires.

1. Le mot de raison sur la mauvaise partie : "Nets are cheaper than malaria medicine, because families should use them" fait passer la thèse pour la raison. Écris : "Families should use nets, because nets are cheaper than malaria medicine."
2. Seulement "and" : "Families should use nets, and nets are cheaper than malaria medicine" pose deux idées côte à côte sans montrer que l'une appuie l'autre.
3. Une comparaison à moitié : "Families should use nets, because nets are cheaper" laisse le lecteur se demander : moins cher que quoi ?

title: Establish and Maintain a Formal Style
body:
An argumentative essay, a letter to an official or a debate speech needs a formal style from the first sentence to the last.

Structure of an argumentative piece:
  Introduction: state the topic and your stand.
  Reasons: one paragraph for each reason, with evidence.
  Conclusion: sum up your stand.

Three habits keep the style formal:
  1. Full forms, not contractions: do not (not don't), cannot (not can't), it is (not it's), we are (not we're).
  2. Whole words, not text-message short forms: because (not coz), you (not u), today (not 2day), before (not b4), please (not pls).
  3. Calm punctuation: one full stop at the end of a statement. Do not use rows of exclamation marks or words in CAPITAL LETTERS to shout. Your reasons and evidence show how strongly you feel.

Keep the same formal style all the way through, including the conclusion.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Kwame's first draft of a letter to his headteacher:
  "We don't have enough desks in Class 6 coz more pupils came this term. This is a BIG problem!!!"

Formal version:
  "We do not have enough desks in Class 6 because more pupils joined this term. This is a serious problem, as some pupils must share one desk between three."

What changed: "don't" became "do not", "coz" became "because", and the capitals and exclamation marks were replaced by a reason that shows why the problem is serious.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Plan the structure: introduction, reasons, conclusion.
Step 2: Write your draft.
Step 3: Circle every apostrophe in a verb (don't, it's, we're) and write the full form.
Step 4: Look for text-message short forms (u, coz, 2day, b4, pls) and write the whole word.
Step 5: Remove extra exclamation marks and shouting capitals. If you want to show something is serious, add a reason or a fact.
Step 6: Read the conclusion last: is it as formal as the introduction?

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes. The topic here is noise near the school.

1. Contractions: "The noise won't let us hear the teacher" should be "The noise will not let us hear the teacher."
2. Text short forms: "Pls move the music shop b4 exams start" should be "Please move the music shop before the examinations start."
3. Shouting: "The noise is TERRIBLE!!!" does not persuade. Write: "The noise is so loud that pupils cannot hear the teacher."

title: Adopter et garder un style soutenu
body:
Une rédaction argumentative, une lettre à un responsable ou un discours de débat demande un style soutenu de la première à la dernière phrase.

Structure d'un texte argumentatif :
  Introduction : présente le sujet et ta position.
  Raisons : un paragraphe par raison, avec des preuves.
  Conclusion : résume ta position.

Trois habitudes gardent le style soutenu :
  1. Les formes complètes, pas les contractions : do not (pas don't), cannot (pas can't), it is (pas it's), we are (pas we're).
  2. Des mots entiers, pas les abréviations des SMS : because (pas coz), you (pas u), today (pas 2day), before (pas b4), please (pas pls).
  3. Une ponctuation calme : un seul point à la fin d'une affirmation. N'utilise pas de rangées de points d'exclamation ni de mots en MAJUSCULES pour crier. Tes raisons et tes preuves montrent la force de ton avis.

Garde le même style soutenu jusqu'au bout, y compris dans la conclusion.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Le premier brouillon de la lettre de Kwame à son directeur :
  "We don't have enough desks in Class 6 coz more pupils came this term. This is a BIG problem!!!"

Version soutenue :
  "We do not have enough desks in Class 6 because more pupils joined this term. This is a serious problem, as some pupils must share one desk between three."

Ce qui a changé : "don't" est devenu "do not", "coz" est devenu "because", et les majuscules et les points d'exclamation ont été remplacés par une raison qui montre pourquoi le problème est sérieux.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Prépare la structure : introduction, raisons, conclusion.
Étape 2 : Écris ton brouillon.
Étape 3 : Entoure chaque apostrophe dans un verbe (don't, it's, we're) et écris la forme complète.
Étape 4 : Cherche les abréviations des SMS (u, coz, 2day, b4, pls) et écris le mot entier.
Étape 5 : Enlève les points d'exclamation en trop et les majuscules qui crient. Si tu veux montrer qu'une chose est grave, ajoute une raison ou un fait.
Étape 6 : Relis la conclusion en dernier : est-elle aussi soutenue que l'introduction ?

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes. Le sujet ici est le bruit près de l'école.

1. Les contractions : "The noise won't let us hear the teacher" doit devenir "The noise will not let us hear the teacher."
2. Les abréviations de SMS : "Pls move the music shop b4 exams start" doit devenir "Please move the music shop before the examinations start."
3. Crier : "The noise is TERRIBLE!!!" ne convainc pas. Écris : "The noise is so loud that pupils cannot hear the teacher."

title: Conclude an Argument with a Rhetorical Question
body:
The conclusion is the last thing the reader or audience remembers. A strong conclusion has two parts.

1. A concluding statement that follows from your argument: sum up your stand and your main reasons, firmly and confidently.
   Begin with words such as "In conclusion," or "To sum up,". In a debate, address the audience first, for example "Madam Chairperson,".

2. A rhetorical question: a question that does not need an answer, because the answer is obvious. It makes the listener agree with you in their head.
   A real question asks for information: "How many pupils are in our school?"
   A rhetorical question makes a point: "Can any pupil learn well on an empty stomach?" (Obvious answer: no.)
   The obvious answer must support YOUR side, not the other side.

Do not end with doubt. Words such as "maybe", "I am not sure" or "I could be wrong" make the reader stop believing you.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Topic: every school should have recycling bins. Kafui is for the motion.

Her reasons: bins keep the compound clean, and recycled plastic can be sold to raise money for the school.

Her conclusion:
"To sum up, recycling bins keep our compound clean and turn waste into money, so every school should have them. Why throw away what could pay for our new books?"

The statement repeats her stand and reasons firmly. The question needs no answer: the obvious answer ("there is no reason to throw it away") supports her side.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Reread your stand and your main reasons.
Step 2: Write one or two sentences that sum them up, starting with "In conclusion," or "To sum up,".
Step 3: Remove any words that show doubt, such as maybe, perhaps or I am not sure.
Step 4: Write a question whose answer is obvious.
Step 5: Answer it in your head. Does the obvious answer support your side?
Step 6: In a debate, begin with the vocative, for example "Madam Chairperson," or "Honourable judges,".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes. The stand here is that schools should run buses for pupils.

1. A real question: "How much does a bus cost?" asks for a fact. It does not make a point. Try: "Should any child be too tired to learn before the first lesson?"
2. A question for the other side: "Isn't walking good exercise anyway?" leads the reader to answer "yes", which argues against buses.
3. Doubt at the end: "In conclusion, buses might help, but I may be wrong" undoes the whole argument. Write: "In conclusion, school buses save time and keep pupils safe."

title: Conclure une argumentation par une question rhétorique
body:
La conclusion est la dernière chose dont le lecteur ou le public se souvient. Une conclusion forte a deux parties.

1. Une phrase de conclusion qui découle de ton argumentation : résume ta position et tes raisons principales, avec fermeté et assurance.
   Commence par des mots comme "In conclusion," ou "To sum up,". Dans un débat, adresse-toi d'abord au public, par exemple "Madam Chairperson,".

2. Une question rhétorique : une question qui n'attend pas de réponse, parce que la réponse est évidente. Elle pousse l'auditeur à te donner raison dans sa tête.
   Une vraie question demande une information : "How many pupils are in our school?"
   Une question rhétorique défend une idée : "Can any pupil learn well on an empty stomach?" (Réponse évidente : non.)
   La réponse évidente doit appuyer TON côté, pas l'autre côté.

Ne termine pas par un doute. Des mots comme "maybe", "I am not sure" ou "I could be wrong" font que le lecteur ne te croit plus.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Sujet : chaque école devrait avoir des poubelles de recyclage. Kafui est pour la motion.

Ses raisons : les poubelles gardent la cour propre, et le plastique recyclé peut être vendu pour rapporter de l'argent à l'école.

Sa conclusion :
"To sum up, recycling bins keep our compound clean and turn waste into money, so every school should have them. Why throw away what could pay for our new books?"

La phrase reprend sa position et ses raisons avec fermeté. La question n'attend pas de réponse : la réponse évidente ("il n'y a aucune raison de le jeter") appuie son côté.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Relis ta position et tes raisons principales.
Étape 2 : Écris une ou deux phrases qui les résument, en commençant par "In conclusion," ou "To sum up,".
Étape 3 : Enlève tous les mots qui montrent un doute, comme maybe, perhaps ou I am not sure.
Étape 4 : Écris une question dont la réponse est évidente.
Étape 5 : Réponds-y dans ta tête. La réponse évidente appuie-t-elle ton côté ?
Étape 6 : Dans un débat, commence par l'apostrophe, par exemple "Madam Chairperson," ou "Honourable judges,".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes. La position ici est que les écoles devraient avoir des bus pour les élèves.

1. Une vraie question : "How much does a bus cost?" demande un fait. Elle ne défend pas d'idée. Essaie : "Should any child be too tired to learn before the first lesson?"
2. Une question pour l'autre côté : "Isn't walking good exercise anyway?" pousse le lecteur à répondre "oui", ce qui va contre les bus.
3. Un doute à la fin : "In conclusion, buses might help, but I may be wrong" défait toute l'argumentation. Écris : "In conclusion, school buses save time and keep pupils safe."

title: Write Short Paragraphs to Describe Incidents
body:
An incident is something unexpected that happens, such as an accident, a fire outbreak, a flood or a fall. When you describe an incident, the reader wants the facts.

Answer the key questions in your first sentences:
  When did it happen? (day and time)
  Where did it happen? (the exact place)
  Who was involved?
  What happened, and what was the result?

Report only what you saw or what was confirmed. If you do not know the cause, do not guess; write "The cause is not yet known" or "Police are investigating."

Use a calm, factual tone: the past tense, plain words and full stops. An incident report is not a story: leave out sound effects such as "BANG!", rows of exclamation marks and dramatic comparisons.

Go through the writing process: choose the incident, brainstorm the facts, organise them, draft, edit with a partner and present.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Incident: a fire at a shop.

"At about 9 p.m. on Sunday, a fire started in a provision shop opposite the lorry station in Techiman. Neighbours poured water on it until the fire service arrived and put it out. Nobody was hurt, but most of the goods were burnt. The cause of the fire is not yet known."

When: about 9 p.m. on Sunday. Where: a provision shop opposite the lorry station in Techiman. What happened and the result: the fire, how it was put out, the damage. The writer does not guess the cause and keeps a calm tone.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Choose an incident you saw or heard about from a reliable person.
Step 2: Write down when, where, who, what happened and the result.
Step 3: Put the facts in order: what happened first, next and last.
Step 4: Draft a short paragraph. Start with when and where.
Step 5: Cross out any guess about who is to blame, and any sound effects or exclamation marks.
Step 6: Ask a partner to check that every key question is answered, then present your paragraph.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes. The incident here is a tree falling on a car.

1. No time or place: "A tree fell on a car. The car was damaged" does not tell the reader when or where. Add: "During the storm on Monday evening, outside the post office."
2. Guessing blame: "The owner of the tree is clearly to blame" is not a fact you saw. Write only what is known.
3. A dramatic story: "CRACK! The giant tree crashed down like a falling giant!!!" belongs in a story, not a report. Write: "A large tree fell onto a parked car."

title: Écrire de courts paragraphes pour décrire un incident
body:
Un incident est un événement inattendu, comme un accident, un incendie, une inondation ou une chute. Quand tu décris un incident, le lecteur veut les faits.

Réponds aux questions clés dans tes premières phrases :
  Quand est-ce arrivé ? (le jour et l'heure)
  Où est-ce arrivé ? (le lieu exact)
  Qui était concerné ?
  Que s'est-il passé, et quel a été le résultat ?

Rapporte seulement ce que tu as vu ou ce qui a été confirmé. Si tu ne connais pas la cause, ne devine pas ; écris "The cause is not yet known" ou "Police are investigating."

Utilise un ton calme et factuel : le passé, des mots simples et des points. Un compte rendu d'incident n'est pas une histoire : enlève les bruitages comme "BANG!", les rangées de points d'exclamation et les comparaisons dramatiques.

Suis le processus d'écriture : choisis l'incident, note les faits, organise-les, écris le brouillon, corrige avec un camarade et présente.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Incident : un incendie dans une boutique.

"At about 9 p.m. on Sunday, a fire started in a provision shop opposite the lorry station in Techiman. Neighbours poured water on it until the fire service arrived and put it out. Nobody was hurt, but most of the goods were burnt. The cause of the fire is not yet known."

Quand : vers 21 h dimanche. Où : une boutique d'alimentation en face de la gare routière de Techiman. Ce qui s'est passé et le résultat : le feu, comment il a été éteint, les dégâts. L'auteur ne devine pas la cause et garde un ton calme.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Choisis un incident que tu as vu ou dont une personne fiable t'a parlé.
Étape 2 : Note quand, où, qui, ce qui s'est passé et le résultat.
Étape 3 : Mets les faits dans l'ordre : ce qui s'est passé d'abord, ensuite et à la fin.
Étape 4 : Écris un court paragraphe. Commence par quand et où.
Étape 5 : Barre toute supposition sur le coupable, ainsi que les bruitages et les points d'exclamation.
Étape 6 : Demande à un camarade de vérifier que chaque question clé a une réponse, puis présente ton paragraphe.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes. L'incident ici est la chute d'un arbre sur une voiture.

1. Pas de moment ni de lieu : "A tree fell on a car. The car was damaged" ne dit pas au lecteur quand ni où. Ajoute : "During the storm on Monday evening, outside the post office."
2. Deviner le coupable : "The owner of the tree is clearly to blame" n'est pas un fait que tu as vu. Écris seulement ce qui est connu.
3. Une histoire dramatique : "CRACK! The giant tree crashed down like a falling giant!!!" convient à une histoire, pas à un compte rendu. Écris : "A large tree fell onto a parked car."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Write Articles on Varied Topics
body:
An article is written for many readers, for example in the school magazine, on the notice board or in a newspaper such as the Junior Graphic. Articles can be about news, health, sport, culture, the environment, science or technology.

Features of an article:
  Headline: a short title that tells the reader what the article is about, using key words: "Floods Close Two Schools".
  Byline: who wrote it: "By Ama Mensah, Class 6".
  Opening paragraph: the most important point first. Say who, what, when and where in the first one or two sentences.
  Body: more details, facts and sometimes the words of people involved.
  Ending: a final fact, what will happen next, or advice for readers.

An article is not a letter. It has no "Dear ..." and no "Yours ...". It speaks to all readers, not to one friend.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Topic: the school's clean-up day.

Headline: Pupils Clean Up School Compound
Byline: By Kweku Asare, Class 6B
Opening: On Saturday morning, more than one hundred pupils and teachers cleared rubbish and weeds from the school compound.
Body: The Environmental Club gave out gloves and brooms. "Our school looks new again," said the club president, Adwoa Sarpong.
Ending: The club plans to hold a clean-up day on the first Saturday of every month.

The headline names the event, the opening gives the main point at once, and the piece speaks to every reader.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Choose a topic: an event, a health tip, a sports result, a festival or a new discovery.
Step 2: Brainstorm the facts: who, what, when, where, why.
Step 3: Write a short headline with the key words of the topic.
Step 4: Write the opening: put the most important point in the first sentence.
Step 5: Add details in the body and finish with what happens next or a tip for readers.
Step 6: Check that there is no "Dear ..." and that any reader could understand it, then edit with a partner.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes. The article here is about inter-house athletics.

1. A headline that says nothing: "What a Day!" does not tell the reader the topic. Try: "Red House Wins Inter-House Athletics".
2. Background first: "Running is an old sport that people have enjoyed for many years" hides the news. Start with: "Red House won the inter-house athletics on Thursday."
3. A letter instead of an article: "Dear Efua, I must tell you about the athletics" speaks to one friend. An article speaks to all readers.

title: Écrire des articles sur des sujets variés
body:
Un article est écrit pour beaucoup de lecteurs, par exemple dans le magazine de l'école, au tableau d'affichage ou dans un journal comme le Junior Graphic. Les articles peuvent parler d'actualité, de santé, de sport, de culture, d'environnement, de sciences ou de technologie.

Les caractéristiques d'un article :
  Le titre : un titre court qui dit au lecteur de quoi parle l'article, avec des mots clés : "Floods Close Two Schools".
  La signature : qui l'a écrit : "By Ama Mensah, Class 6".
  Le premier paragraphe : le point le plus important d'abord. Dis qui, quoi, quand et où dans la première ou les deux premières phrases.
  Le corps : plus de détails, des faits et parfois les paroles des personnes concernées.
  La fin : un dernier fait, ce qui va se passer ensuite, ou un conseil aux lecteurs.

Un article n'est pas une lettre. Il n'a ni "Dear ..." ni "Yours ...". Il s'adresse à tous les lecteurs, pas à un seul ami.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Sujet : la journée de nettoyage de l'école.

Titre : Pupils Clean Up School Compound
Signature : By Kweku Asare, Class 6B
Début : On Saturday morning, more than one hundred pupils and teachers cleared rubbish and weeds from the school compound.
Corps : The Environmental Club gave out gloves and brooms. "Our school looks new again," said the club president, Adwoa Sarpong.
Fin : The club plans to hold a clean-up day on the first Saturday of every month.

Le titre nomme l'événement, le début donne tout de suite le point principal, et le texte s'adresse à tous les lecteurs.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Choisis un sujet : un événement, un conseil de santé, un résultat sportif, une fête ou une découverte.
Étape 2 : Note les faits : qui, quoi, quand, où, pourquoi.
Étape 3 : Écris un titre court avec les mots clés du sujet.
Étape 4 : Écris le début : mets le point le plus important dans la première phrase.
Étape 5 : Ajoute des détails dans le corps et termine par ce qui va se passer ou un conseil aux lecteurs.
Étape 6 : Vérifie qu'il n'y a pas de "Dear ..." et que n'importe quel lecteur pourrait comprendre, puis corrige avec un camarade.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes. L'article ici parle des compétitions d'athlétisme entre maisons.

1. Un titre qui ne dit rien : "What a Day!" ne dit pas au lecteur le sujet. Essaie : "Red House Wins Inter-House Athletics".
2. Le contexte d'abord : "Running is an old sport that people have enjoyed for many years" cache la nouvelle. Commence par : "Red House won the inter-house athletics on Thursday."
3. Une lettre au lieu d'un article : "Dear Efua, I must tell you about the athletics" s'adresse à une seule amie. Un article s'adresse à tous les lecteurs.

title: Write to a Friend to Give Your Views
body:
An informal letter is a letter to someone you know well, such as a friend or a cousin. When a friend asks what you think about something, you can reply with a letter that gives your view and your reasons.

Informal letter format:
  Top right: YOUR address and the date. (There is no receiver's address.)
  Greeting: Dear + first name, for example "Dear Esi,".
  Opening: a friendly line, such as asking how they are or thanking them for their letter.
  Body: the view your friend asked for, with your reasons, in a friendly tone.
  Closing: a warm ending such as "Your friend," "Your loving cousin," or "Best wishes," followed by your first name.

How a formal letter is different:
  It has two addresses: the writer's address and the receiver's address.
  It begins "Dear Sir," or "Dear Madam," and ends "Yours faithfully," with the full name.

Before writing, identify your purpose (to give the view your friend asked for) and your audience (your friend), and make a mind map of your reasons.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Kwabena's cousin Nana asked: "Do you think I should join the school choir?"

Kwabena's plan:
  Top right: his address in Sunyani and the date.
  Greeting: Dear Nana,
  Opening: Thank you for your letter. I am glad you enjoyed your holiday.
  Body: I think you should join the choir, because you have a sweet voice and the choir travels to other schools for competitions.
  Closing: Your loving cousin, Kwabena

Only his own address is at the top, the greeting and closing are friendly, and the body answers exactly the question Nana asked.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Read your friend's question again. What view do they want from you?
Step 2: Make a mind map: your view in the middle, your reasons around it.
Step 3: Write your own address and the date at the top right. Do not add your friend's address.
Step 4: Write "Dear" and your friend's first name, then a friendly opening line.
Step 5: Give your view and explain it with your reasons.
Step 6: End with a warm closing such as "Your friend," and your first name. Swap letters with another group to edit.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes. Here, your friend Selorm asked whether he should learn to play the guitar.

1. Two addresses: putting Selorm's address under yours makes it look like a formal letter. In a letter to a friend, write only your own address and the date.
2. A formal ending: "Yours faithfully, Akosua Boateng" is for letters to officials. Write "Your friend, Akosua".
3. Answering a different question: a letter all about your new school bag does not tell Selorm what you think about the guitar. Give the view he asked for.

title: Écrire à un ami pour donner son avis
body:
Une lettre informelle s'adresse à quelqu'un que tu connais bien, comme un ami ou un cousin. Quand un ami te demande ce que tu penses de quelque chose, tu peux lui répondre par une lettre qui donne ton avis et tes raisons.

Présentation d'une lettre informelle :
  En haut à droite : TON adresse et la date. (Il n'y a pas d'adresse du destinataire.)
  Formule d'appel : Dear + prénom, par exemple "Dear Esi,".
  Début : une phrase amicale, par exemple demander de ses nouvelles ou le remercier pour sa lettre.
  Corps : l'avis que ton ami a demandé, avec tes raisons, sur un ton amical.
  Formule finale : une fin chaleureuse comme "Your friend," "Your loving cousin," ou "Best wishes," suivie de ton prénom.

En quoi une lettre formelle est différente :
  Elle a deux adresses : celle de l'auteur et celle du destinataire.
  Elle commence par "Dear Sir," ou "Dear Madam," et finit par "Yours faithfully," avec le nom complet.

Avant d'écrire, identifie ton but (donner l'avis que ton ami a demandé) et ton destinataire (ton ami), et fais une carte mentale de tes raisons.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Nana, la cousine de Kwabena, lui a demandé : "Do you think I should join the school choir?"

Le plan de Kwabena :
  En haut à droite : son adresse à Sunyani et la date.
  Formule d'appel : Dear Nana,
  Début : Thank you for your letter. I am glad you enjoyed your holiday.
  Corps : I think you should join the choir, because you have a sweet voice and the choir travels to other schools for competitions.
  Formule finale : Your loving cousin, Kwabena

Seule son adresse est en haut, la formule d'appel et la formule finale sont amicales, et le corps répond exactement à la question de Nana.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Relis la question de ton ami. Quel avis veut-il de toi ?
Étape 2 : Fais une carte mentale : ton avis au milieu, tes raisons autour.
Étape 3 : Écris ton adresse et la date en haut à droite. N'ajoute pas l'adresse de ton ami.
Étape 4 : Écris "Dear" et le prénom de ton ami, puis une phrase d'ouverture amicale.
Étape 5 : Donne ton avis et explique-le avec tes raisons.
Étape 6 : Termine par une formule chaleureuse comme "Your friend," et ton prénom. Échange les lettres avec un autre groupe pour les corriger.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes. Ici, ton ami Selorm t'a demandé s'il devrait apprendre à jouer de la guitare.

1. Deux adresses : mettre l'adresse de Selorm sous la tienne donne l'air d'une lettre formelle. Dans une lettre à un ami, écris seulement ton adresse et la date.
2. Une formule finale formelle : "Yours faithfully, Akosua Boateng" sert pour les lettres aux responsables. Écris "Your friend, Akosua".
3. Répondre à une autre question : une lettre qui ne parle que de ton nouveau sac d'école ne dit pas à Selorm ce que tu penses de la guitare. Donne l'avis qu'il a demandé.

title: Follow Mechanical Conventions in a Formal Letter
body:
Mechanical conventions are the rules for capital letters and punctuation. A formal letter must follow them carefully. Check these three points in particular.

1. Direct speech: the first word of the spoken words always starts with a capital letter, even in the middle of your sentence.
   The pastor said, "Everyone is welcome on Sunday."

2. Hyphens:
   in numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine written as words: sixty-four, eighty-one;
   in ages and other compound describing words before a noun: a seven-year-old girl, a two-day workshop.

3. The salutation and closing of a formal letter:
   "Dear Sir," or "Dear Madam," followed by a comma;
   "Yours faithfully," with a capital Y, a small f, and a comma; then your signature and full name.

Remember the other marks too: a full stop at the end of a statement, a question mark after a question, an exclamation mark only for strong feeling, quotation marks around spoken words, and an apostrophe for possession or a missing letter.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
The end of Selasi's letter to the District Director, before and after checking:

Before:
  Our librarian said, "we have only sixty four books for the whole school."
  Yours Faithfully,

After:
  Our librarian said, "We have only sixty-four books for the whole school."
  Yours faithfully,

1. "We" starts the spoken words, so it needs a capital.
2. Sixty-four is a compound number, so it needs a hyphen.
3. In "Yours faithfully," only the first word has a capital.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Write your formal letter in full.
Step 2: Find every pair of quotation marks. Is the first spoken word written with a capital letter?
Step 3: Find every number written in words between twenty-one and ninety-nine. Add a hyphen.
Step 4: Find every age or compound describing word before a noun (ten-year-old, two-day). Add the hyphens.
Step 5: Check the salutation (Dear Sir,) and the closing (Yours faithfully,), with a small f and a comma.
Step 6: Check the end of every sentence: full stop, question mark or exclamation mark.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. A small letter in direct speech: My father said, "please help me." The spoken words begin with "Please", so it needs a capital P.
2. A missing hyphen: "seventy three chairs" and "a nine year old boy" should be "seventy-three chairs" and "a nine-year-old boy".
3. Capitals in the closing: "Yours Faithfully," is wrong. Only "Yours" has a capital: "Yours faithfully,"

title: Respecter les conventions d'écriture dans une lettre formelle
body:
Les conventions d'écriture sont les règles des majuscules et de la ponctuation. Une lettre formelle doit les suivre avec soin. Vérifie surtout ces trois points.

1. Le discours direct : le premier mot des paroles prononcées prend toujours une majuscule, même au milieu de ta phrase.
   The pastor said, "Everyone is welcome on Sunday."

2. Les traits d'union :
   dans les nombres de twenty-one à ninety-nine écrits en lettres : sixty-four, eighty-one ;
   dans les âges et les autres mots descriptifs composés placés avant un nom : a seven-year-old girl, a two-day workshop.

3. La formule d'appel et la formule finale d'une lettre formelle :
   "Dear Sir," ou "Dear Madam," suivi d'une virgule ;
   "Yours faithfully," avec un Y majuscule, un f minuscule et une virgule ; puis ta signature et ton nom complet.

N'oublie pas les autres signes : un point à la fin d'une affirmation, un point d'interrogation après une question, un point d'exclamation seulement pour un sentiment fort, des guillemets autour des paroles, et une apostrophe pour la possession ou une lettre manquante.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
La fin de la lettre de Selasi au directeur de district, avant et après vérification :

Avant :
  Our librarian said, "we have only sixty four books for the whole school."
  Yours Faithfully,

Après :
  Our librarian said, "We have only sixty-four books for the whole school."
  Yours faithfully,

1. "We" commence les paroles, donc il prend une majuscule.
2. Sixty-four est un nombre composé, donc il prend un trait d'union.
3. Dans "Yours faithfully," seul le premier mot prend une majuscule.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Écris ta lettre formelle en entier.
Étape 2 : Trouve chaque paire de guillemets. Le premier mot prononcé a-t-il une majuscule ?
Étape 3 : Trouve chaque nombre écrit en lettres entre twenty-one et ninety-nine. Ajoute un trait d'union.
Étape 4 : Trouve chaque âge ou mot descriptif composé avant un nom (ten-year-old, two-day). Ajoute les traits d'union.
Étape 5 : Vérifie la formule d'appel (Dear Sir,) et la formule finale (Yours faithfully,), avec un f minuscule et une virgule.
Étape 6 : Vérifie la fin de chaque phrase : point, point d'interrogation ou point d'exclamation.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Une minuscule dans le discours direct : My father said, "please help me." Les paroles commencent par "Please", donc il faut un P majuscule.
2. Un trait d'union oublié : "seventy three chairs" et "a nine year old boy" doivent devenir "seventy-three chairs" et "a nine-year-old boy".
3. Des majuscules dans la formule finale : "Yours Faithfully," est faux. Seul "Yours" prend une majuscule : "Yours faithfully,"

title: Use Commas, Quotation Marks and the Apostrophe for Plural Possession
body:
1. Commas around a describing phrase
A phrase that comes straight after a noun and tells us more about it is placed between TWO commas:
  Mr Tetteh, our music teacher, plays the organ.
If you remove the phrase, the sentence still makes sense: Mr Tetteh plays the organ.

2. Quotation marks for direct speech
Put quotation marks around ALL the words the person said, and only those words:
  "I like football," said Ama.
  Mary asked, "Kofi, do you like my pen?"
The closing quotation mark comes after the last spoken word and its punctuation.

3. The apostrophe for plural possession
When the owners are plural and the plural ends in -s, put the apostrophe AFTER the s:
  one girl's bag (one owner)   the girls' bags (many owners)
  This is girls' work.
Write the plural first (girls), then add the apostrophe (girls').

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Unpunctuated: Esi my older sister said the dancers costumes are ready

Step by step:
  "my older sister" tells us more about Esi, so it goes between two commas: Esi, my older sister,
  The words she said are "The dancers' costumes are ready." They all go inside the quotation marks, starting with a capital.
  The costumes belong to many dancers, so the apostrophe goes after the s: dancers'

Punctuated: Esi, my older sister, said, "The dancers' costumes are ready."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find any phrase that describes the noun just before it. Put a comma before it AND after it.
Step 2: Find the exact words that were spoken.
Step 3: Put an opening quotation mark before the first spoken word and a closing one after the last.
Step 4: Find any owner noun. Is there one owner or more than one?
Step 5: For more than one owner, write the plural ending in -s, then put the apostrophe after it.
Step 6: Read the sentence again and check all three.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Only one comma: "Nii, the goalkeeper caught the ball" makes it look as if someone is talking to Nii. Write: "Nii, the goalkeeper, caught the ball."
2. The apostrophe in the wrong place: "the drivers's union" and "the driver's union" (for many drivers) are wrong. Write "the drivers' union".
3. Closing the quotation marks too early: He said, "Bring" the chairs inside. All his words were spoken, so write: He said, "Bring the chairs inside."

title: Utiliser la virgule, les guillemets et l'apostrophe du pluriel possessif
body:
1. Les virgules autour d'un groupe descriptif
Un groupe de mots placé juste après un nom pour en dire plus se met entre DEUX virgules :
  Mr Tetteh, our music teacher, plays the organ.
Si on enlève le groupe, la phrase a toujours un sens : Mr Tetteh plays the organ.

2. Les guillemets pour le discours direct
Mets des guillemets autour de TOUTES les paroles prononcées, et seulement autour d'elles :
  "I like football," said Ama.
  Mary asked, "Kofi, do you like my pen?"
Le guillemet fermant vient après le dernier mot prononcé et sa ponctuation.

3. L'apostrophe du pluriel possessif
Quand les possesseurs sont au pluriel et que le pluriel finit par -s, mets l'apostrophe APRÈS le s :
  one girl's bag (un seul possesseur)   the girls' bags (plusieurs possesseurs)
  This is girls' work.
Écris d'abord le pluriel (girls), puis ajoute l'apostrophe (girls').

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Sans ponctuation : Esi my older sister said the dancers costumes are ready

Pas à pas :
  "my older sister" en dit plus sur Esi, donc il va entre deux virgules : Esi, my older sister,
  Ses paroles sont "The dancers' costumes are ready." Elles vont toutes entre les guillemets, avec une majuscule au début.
  Les costumes appartiennent à plusieurs danseurs, donc l'apostrophe va après le s : dancers'

Ponctué : Esi, my older sister, said, "The dancers' costumes are ready."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Trouve tout groupe de mots qui décrit le nom juste avant. Mets une virgule avant ET après.
Étape 2 : Trouve les paroles exactes qui ont été dites.
Étape 3 : Mets un guillemet ouvrant avant le premier mot prononcé et un guillemet fermant après le dernier.
Étape 4 : Trouve tout nom de possesseur. Y a-t-il un possesseur ou plusieurs ?
Étape 5 : S'il y en a plusieurs, écris le pluriel en -s, puis mets l'apostrophe après.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase et vérifie les trois points.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Une seule virgule : "Nii, the goalkeeper caught the ball" fait croire qu'on parle à Nii. Écris : "Nii, the goalkeeper, caught the ball."
2. L'apostrophe au mauvais endroit : "the drivers's union" et "the driver's union" (pour plusieurs chauffeurs) sont faux. Écris "the drivers' union".
3. Fermer les guillemets trop tôt : He said, "Bring" the chairs inside. Tous ces mots ont été prononcés, donc écris : He said, "Bring the chairs inside."

title: Use Noun Phrases to Describe in Writing
body:
A noun phrase is a group of words built around one noun (the head noun). The other words describe it.

Describing words can come before the noun:
  a tall mango tree   the old wooden gate
A noun can also describe another noun. It stays singular:
  a shoe shop (not a shoes shop), a bus stop, a two-hour lesson, a five-kilometre walk

Describing phrases can come after the noun:
  the boy in the blue shirt   a bag full of oranges   the woman who sells bread

Three rules for clear writing:
  1. Put the describing phrase straight after the noun it describes. "A boy rode past on a bicycle in a red cap" sounds as if the bicycle wears the cap. Write: "A boy in a red cap rode past on a bicycle."
  2. Choose a precise head noun. Avoid "thing" and "stuff": write "a torch", "a pile of firewood".
  3. Keep a noun used as a describer singular: a vegetable garden, a two-week holiday.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Kwesi's first draft: "A man sold stuff at the cars park in a big straw hat."

1. "stuff" is vague. What did he sell? "coconuts".
2. "cars park" uses a plural noun as a describer. Write "car park".
3. "in a big straw hat" describes the man, not the car park. Move it next to "man".

Revised: "A man in a big straw hat sold coconuts at the car park."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the noun you want to describe.
Step 2: Make it precise: replace thing, stuff or something with the real name.
Step 3: Add describing words before it, or a describing phrase after it.
Step 4: Check that the phrase sits right next to the noun it describes.
Step 5: If one noun describes another (a ___ shop, a ___ stop), keep the first noun singular.
Step 6: Read the sentence aloud. Could anyone picture the wrong thing?

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Phrase in the wrong place: "I gave a pencil to my friend with a sharp point" makes the friend sound sharp. Write: "I gave a pencil with a sharp point to my friend."
2. A vague noun: "She carried a heavy thing on her head" tells the reader little. Write: "She carried a heavy basin of water on her head."
3. A plural describer: "a books club" and "a three-weeks course" should be "a book club" and "a three-week course".

title: Utiliser des groupes nominaux pour décrire à l'écrit
body:
Un groupe nominal est un groupe de mots construit autour d'un nom (le nom noyau). Les autres mots le décrivent.

Les mots descriptifs peuvent venir avant le nom :
  a tall mango tree   the old wooden gate
Un nom peut aussi décrire un autre nom. Il reste au singulier :
  a shoe shop (pas a shoes shop), a bus stop, a two-hour lesson, a five-kilometre walk

Les groupes descriptifs peuvent venir après le nom :
  the boy in the blue shirt   a bag full of oranges   the woman who sells bread

Trois règles pour écrire clairement :
  1. Place le groupe descriptif juste après le nom qu'il décrit. "A boy rode past on a bicycle in a red cap" fait croire que c'est le vélo qui porte la casquette. Écris : "A boy in a red cap rode past on a bicycle."
  2. Choisis un nom noyau précis. Évite "thing" et "stuff" : écris "a torch", "a pile of firewood".
  3. Garde au singulier un nom qui en décrit un autre : a vegetable garden, a two-week holiday.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Le premier brouillon de Kwesi : "A man sold stuff at the cars park in a big straw hat."

1. "stuff" est vague. Que vendait-il ? "coconuts".
2. "cars park" utilise un nom pluriel pour décrire. Écris "car park".
3. "in a big straw hat" décrit l'homme, pas le parking. Place-le à côté de "man".

Version révisée : "A man in a big straw hat sold coconuts at the car park."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Trouve le nom que tu veux décrire.
Étape 2 : Rends-le précis : remplace thing, stuff ou something par le vrai nom.
Étape 3 : Ajoute des mots descriptifs avant lui, ou un groupe descriptif après lui.
Étape 4 : Vérifie que le groupe est juste à côté du nom qu'il décrit.
Étape 5 : Si un nom en décrit un autre (a ___ shop, a ___ stop), garde le premier nom au singulier.
Étape 6 : Lis la phrase à voix haute. Quelqu'un pourrait-il imaginer la mauvaise chose ?

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Le groupe au mauvais endroit : "I gave a pencil to my friend with a sharp point" fait croire que l'ami est pointu. Écris : "I gave a pencil with a sharp point to my friend."
2. Un nom vague : "She carried a heavy thing on her head" dit peu de chose au lecteur. Écris : "She carried a heavy basin of water on her head."
3. Un nom descriptif au pluriel : "a books club" et "a three-weeks course" doivent devenir "a book club" et "a three-week course".

title: Use Gender, Count and Plural Nouns Correctly in Writing
body:
1. Gender nouns
Some nouns have one form for a male and another for a female. Match the noun to the person or animal, and to he/his or she/her.
  king / queen   prince / princess   nephew / niece   uncle / aunt
  bridegroom / bride   lion / lioness   cock / hen   bull / cow

2. Count and non-count nouns
Count nouns can be counted: one egg, three eggs. Use many and few with them.
Non-count nouns cannot be counted one by one: water, money, rice, luggage, furniture, information, grain. Use much and little with them.
  many eggs, few chairs   but   much water, little money

3. Nouns that are always plural
Some nouns have no singular form in everyday use and always take a plural verb:
  scissors, trousers, spectacles, clothes, goods, cattle, poultry, police
  The police are here.   My trousers are torn.   The cattle were grazing.

Remember too: names of organisations and events start with capitals (Ghana Education Service, Independence Day).

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Draft sentence: "The bull licked her calf, but there was few grass, so the cattle was hungry."

1. "her calf" shows a female animal, so "bull" should be "cow".
2. "grass" is non-count, so "few" should be "little".
3. "cattle" is always plural, so "was" should be "were".

Corrected: "The cow licked her calf, but there was little grass, so the cattle were hungry."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find each noun for a person or animal. Does its gender form match he/his or she/her?
Step 2: Find each quantity word: many, few, much, little.
Step 3: Ask: can I count the noun one by one? If yes, use many or few. If no, use much or little.
Step 4: Find nouns such as scissors, trousers, clothes, goods, cattle, poultry and police.
Step 5: Check that their verbs are plural: are, were, have.
Step 6: Read the sentence again and check all three.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. The wrong gender form: "My uncle wore her best dress to church" does not match. Write "My aunt wore her best dress to church."
2. Many or few with a non-count noun: "We have many furniture" and "few information" are wrong. Write "much furniture" and "little information".
3. Always-plural nouns used as singular: "My spectacles is broken" and "The goods has arrived" are wrong. Write "My spectacles are broken" and "The goods have arrived."

title: Bien employer le genre, les noms comptables et les pluriels à l'écrit
body:
1. Les noms qui changent selon le genre
Certains noms ont une forme pour le masculin et une autre pour le féminin. Accorde le nom avec la personne ou l'animal, et avec he/his ou she/her.
  king / queen   prince / princess   nephew / niece   uncle / aunt
  bridegroom / bride   lion / lioness   cock / hen   bull / cow

2. Les noms comptables et non comptables
Les noms comptables se comptent : one egg, three eggs. On utilise many et few avec eux.
Les noms non comptables ne se comptent pas un par un : water, money, rice, luggage, furniture, information, grain. On utilise much et little avec eux.
  many eggs, few chairs   mais   much water, little money

3. Les noms toujours au pluriel
Certains noms n'ont pas de singulier dans l'usage courant et prennent toujours un verbe au pluriel :
  scissors, trousers, spectacles, clothes, goods, cattle, poultry, police
  The police are here.   My trousers are torn.   The cattle were grazing.

N'oublie pas non plus : les noms d'organisations et d'événements prennent des majuscules (Ghana Education Service, Independence Day).

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Phrase du brouillon : "The bull licked her calf, but there was few grass, so the cattle was hungry."

1. "her calf" montre un animal femelle, donc "bull" doit devenir "cow".
2. "grass" est non comptable, donc "few" doit devenir "little".
3. "cattle" est toujours au pluriel, donc "was" doit devenir "were".

Version corrigée : "The cow licked her calf, but there was little grass, so the cattle were hungry."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Trouve chaque nom de personne ou d'animal. Sa forme (masculin ou féminin) correspond-elle à he/his ou she/her ?
Étape 2 : Trouve chaque mot de quantité : many, few, much, little.
Étape 3 : Demande-toi : puis-je compter ce nom un par un ? Si oui, utilise many ou few. Sinon, utilise much ou little.
Étape 4 : Trouve les noms comme scissors, trousers, clothes, goods, cattle, poultry et police.
Étape 5 : Vérifie que leurs verbes sont au pluriel : are, were, have.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase et vérifie les trois points.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. La mauvaise forme de genre : "My uncle wore her best dress to church" ne va pas. Écris "My aunt wore her best dress to church."
2. Many ou few avec un nom non comptable : "We have many furniture" et "few information" sont faux. Écris "much furniture" et "little information".
3. Des noms toujours au pluriel traités comme singuliers : "My spectacles is broken" et "The goods has arrived" sont faux. Écris "My spectacles are broken" et "The goods have arrived."

title: Use -ing Nouns to Refer to Activities
body:
An -ing noun names an activity: I enjoy singing. I like swimming. Cooking is fun.

When you write about activities, follow three rules.

1. An -ing noun as the subject takes a singular verb, because it names one activity:
   Reading helps me relax.   Farming is hard work.   Running has made me stronger.

2. An -ing activity noun does not take -s, even if you do the activity often:
   I enjoy dancing (not dancings).   Her hobbies are painting and knitting.

3. When you mean the activity in general, do not put a or the in front:
   Gardening teaches patience. (not The gardening teaches patience.)
   I love drumming. (not I love the drumming.)

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Akosua's draft: "I love the drumming, and dancings make me happy."

1. "the drumming": she means drumming in general, so drop "the".
2. "dancings": an -ing activity noun takes no -s.
3. "make": dancing is one activity, so the verb is singular, "makes".

Corrected: "I love drumming, and dancing makes me happy."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Underline every -ing word that names an activity.
Step 2: Remove any -s you have added to it.
Step 3: If it means the activity in general, remove a or the in front of it.
Step 4: If the -ing noun is the subject, find its verb.
Step 5: Make the verb singular: is, was, has, helps, makes.
Step 6: Read your sentence aloud to check.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. A plural verb: "Jogging are good for the heart" is wrong. Jogging is one activity: "Jogging is good for the heart."
2. An -s on the activity: "My brother likes paintings and carvings" means pictures and carved objects, not the activities. For the activities, write "painting and carving".
3. An article for an activity in general: "The weaving is an old skill in Bonwire" should be "Weaving is an old skill in Bonwire."

title: Utiliser les noms en -ing pour parler d'activités
body:
Un nom en -ing désigne une activité : I enjoy singing. I like swimming. Cooking is fun.

Quand tu écris sur des activités, suis trois règles.

1. Un nom en -ing sujet prend un verbe au singulier, car il désigne une seule activité :
   Reading helps me relax.   Farming is hard work.   Running has made me stronger.

2. Un nom d'activité en -ing ne prend pas de -s, même si tu pratiques souvent l'activité :
   I enjoy dancing (pas dancings).   Her hobbies are painting and knitting.

3. Quand tu parles de l'activité en général, ne mets pas a ou the devant :
   Gardening teaches patience. (pas The gardening teaches patience.)
   I love drumming. (pas I love the drumming.)

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Le brouillon d'Akosua : "I love the drumming, and dancings make me happy."

1. "the drumming" : elle parle du tambour en général, donc enlève "the".
2. "dancings" : un nom d'activité en -ing ne prend pas de -s.
3. "make" : la danse est une seule activité, donc le verbe est au singulier, "makes".

Version corrigée : "I love drumming, and dancing makes me happy."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Souligne chaque mot en -ing qui désigne une activité.
Étape 2 : Enlève tout -s que tu as ajouté.
Étape 3 : S'il s'agit de l'activité en général, enlève a ou the devant.
Étape 4 : Si le nom en -ing est sujet, trouve son verbe.
Étape 5 : Mets le verbe au singulier : is, was, has, helps, makes.
Étape 6 : Lis ta phrase à voix haute pour vérifier.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Un verbe au pluriel : "Jogging are good for the heart" est faux. Le jogging est une seule activité : "Jogging is good for the heart."
2. Un -s sur l'activité : "My brother likes paintings and carvings" veut dire des tableaux et des objets sculptés, pas les activités. Pour les activités, écris "painting and carving".
3. Un article devant une activité en général : "The weaving is an old skill in Bonwire" doit devenir "Weaving is an old skill in Bonwire."

title: Use Abstract Nouns to Refer to Concepts and Ideas
body:
Abstract nouns name ideas, qualities and feelings that you cannot touch: intelligence, knowledge, idea, patience, honesty, courage, freedom, respect.
  I admire Ama because of her patience.
  He appears to have a good knowledge of what we are saying.

To use them well in writing:

1. Choose the noun whose meaning fits the situation. Courage is facing danger; patience is waiting calmly; honesty is telling the truth; loyalty is staying faithful to someone.

2. Use the preposition that usually follows the noun:
   knowledge of   respect for   interest in   pride in   fear of   confidence in   the right to

3. Do not confuse an abstract noun with a word that sounds the same:
   pain (hurt) / pane (the glass in a window)
   aid (help) / aide (an assistant)
   Check the meaning of any abstract noun that sounds like another word.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Draft: "Efua jumped into the river to save the child. Everyone praised her calmness and had great respect on her, even though she felt great pane in her leg."

1. Meaning: jumping into a river to save someone shows courage, not calmness.
2. Preposition: we say "respect for", not "respect on".
3. Spelling: "pane" is window glass. The abstract noun for hurt is "pain".

Revised: "Everyone praised her courage and had great respect for her, even though she felt great pain in her leg."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Think about the idea you want to name: what did the person show or feel?
Step 2: Choose the abstract noun that matches that idea exactly.
Step 3: Check the preposition after it (knowledge of, interest in, respect for, the right to).
Step 4: Check the spelling: is it the abstract noun or a word that only sounds the same?
Step 5: Read the sentence aloud and ask whether the meaning is clear.
Step 6: Use a dictionary when you are not sure.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. The wrong preposition: "She has a great interest on music" should be "a great interest in music"; "fear for snakes" should be "fear of snakes".
2. A sound-alike word: "The broken window pain let in the rain" should be "pane"; "first aide" should be "first aid".
3. A meaning that does not fit: "He told the truth even when it cost him his prize. We admired his greed." Telling the truth shows honesty, so write "We admired his honesty."

title: Utiliser des noms abstraits pour parler de notions et d'idées
body:
Les noms abstraits désignent des idées, des qualités et des sentiments qu'on ne peut pas toucher : intelligence, knowledge, idea, patience, honesty, courage, freedom, respect.
  I admire Ama because of her patience.
  He appears to have a good knowledge of what we are saying.

Pour bien les employer à l'écrit :

1. Choisis le nom dont le sens convient à la situation. Courage, c'est affronter un danger ; patience, c'est attendre calmement ; honesty, c'est dire la vérité ; loyalty, c'est rester fidèle à quelqu'un.

2. Utilise la préposition qui suit habituellement le nom :
   knowledge of   respect for   interest in   pride in   fear of   confidence in   the right to

3. Ne confonds pas un nom abstrait avec un mot qui se prononce pareil :
   pain (la douleur) / pane (la vitre d'une fenêtre)
   aid (l'aide) / aide (un assistant)
   Vérifie le sens de tout nom abstrait qui se prononce comme un autre mot.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Brouillon : "Efua jumped into the river to save the child. Everyone praised her calmness and had great respect on her, even though she felt great pane in her leg."

1. Le sens : sauter dans une rivière pour sauver quelqu'un montre du courage, pas du calme.
2. La préposition : on dit "respect for", pas "respect on".
3. L'orthographe : "pane" est une vitre. Le nom abstrait pour la douleur est "pain".

Version révisée : "Everyone praised her courage and had great respect for her, even though she felt great pain in her leg."

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Pense à l'idée que tu veux nommer : qu'est-ce que la personne a montré ou ressenti ?
Étape 2 : Choisis le nom abstrait qui correspond exactement à cette idée.
Étape 3 : Vérifie la préposition qui suit (knowledge of, interest in, respect for, the right to).
Étape 4 : Vérifie l'orthographe : est-ce le nom abstrait ou un mot qui se prononce seulement pareil ?
Étape 5 : Lis la phrase à voix haute et demande-toi si le sens est clair.
Étape 6 : Utilise un dictionnaire quand tu n'es pas sûr.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. La mauvaise préposition : "She has a great interest on music" doit devenir "a great interest in music" ; "fear for snakes" doit devenir "fear of snakes".
2. Un mot qui se prononce pareil : "The broken window pain let in the rain" doit devenir "pane" ; "first aide" doit devenir "first aid".
3. Un sens qui ne convient pas : "He told the truth even when it cost him his prize. We admired his greed." Dire la vérité montre l'honnêteté, donc écris "We admired his honesty."

title: Simple Past or Present Perfect?
body:
Simple past: an action finished at a known time in the past.
  We visited Elmina Castle last year.   When did you arrive?
Present perfect (has/have + past participle): an action linked to now, with no finished time given.
  We have visited Elmina Castle twice.   I have lived here for six years.

Three points to get right in speech and in writing:

1. Questions with "When": "When" asks about a finished time, so use the simple past.
   When did the bus leave? (not When has the bus left?)

2. For and since with the present perfect:
   for + a length of time: for two hours, for three weeks, for six years
   since + a starting point: since Monday, since 2020, since nine o'clock

3. Been and gone:
   has been to = went and has come back. "Ato has been to Ho" (he is home again).
   has gone to = went and is still there. "Ato has gone to Ho" (he is in Ho now).

title: Worked Example
body:
Abena writes a short message to her class group:
  "Grandma has gone to Bolgatanga, so she cannot come to our play. She has lived there since 2015, and she has been to Accra only once. When did you buy the tickets?"

"has gone": Grandma is still in Bolgatanga.
"since 2015": a starting point.
"has been to Accra": a visit that is over.
"When did you buy": a question about a finished time, so the simple past.

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Is the action finished at a known time (yesterday, in 2019, last week)? Use the simple past.
Step 2: Is it linked to now, with no finished time? Use has/have + past participle.
Step 3: Does your question start with "When"? Use did + base verb.
Step 4: With the present perfect, use for + a length of time, or since + a starting point.
Step 5: Is the person back from the place? Write "been". Still there? Write "gone".
Step 6: Read your sentence and check the time words again.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. "When" with the present perfect: "When have you finished your homework?" should be "When did you finish your homework?"
2. Since with a length of time: "I have waited since forty minutes" should be "for forty minutes". Since needs a starting point: "since ten o'clock".
3. Been and gone mixed up: "Dad has been to the farm; he will be back tonight" does not make sense, because Dad is still away. Write "Dad has gone to the farm."

title: Prétérit ou present perfect ?
body:
Le prétérit (simple past) : une action terminée à un moment connu du passé.
  We visited Elmina Castle last year.   When did you arrive?
Le present perfect (has/have + participe passé) : une action liée au présent, sans moment terminé précisé.
  We have visited Elmina Castle twice.   I have lived here for six years.

Trois points à bien maîtriser à l'oral et à l'écrit :

1. Les questions avec "When" : "When" interroge sur un moment terminé, donc on utilise le prétérit.
   When did the bus leave? (pas When has the bus left?)

2. For et since avec le present perfect :
   for + une durée : for two hours, for three weeks, for six years
   since + un point de départ : since Monday, since 2020, since nine o'clock

3. Been et gone :
   has been to = y est allé et en est revenu. "Ato has been to Ho" (il est de retour).
   has gone to = y est allé et y est encore. "Ato has gone to Ho" (il est à Ho maintenant).

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Abena écrit un court message au groupe de sa classe :
  "Grandma has gone to Bolgatanga, so she cannot come to our play. She has lived there since 2015, and she has been to Accra only once. When did you buy the tickets?"

"has gone" : grand-mère est encore à Bolgatanga.
"since 2015" : un point de départ.
"has been to Accra" : une visite terminée.
"When did you buy" : une question sur un moment terminé, donc le prétérit.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : L'action est-elle terminée à un moment connu (yesterday, in 2019, last week) ? Utilise le prétérit.
Étape 2 : Est-elle liée au présent, sans moment terminé ? Utilise has/have + participe passé.
Étape 3 : Ta question commence-t-elle par "When" ? Utilise did + verbe de base.
Étape 4 : Avec le present perfect, utilise for + une durée, ou since + un point de départ.
Étape 5 : La personne est-elle revenue du lieu ? Écris "been". Y est-elle encore ? Écris "gone".
Étape 6 : Relis ta phrase et vérifie encore les mots de temps.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. "When" avec le present perfect : "When have you finished your homework?" doit devenir "When did you finish your homework?"
2. Since avec une durée : "I have waited since forty minutes" doit devenir "for forty minutes". Since demande un point de départ : "since ten o'clock".
3. Been et gone confondus : "Dad has been to the farm; he will be back tonight" n'a pas de sens, car papa est encore absent. Écris "Dad has gone to the farm."

title: Simple Past Form and Participle Form
body:
Many common verbs have three different forms:
  base      simple past   past participle
  speak     spoke         spoken
  begin     began         begun
  forget    forgot        forgotten
  hide      hid           hidden
  throw     threw         thrown

Use each form in its own place:

1. The simple past stands alone: Yesterday I spoke to the headteacher.
2. The past participle needs a helper in front: has, have, had, or was/were.
   I have spoken to her.   The ball was thrown over the wall.
3. After did or did not, use the base form: Did you speak to her? I did not forget.

When you write a story about what happened, for example after school on Monday, check every verb: is it alone, after a helper, or after did?

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Part of Yaa's story, "After School on Monday", before and after editing:

Before: "I hidden my bag under the desk, but it was threw outside by the wind. I did not forgot to look for it."

After: "I hid my bag under the desk, but it was thrown outside by the wind. I did not forget to look for it."

hid: the simple past alone.
was thrown: the participle after was.
did not forget: the base form after did not.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Write your story about what happened.
Step 2: Underline every verb that tells what happened.
Step 3: If the verb stands alone, use the simple past (went, saw, ate).
Step 4: If it comes after has, have, had, was or were, use the past participle (gone, seen, eaten).
Step 5: If it comes after did or did not, use the base form (go, see, eat).
Step 6: Swap stories with a partner and check each other's verbs.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. The participle alone: "We done our chores" and "She gone home" need a helper or the simple past: "We did our chores", "She went home".
2. The simple past after a helper: "The window was broke" and "He has drove the car" should be "was broken" and "has driven".
3. A past form after did: "Did you knew the answer?" and "I did not saw him" should be "Did you know" and "I did not see".

title: La forme du prétérit et la forme du participe
body:
Beaucoup de verbes courants ont trois formes différentes :
  base      prétérit      participe passé
  speak     spoke         spoken
  begin     began         begun
  forget    forgot        forgotten
  hide      hid           hidden
  throw     threw         thrown

Utilise chaque forme à sa place :

1. Le prétérit s'emploie seul : Yesterday I spoke to the headteacher.
2. Le participe passé a besoin d'un auxiliaire devant : has, have, had, ou was/were.
   I have spoken to her.   The ball was thrown over the wall.
3. Après did ou did not, utilise la forme de base : Did you speak to her? I did not forget.

Quand tu écris une histoire sur ce qui s'est passé, par exemple après l'école lundi, vérifie chaque verbe : est-il seul, après un auxiliaire, ou après did ?

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Une partie de l'histoire de Yaa, "After School on Monday", avant et après correction :

Avant : "I hidden my bag under the desk, but it was threw outside by the wind. I did not forgot to look for it."

Après : "I hid my bag under the desk, but it was thrown outside by the wind. I did not forget to look for it."

hid : le prétérit seul.
was thrown : le participe après was.
did not forget : la forme de base après did not.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Écris ton histoire sur ce qui s'est passé.
Étape 2 : Souligne chaque verbe qui dit ce qui s'est passé.
Étape 3 : Si le verbe est seul, utilise le prétérit (went, saw, ate).
Étape 4 : S'il vient après has, have, had, was ou were, utilise le participe passé (gone, seen, eaten).
Étape 5 : S'il vient après did ou did not, utilise la forme de base (go, see, eat).
Étape 6 : Échange ton histoire avec un camarade et vérifiez les verbes l'un de l'autre.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Le participe seul : "We done our chores" et "She gone home" demandent un auxiliaire ou le prétérit : "We did our chores", "She went home".
2. Le prétérit après un auxiliaire : "The window was broke" et "He has drove the car" doivent devenir "was broken" et "has driven".
3. Une forme passée après did : "Did you knew the answer?" et "I did not saw him" doivent devenir "Did you know" et "I did not see".
