title: Use a Range of Verb Forms: the Past Perfect
body:
When you tell about two actions in the past, the past perfect (had + past participle) shows which one happened FIRST.
  When you came, I had already finished the work.
  (First: I finished the work. Later: you came.)

The later action is in the simple past. The earlier action takes had.

Three things to remember:
1. Had goes on the EARLIER action, never on the later one.
2. If there is only one past event, the simple past is enough: "Yesterday we went to church." (not "Yesterday we had gone to church.")
3. In a story about the past, use had, not has or have: "By the time the bus arrived, we had waited an hour." (not "we have waited")

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Nana narrates an event:
  "On Sunday, my cousins visited us. When they arrived, Mum had already cooked fufu, and Dad had swept the compound."

"visited" and "arrived": simple past for the main events.
"had cooked" and "had swept": these happened before the cousins arrived, so they take had.
The first sentence has only one event, so it needs no had.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: List the past actions in your sentence.
Step 2: Number them in the order they really happened.
Step 3: If there is only one action, use the simple past.
Step 4: If there are two, put had + past participle on action 1 (the earlier one).
Step 5: Put action 2 (the later one) in the simple past.
Step 6: Check that you wrote had, not has or have.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Had on the later action: "I switched off the light, and then I had gone to bed" puts had on the second action. Write: "I went to bed after I had switched off the light."
2. Had for a single event: "Last week, our class had visited the museum" has only one event. Write: "Last week, our class visited the museum."
3. Have instead of had: "When the teacher returned, the pupils have cleaned the board" should be "had cleaned".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Utiliser plusieurs formes verbales : le plus-que-parfait
body:
Quand tu racontes deux actions passées, le plus-que-parfait (had + participe passé) montre laquelle s'est passée EN PREMIER.
  When you came, I had already finished the work.
  (D'abord : j'ai fini le travail. Ensuite : tu es venu.)

L'action la plus récente est au prétérit. L'action la plus ancienne prend had.

Trois choses à retenir :
1. Had va sur l'action la PLUS ANCIENNE, jamais sur la plus récente.
2. S'il n'y a qu'un seul événement passé, le prétérit suffit : "Yesterday we went to church." (pas "Yesterday we had gone to church.")
3. Dans une histoire au passé, utilise had, pas has ni have : "By the time the bus arrived, we had waited an hour." (pas "we have waited")

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Nana raconte un événement :
  "On Sunday, my cousins visited us. When they arrived, Mum had already cooked fufu, and Dad had swept the compound."

"visited" et "arrived" : le prétérit pour les événements principaux.
"had cooked" et "had swept" : ces actions ont eu lieu avant l'arrivée des cousins, donc elles prennent had.
La première phrase n'a qu'un seul événement, donc elle n'a pas besoin de had.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Note les actions passées de ta phrase.
Étape 2 : Numérote-les dans l'ordre où elles se sont vraiment passées.
Étape 3 : S'il n'y a qu'une action, utilise le prétérit.
Étape 4 : S'il y en a deux, mets had + participe passé sur l'action 1 (la plus ancienne).
Étape 5 : Mets l'action 2 (la plus récente) au prétérit.
Étape 6 : Vérifie que tu as écrit had, et pas has ni have.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Had sur l'action la plus récente : "I switched off the light, and then I had gone to bed" met had sur la deuxième action. Écris : "I went to bed after I had switched off the light."
2. Had pour un seul événement : "Last week, our class had visited the museum" n'a qu'un seul événement. Écris : "Last week, our class visited the museum."
3. Have au lieu de had : "When the teacher returned, the pupils have cleaned the board" doit devenir "had cleaned".

title: Match Subjects and Verbs in Every Tense
body:
The verb must agree with its subject in the simple present and the present perfect:
  simple present: he/she/it or one person: plays, is   |   plural: play, are
  present perfect: singular: has played   |   plural: have played
  past perfect: had played for every subject.

Three subjects that often cause mistakes:

1. Two subjects joined by "and" make a plural subject:
   Akua and her brother walk to school.   My uncle and my aunt have built a house.

2. An amount of money, time or distance is treated as ONE thing, so it takes a singular verb:
   Five hundred cedis is a lot of money.   Three hours is a long journey.   Ten kilometres is too far to walk.

3. Irregular plurals have no -s but are still plural:
   children, people, men, women, teeth, feet, mice, geese
   The children have gone home.   People are waiting.   My teeth hurt.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Mensah's essay, "Our Market Day", before and after editing:

Before: "My mother and my sister sells tomatoes. Two hours are the time it takes to set up. The people has already arrived by eight."

After: "My mother and my sister sell tomatoes. Two hours is the time it takes to set up. The people have already arrived by eight."

1. "My mother and my sister": two subjects joined by and, so "sell".
2. "Two hours": one amount of time, so "is".
3. "people": an irregular plural, so "have".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the subject of each verb.
Step 2: Does the subject have two parts joined by "and"? Use a plural verb (are, have, play).
Step 3: Is the subject an amount of money, time or distance? Use a singular verb (is, has, takes).
Step 4: Is the subject an irregular plural such as children, people, men, women or teeth? Use a plural verb.
Step 5: In the past perfect, use had for every subject.
Step 6: Read each sentence again with its subject and verb together.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. "And" with a singular verb: "Kwame and Yaw has finished the poster" should be "have finished".
2. An amount with a plural verb: "Forty minutes are enough for the test" should be "Forty minutes is enough".
3. An irregular plural with a singular verb: "The geese walks to the pond every morning" should be "The geese walk"; "The men has left" should be "The men have left".

title: Accorder le sujet et le verbe à tous les temps
body:
Le verbe doit s'accorder avec son sujet au présent simple et au present perfect :
  présent simple : he/she/it ou une seule personne : plays, is   |   pluriel : play, are
  present perfect : singulier : has played   |   pluriel : have played
  plus-que-parfait : had played pour tous les sujets.

Trois sujets qui causent souvent des erreurs :

1. Deux sujets reliés par "and" forment un sujet pluriel :
   Akua and her brother walk to school.   My uncle and my aunt have built a house.

2. Une somme d'argent, une durée ou une distance est traitée comme UNE seule chose, donc elle prend un verbe au singulier :
   Five hundred cedis is a lot of money.   Three hours is a long journey.   Ten kilometres is too far to walk.

3. Les pluriels irréguliers n'ont pas de -s mais restent au pluriel :
   children, people, men, women, teeth, feet, mice, geese
   The children have gone home.   People are waiting.   My teeth hurt.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
La rédaction de Mensah, "Our Market Day", avant et après correction :

Avant : "My mother and my sister sells tomatoes. Two hours are the time it takes to set up. The people has already arrived by eight."

Après : "My mother and my sister sell tomatoes. Two hours is the time it takes to set up. The people have already arrived by eight."

1. "My mother and my sister" : deux sujets reliés par and, donc "sell".
2. "Two hours" : une seule durée, donc "is".
3. "people" : un pluriel irrégulier, donc "have".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Trouve le sujet de chaque verbe.
Étape 2 : Le sujet a-t-il deux parties reliées par "and" ? Utilise un verbe au pluriel (are, have, play).
Étape 3 : Le sujet est-il une somme d'argent, une durée ou une distance ? Utilise un verbe au singulier (is, has, takes).
Étape 4 : Le sujet est-il un pluriel irrégulier comme children, people, men, women ou teeth ? Utilise un verbe au pluriel.
Étape 5 : Au plus-que-parfait, utilise had pour tous les sujets.
Étape 6 : Relis chaque phrase en regardant ensemble le sujet et le verbe.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. "And" avec un verbe au singulier : "Kwame and Yaw has finished the poster" doit devenir "have finished".
2. Une quantité avec un verbe au pluriel : "Forty minutes are enough for the test" doit devenir "Forty minutes is enough".
3. Un pluriel irrégulier avec un verbe au singulier : "The geese walks to the pond every morning" doit devenir "The geese walk" ; "The men has left" doit devenir "The men have left".

title: Use Superlatives to Compare
body:
We use the superlative to compare one person or thing with all the others in a group of three or more.

Regular adjectives:
  short words add -est: tall, taller, the tallest   |   big, bigger, the biggest   |   happy, happier, the happiest
  long words use most: careful, more careful, the most careful
Irregular adjectives:
  good, better, the best   |   bad, worse, the worst   |   many/much, more, the most   |   little, less, the least   |   far, farther, the farthest

Three rules for writing superlatives:
1. Two people or things: use the comparative (Kofi is taller than Ama).
   Three or more: use the superlative (Kofi is the tallest boy in the team).
2. Put "the" before the superlative: the best player, the most useful tool.
3. After a superlative, use "in" before a place or group (the tallest in the class)
   and "of" before a number or "all" (the oldest of the four, the best of all).
   Do not use "than" after a superlative.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Adjoa's description, "Our Family Stalls", before and after editing:

Before: "Grandma's stall is bigger of all the stalls. Uncle Kojo sells best yams in Techiman. His yams are the cheapest than everyone else's."

After: "Grandma's stall is the biggest of all the stalls. Uncle Kojo sells the best yams in Techiman. His yams are the cheapest in the market."

1. "of all the stalls": many stalls are compared, so the superlative "the biggest".
2. "best yams": a superlative needs "the", so "the best yams" (best is the irregular superlative of good).
3. "the cheapest than": a superlative is followed by in or of, so "the cheapest in the market".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Count how many people or things are being compared.
Step 2: Two? Use the comparative with than. Three or more? Use the superlative.
Step 3: Form the superlative: -est for short words, most for long words, or the irregular form (best, worst, most, least, farthest).
Step 4: Put "the" in front of the superlative.
Step 5: After the superlative, use in before a place or group, or of before a number or "all". Never use than.
Step 6: Read the sentence again to check all three points.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. A comparative for a whole group: "Esi is cleverer of all the girls" should be "Esi is the cleverest of all the girls".
2. No "the": "He told funniest joke at the party" should be "He told the funniest joke at the party".
3. "Than" after a superlative: "This is the longest bridge than the others" should be "This is the longest bridge in the region".

title: Utiliser le superlatif pour comparer
body:
On utilise le superlatif pour comparer une personne ou une chose à toutes les autres d'un groupe de trois ou plus.

Adjectifs réguliers :
  mots courts, on ajoute -est : tall, taller, the tallest   |   big, bigger, the biggest   |   happy, happier, the happiest
  mots longs, on utilise most : careful, more careful, the most careful
Adjectifs irréguliers :
  good, better, the best   |   bad, worse, the worst   |   many/much, more, the most   |   little, less, the least   |   far, farther, the farthest

Trois règles pour écrire le superlatif :
1. Deux personnes ou deux choses : utilise le comparatif (Kofi is taller than Ama).
   Trois ou plus : utilise le superlatif (Kofi is the tallest boy in the team).
2. Mets "the" devant le superlatif : the best player, the most useful tool.
3. Après un superlatif, utilise "in" devant un lieu ou un groupe (the tallest in the class)
   et "of" devant un nombre ou "all" (the oldest of the four, the best of all).
   N'utilise pas "than" après un superlatif.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
La description d'Adjoa, "Our Family Stalls", avant et après correction :

Avant : "Grandma's stall is bigger of all the stalls. Uncle Kojo sells best yams in Techiman. His yams are the cheapest than everyone else's."

Après : "Grandma's stall is the biggest of all the stalls. Uncle Kojo sells the best yams in Techiman. His yams are the cheapest in the market."

1. "of all the stalls" : on compare beaucoup d'étals, donc le superlatif "the biggest".
2. "best yams" : un superlatif a besoin de "the", donc "the best yams" (best est le superlatif irrégulier de good).
3. "the cheapest than" : un superlatif est suivi de in ou of, donc "the cheapest in the market".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Compte combien de personnes ou de choses sont comparées.
Étape 2 : Deux ? Utilise le comparatif avec than. Trois ou plus ? Utilise le superlatif.
Étape 3 : Forme le superlatif : -est pour les mots courts, most pour les mots longs, ou la forme irrégulière (best, worst, most, least, farthest).
Étape 4 : Mets "the" devant le superlatif.
Étape 5 : Après le superlatif, utilise in devant un lieu ou un groupe, ou of devant un nombre ou "all". N'utilise jamais than.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase pour vérifier ces trois points.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Un comparatif pour tout un groupe : "Esi is cleverer of all the girls" doit devenir "Esi is the cleverest of all the girls".
2. Pas de "the" : "He told funniest joke at the party" doit devenir "He told the funniest joke at the party".
3. "Than" après un superlatif : "This is the longest bridge than the others" doit devenir "This is the longest bridge in the region".

title: Show Degree and Reason
body:
Adverbs of degree tell us how much: very, so, such, quite, rather, extremely, almost.
Adverbs and linking words of reason tell us why: because, since, as, that is why.

Three rules for writing them:

1. "So" or "such"?
   so + an adjective or adverb on its own: so hot, so kind, so quickly (also so many, so much)
   such + (a/an) + adjective + noun: such a hot day, such kind people
   Both can be followed by "that" and a result: The water was so cold that we shivered.

2. "Very" goes before an adjective or an adverb (very tall, very slowly), not before a verb.
   With a verb, put "very much" after the verb or its object: We like music very much.
   (You may also say "really" before a verb: We really like music.)

3. "Because" goes before the REASON, the part that answers "Why?":
   The road was closed because a tree had fallen.   (Why was it closed? A tree had fallen.)

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Kojo's paragraph, "Our Sports Day", before and after editing:

Before: "It was so a hot afternoon. We very enjoyed the races. Our team won the cup because we celebrated loudly."

After: "It was such a hot afternoon. We enjoyed the races very much. We celebrated loudly because our team won the cup."

1. "a hot afternoon" is a noun phrase, so "such a hot afternoon".
2. "enjoyed" is a verb, so "very much" goes after "the races".
3. Winning the cup is the reason for celebrating, so "because" goes before "our team won the cup".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find each word that shows degree (so, such, very) and each word that shows reason (because).
Step 2: After so, is there only an adjective or adverb? Keep so. Is there a noun? Use such.
Step 3: Is very in front of a verb? Move it: put very much after the verb or its object.
Step 4: For because, ask "Why?" about the other part of the sentence.
Step 5: The answer to "Why?" must come straight after because.
Step 6: Read the sentence again to check that it makes sense.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. So and such mixed up: "so a big crowd" should be "such a big crowd"; "such noisy" should be "so noisy".
2. Very before a verb: "She very loves her grandmother" should be "She loves her grandmother very much".
3. Because before the result: "Our team won the match because we were happy" should be "We were happy because our team won the match".

title: Exprimer le degré et la cause
body:
Les adverbes de degré indiquent à quel point : very, so, such, quite, rather, extremely, almost.
Les adverbes et les mots de liaison de cause indiquent pourquoi : because, since, as, that is why.

Trois règles pour les écrire :

1. "So" ou "such" ?
   so + un adjectif ou un adverbe seul : so hot, so kind, so quickly (et aussi so many, so much)
   such + (a/an) + adjectif + nom : such a hot day, such kind people
   Les deux peuvent être suivis de "that" et d'une conséquence : The water was so cold that we shivered.

2. "Very" se place devant un adjectif ou un adverbe (very tall, very slowly), pas devant un verbe.
   Avec un verbe, mets "very much" après le verbe ou son complément : We like music very much.
   (On peut aussi dire "really" devant un verbe : We really like music.)

3. "Because" se place devant la CAUSE, la partie qui répond à "Pourquoi ?" :
   The road was closed because a tree had fallen.   (Pourquoi la route était-elle fermée ? Un arbre était tombé.)

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Le paragraphe de Kojo, "Our Sports Day", avant et après correction :

Avant : "It was so a hot afternoon. We very enjoyed the races. Our team won the cup because we celebrated loudly."

Après : "It was such a hot afternoon. We enjoyed the races very much. We celebrated loudly because our team won the cup."

1. "a hot afternoon" est un groupe nominal, donc "such a hot afternoon".
2. "enjoyed" est un verbe, donc "very much" se place après "the races".
3. Gagner la coupe est la cause de la fête, donc "because" se place devant "our team won the cup".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Trouve chaque mot qui indique le degré (so, such, very) et chaque mot qui indique la cause (because).
Étape 2 : Après so, y a-t-il seulement un adjectif ou un adverbe ? Garde so. Y a-t-il un nom ? Utilise such.
Étape 3 : Very est-il devant un verbe ? Déplace-le : mets very much après le verbe ou son complément.
Étape 4 : Pour because, pose la question "Pourquoi ?" sur l'autre partie de la phrase.
Étape 5 : La réponse à "Pourquoi ?" doit venir juste après because.
Étape 6 : Relis la phrase pour vérifier qu'elle a du sens.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. So et such confondus : "so a big crowd" doit devenir "such a big crowd" ; "such noisy" doit devenir "so noisy".
2. Very devant un verbe : "She very loves her grandmother" doit devenir "She loves her grandmother very much".
3. Because devant la conséquence : "Our team won the match because we were happy" doit devenir "We were happy because our team won the match".

title: Prepositions for Comparison, Support and Means
body:
Prepositions show how words are linked. Three groups are often mixed up in writing.

1. Comparison
   A comparative is followed by than: taller than, older than, more useful than.
   Some words take their own preposition:
     prefer something TO something else      similar TO      different FROM      the same AS

2. Support or opposition
   for = on the side of, supporting:   We voted for Ama.   The crowd cheered for the home team.
   against = opposing:   Ten pupils voted against the plan.   We must fight against malaria.

3. Means (how something is done)
   by + a way of travelling or sending, with no "a" or "the": by bus, by car, by phone, by post, by hand
   (but: on foot)
   with + a tool or thing you hold or use: with a knife, with a pen, with a hoe, with our hands

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Esi's report, "Our Class Election", before and after editing:

Before: "Most of us voted against Kwame because we wanted him as prefect. We marked our papers by pencils. Kwame's speech was similar with Ama's, but I preferred his speech than hers."

After: "Most of us voted for Kwame because we wanted him as prefect. We marked our papers with pencils. Kwame's speech was similar to Ama's, but I preferred his speech to hers."

1. The pupils wanted Kwame, so they voted for him, not against him.
2. A pencil is a tool you hold, so "with pencils".
3. "similar" takes to, and "prefer" takes to.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find each preposition in your sentence.
Step 2: Is it a comparison? After a comparative, use than. After prefer and similar, use to; after different, use from; after the same, use as.
Step 3: Is it about supporting or opposing? Use for to support and against to oppose. Check that it matches the rest of the sentence.
Step 4: Is it about how something is done? Use by for travel or sending (by bus, by phone) and with for a tool (with a knife).
Step 5: Read the sentence again and ask: does the preposition give the meaning I want?

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. The wrong word in a comparison: "Yams are different than cocoyams" should be "Yams are different from cocoyams"; "I prefer football than ampe" should be "I prefer football to ampe".
2. For and against mixed up: "The chief spoke against the new clinic because he wanted it built" should be "spoke for the new clinic".
3. By and with mixed up: "She sent the money with phone" should be "by phone"; "He opened the tin by a spoon" should be "with a spoon".

title: Les prépositions de comparaison, de soutien ou d'opposition et de moyen
body:
Les prépositions montrent comment les mots sont reliés. Trois groupes sont souvent confondus à l'écrit.

1. La comparaison
   Un comparatif est suivi de than : taller than, older than, more useful than.
   Certains mots ont leur propre préposition :
     prefer something TO something else      similar TO      different FROM      the same AS

2. Le soutien ou l'opposition
   for = du côté de, pour soutenir :   We voted for Ama.   The crowd cheered for the home team.
   against = contre :   Ten pupils voted against the plan.   We must fight against malaria.

3. Le moyen (comment on fait quelque chose)
   by + un moyen de transport ou d'envoi, sans "a" ni "the" : by bus, by car, by phone, by post, by hand
   (mais : on foot)
   with + un outil ou une chose qu'on tient ou qu'on utilise : with a knife, with a pen, with a hoe, with our hands

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Le compte rendu d'Esi, "Our Class Election", avant et après correction :

Avant : "Most of us voted against Kwame because we wanted him as prefect. We marked our papers by pencils. Kwame's speech was similar with Ama's, but I preferred his speech than hers."

Après : "Most of us voted for Kwame because we wanted him as prefect. We marked our papers with pencils. Kwame's speech was similar to Ama's, but I preferred his speech to hers."

1. Les élèves voulaient Kwame, donc ils ont voté pour lui (for), pas contre lui (against).
2. Un crayon est un outil qu'on tient, donc "with pencils".
3. "similar" se construit avec to, et "prefer" aussi.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Trouve chaque préposition dans ta phrase.
Étape 2 : Est-ce une comparaison ? Après un comparatif, utilise than. Après prefer et similar, utilise to ; après different, utilise from ; après the same, utilise as.
Étape 3 : S'agit-il de soutenir ou de s'opposer ? Utilise for pour soutenir et against pour s'opposer. Vérifie que cela va avec le reste de la phrase.
Étape 4 : S'agit-il de la façon de faire quelque chose ? Utilise by pour voyager ou envoyer (by bus, by phone) et with pour un outil (with a knife).
Étape 5 : Relis la phrase et demande-toi : la préposition donne-t-elle le sens que je veux ?

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Le mauvais mot dans une comparaison : "Yams are different than cocoyams" doit devenir "Yams are different from cocoyams" ; "I prefer football than ampe" doit devenir "I prefer football to ampe".
2. For et against confondus : "The chief spoke against the new clinic because he wanted it built" doit devenir "spoke for the new clinic".
3. By et with confondus : "She sent the money with phone" doit devenir "by phone" ; "He opened the tin by a spoon" doit devenir "with a spoon".

title: Conjunctions for Purpose, Time and Condition
body:
Conjunctions join a clause to the rest of the sentence:
  purpose: so that        time: when, while, as soon as, before, after        condition: if, unless

Three rules for writing them:

1. Talking about the future: after when, while, as soon as, if and unless, use the PRESENT tense.
   Will goes only in the other clause.
   When the bell rings, we will go out.   If it rains, the match will be cancelled.

2. "Unless" already means "if not". Do not add another "not" after it.
   Unless you hurry, you will be late.   (= If you do not hurry, you will be late.)

3. "So that" shows PURPOSE: why someone does something on purpose. It is usually followed by can, could, will or would.
   She saved her money so that she could buy a bicycle.
   "So" (often after a comma) shows a RESULT: what happened because of something.
   It rained heavily, so the match was cancelled.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Ato's story, "The Football Match", before and after editing:

Before: "If the rain will stop, we will play. Unless we do not finish our homework, Mother will not let us go. The ball was flat so that we borrowed one."

After: "If the rain stops, we will play. Unless we finish our homework, Mother will not let us go. The ball was flat, so we borrowed one."

1. "If the rain will stop" talks about the future after if, so the present tense: "If the rain stops".
2. "Unless we do not finish" has two negatives; unless already means if not, so "Unless we finish".
3. Borrowing a ball is a result of the flat ball, not a purpose, so ", so we borrowed one".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the conjunction and the clause that comes after it.
Step 2: Is it if, when, while, as soon as or unless about the future? Use the present tense in that clause; keep will for the other clause.
Step 3: Is it unless? Make sure there is no extra not after it. Test it by saying "if ... not" instead.
Step 4: Is it so that? Ask: did someone do this on purpose? If not, it is a result, so use so.
Step 5: Read the sentence again to check the meaning.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Will after if or when: "As soon as Papa will come home, we will eat" should be "As soon as Papa comes home, we will eat".
2. Not after unless: "Unless you do not rest, your leg will not heal" should be "Unless you rest, your leg will not heal".
3. So that for a result: "The tap broke so that the kitchen floor got wet" should be "The tap broke, so the kitchen floor got wet".

title: Les conjonctions de but, de temps et de condition
body:
Les conjonctions relient une proposition au reste de la phrase :
  but : so that        temps : when, while, as soon as, before, after        condition : if, unless

Trois règles pour les écrire :

1. Pour parler du futur : après when, while, as soon as, if et unless, utilise le PRÉSENT.
   Will se place seulement dans l'autre proposition.
   When the bell rings, we will go out.   If it rains, the match will be cancelled.

2. "Unless" veut déjà dire "if not" (si... ne... pas). N'ajoute pas un autre "not" après.
   Unless you hurry, you will be late.   (= If you do not hurry, you will be late.)

3. "So that" exprime le BUT : pourquoi quelqu'un fait quelque chose exprès. Il est souvent suivi de can, could, will ou would.
   She saved her money so that she could buy a bicycle.
   "So" (souvent après une virgule) exprime une CONSÉQUENCE : ce qui s'est passé à cause de quelque chose.
   It rained heavily, so the match was cancelled.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
L'histoire d'Ato, "The Football Match", avant et après correction :

Avant : "If the rain will stop, we will play. Unless we do not finish our homework, Mother will not let us go. The ball was flat so that we borrowed one."

Après : "If the rain stops, we will play. Unless we finish our homework, Mother will not let us go. The ball was flat, so we borrowed one."

1. "If the rain will stop" parle du futur après if, donc on utilise le présent : "If the rain stops".
2. "Unless we do not finish" contient deux négations ; unless veut déjà dire if not, donc "Unless we finish".
3. Emprunter un ballon est une conséquence du ballon dégonflé, pas un but, donc ", so we borrowed one".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Trouve la conjonction et la proposition qui la suit.
Étape 2 : Est-ce if, when, while, as soon as ou unless pour parler du futur ? Utilise le présent dans cette proposition ; garde will pour l'autre proposition.
Étape 3 : Est-ce unless ? Vérifie qu'il n'y a pas de not en trop après. Vérifie en utilisant "if ... not" à la place.
Étape 4 : Est-ce so that ? Demande-toi : quelqu'un a-t-il fait cela exprès ? Sinon, c'est une conséquence, donc utilise so.
Étape 5 : Relis la phrase pour vérifier le sens.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Will après if ou when : "As soon as Papa will come home, we will eat" doit devenir "As soon as Papa comes home, we will eat".
2. Not après unless : "Unless you do not rest, your leg will not heal" doit devenir "Unless you rest, your leg will not heal".
3. So that pour une conséquence : "The tap broke so that the kitchen floor got wet" doit devenir "The tap broke, so the kitchen floor got wet".

title: Find the Subject and Verb in a Complex Sentence
body:
A complex sentence has:
  a MAIN clause, which makes sense on its own, and
  a SUBORDINATE clause, which begins with a word such as when, because, although, if, as, since, after or who,
  and cannot stand alone.

  When the bell rang,   |   the pupils ran out.
  subordinate clause         main clause

The subject of the sentence is the subject of the MAIN clause: the person or thing that does the main verb.
The main verb is the verb of the main clause that shows the tense (ran, is, has started, will go).

Three things to remember:
1. The subject and verb after when, because, although, if or who belong to the subordinate clause, not the main clause.
2. The noun just before the verb is not always the subject. It may belong to a phrase (the man in the red cap)
   or to a who-clause. Ask: who or what does the action?
3. A verb ending in -ing on its own, or a to-form (to play, to see), is not the main verb.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Kofi edits a sentence from his account of a school trip:

"After the bell rang, the pupils in Basic 6 hurried to collect their books."

1. Subordinate clause: "After the bell rang". Its subject (the bell) and verb (rang) are NOT the main ones.
2. Main clause: "the pupils in Basic 6 hurried to collect their books".
3. Who hurried? The pupils, not "Basic 6", which is only part of the phrase "in Basic 6".
4. "to collect" is a to-form, so it is not the main verb. The main verb is "hurried".

Subject: the pupils. Main verb: hurried.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Find the joining word (when, because, although, if, as, since, who...).
Step 2: Mark the subordinate clause that it begins. Put it aside.
Step 3: What is left is the main clause. It must make sense on its own.
Step 4: In the main clause, find the verb that shows the tense. Skip -ing words on their own and to-forms.
Step 5: Ask "Who or what" + the verb. The answer is the subject. Skip nouns that belong to phrases like "of the..." or "in the...".
Step 6: Check: subject + main verb should make a short sentence (The pupils hurried.).

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Choosing the subordinate clause: in "Since the shop was closed, my aunt bought bread at the station", the main subject is not "the shop" but "my aunt", and the main verb is "bought".
2. Choosing the nearest noun: in "The pen with the gold top belongs to Sena", the subject is "the pen", not "the gold top".
3. Choosing an -ing or to-form: in "Feeling hungry, the goats began to eat the fence", the main verb is "began", not "feeling" or "to eat".

title: Trouver le sujet et le verbe dans une phrase complexe
body:
Une phrase complexe contient :
  une proposition PRINCIPALE, qui a du sens toute seule, et
  une proposition SUBORDONNÉE, qui commence par un mot comme when, because, although, if, as, since, after ou who,
  et qui ne peut pas former une phrase complète à elle seule.

  When the bell rang,   |   the pupils ran out.
  proposition subordonnée     proposition principale

Le sujet de la phrase est le sujet de la proposition PRINCIPALE : la personne ou la chose qui fait l'action du verbe principal.
Le verbe principal est le verbe de la proposition principale qui montre le temps (ran, is, has started, will go).

Trois choses à retenir :
1. Le sujet et le verbe qui suivent when, because, although, if ou who appartiennent à la subordonnée, pas à la principale.
2. Le nom juste devant le verbe n'est pas toujours le sujet. Il peut faire partie d'un groupe (the man in the red cap)
   ou d'une proposition avec who. Demande-toi : qui ou quoi fait l'action ?
3. Un verbe en -ing tout seul, ou une forme avec to (to play, to see), n'est pas le verbe principal.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Kofi corrige une phrase de son récit d'une sortie scolaire :

"After the bell rang, the pupils in Basic 6 hurried to collect their books."

1. Proposition subordonnée : "After the bell rang". Son sujet (the bell) et son verbe (rang) ne sont PAS les principaux.
2. Proposition principale : "the pupils in Basic 6 hurried to collect their books".
3. Qui s'est dépêché ? The pupils, pas "Basic 6", qui fait seulement partie du groupe "in Basic 6".
4. "to collect" est une forme avec to, donc ce n'est pas le verbe principal. Le verbe principal est "hurried".

Sujet : the pupils. Verbe principal : hurried.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Trouve le mot de liaison (when, because, although, if, as, since, who...).
Étape 2 : Repère la proposition subordonnée qu'il introduit. Mets-la de côté.
Étape 3 : Ce qui reste est la proposition principale. Elle doit avoir du sens toute seule.
Étape 4 : Dans la proposition principale, trouve le verbe qui montre le temps. Ignore les mots en -ing seuls et les formes avec to.
Étape 5 : Pose la question "Qui ou quoi" + le verbe. La réponse est le sujet. Ignore les noms qui font partie de groupes comme "of the..." ou "in the...".
Étape 6 : Vérifie : sujet + verbe principal doivent former une petite phrase (The pupils hurried.).

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Choisir la subordonnée : dans "Since the shop was closed, my aunt bought bread at the station", le sujet principal n'est pas "the shop" mais "my aunt", et le verbe principal est "bought".
2. Choisir le nom le plus proche : dans "The pen with the gold top belongs to Sena", le sujet est "the pen", pas "the gold top".
3. Choisir une forme en -ing ou avec to : dans "Feeling hungry, the goats began to eat the fence", le verbe principal est "began", pas "feeling" ni "to eat".

title: Build Complex Sentences
body:
A compound sentence joins two main clauses with and, but, so or or.
A complex sentence joins a main clause to a subordinate clause with a word such as:
  because, as, since (reason)      although, even though (contrast)      when, after, before, until (time)      if, unless (condition)
  who, which, that (to describe a noun)

Changing compound sentences into complex ones:
  It was raining, but we went to school.        ->  Although it was raining, we went to school.
  Kofi was hungry, so he ate the bread.          ->  Because Kofi was hungry, he ate the bread.
  The woman sells kenkey. She lives next door.   ->  The woman who lives next door sells kenkey.

Three rules:
1. Choose the joining word that shows the right link: reason, contrast, time or condition.
2. When the subordinate clause comes FIRST, put a comma after it: When the rain stopped, we went out.
   Without the comma, the reader may join the wrong words together.
3. To describe a noun, use who (people), which (things) or that (both). Never use "what":
   say "the bag that I bought", not "the bag what I bought".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Akua changes three sentences from her story, "Market Day", into complex sentences:

1. "The sun was hot, but we walked to the market."
   Contrast, so although, with a comma after the first clause: "Although the sun was hot, we walked to the market."
2. "We met a trader. She sells beads."
   The trader is a person, so: "We met a trader who sells beads."
3. "I chose a necklace. It had blue beads."
   The necklace is a thing, so: "I chose a necklace which had blue beads." (or "that had blue beads", never "what had").

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Read the two ideas you want to join.
Step 2: Decide how they are linked: reason, contrast, time, condition, or describing a noun.
Step 3: Choose the joining word: because for a reason, although for a contrast, when or until for time, if for a condition.
Step 4: To describe a noun, use who for a person and which for a thing or animal (or that for either). Never what.
Step 5: Put the subordinate clause before or after the main clause. If it comes first, put a comma after it.
Step 6: Read the new sentence aloud and check that it means the same as the two ideas.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. A joining word with the wrong meaning: "Because the river was deep, the boys swam across easily" shows contrast, so it should be "Although the river was deep, ...".
2. No comma after a clause that comes first: "Before we ate the goat ran off" should be "Before we ate, the goat ran off".
3. What as a describing word: "the radio what my father repaired" should be "the radio that my father repaired".

title: Construire des phrases complexes
body:
Une phrase composée relie deux propositions principales avec and, but, so ou or.
Une phrase complexe relie une proposition principale à une subordonnée avec un mot comme :
  because, as, since (cause)      although, even though (opposition)      when, after, before, until (temps)      if, unless (condition)
  who, which, that (pour décrire un nom)

Transformer des phrases composées en phrases complexes :
  It was raining, but we went to school.        ->  Although it was raining, we went to school.
  Kofi was hungry, so he ate the bread.          ->  Because Kofi was hungry, he ate the bread.
  The woman sells kenkey. She lives next door.   ->  The woman who lives next door sells kenkey.

Trois règles :
1. Choisis le mot de liaison qui montre le bon lien : cause, opposition, temps ou condition.
2. Quand la subordonnée vient EN PREMIER, mets une virgule après elle : When the rain stopped, we went out.
   Sans la virgule, le lecteur risque de relier les mauvais mots entre eux.
3. Pour décrire un nom, utilise who (personnes), which (choses) ou that (les deux). N'utilise jamais "what" :
   dis "the bag that I bought", pas "the bag what I bought".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Akua transforme trois phrases de son histoire, "Market Day", en phrases complexes :

1. "The sun was hot, but we walked to the market."
   Opposition, donc although, avec une virgule après la première proposition : "Although the sun was hot, we walked to the market."
2. "We met a trader. She sells beads."
   La commerçante est une personne, donc : "We met a trader who sells beads."
3. "I chose a necklace. It had blue beads."
   Le collier est une chose, donc : "I chose a necklace which had blue beads." (ou "that had blue beads", jamais "what had").

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Lis les deux idées que tu veux relier.
Étape 2 : Décide quel est le lien : cause, opposition, temps, condition, ou description d'un nom.
Étape 3 : Choisis le mot de liaison : because pour une cause, although pour une opposition, when ou until pour le temps, if pour une condition.
Étape 4 : Pour décrire un nom, utilise who pour une personne et which pour une chose ou un animal (ou that pour les deux). Jamais what.
Étape 5 : Place la subordonnée avant ou après la principale. Si elle vient en premier, mets une virgule après.
Étape 6 : Lis la nouvelle phrase à voix haute et vérifie qu'elle a le même sens que les deux idées.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Un mot de liaison au mauvais sens : "Because the river was deep, the boys swam across easily" exprime une opposition, donc il faut "Although the river was deep, ...".
2. Pas de virgule après une proposition placée en premier : "Before we ate the goat ran off" doit devenir "Before we ate, the goat ran off".
3. What pour décrire un nom : "the radio what my father repaired" doit devenir "the radio that my father repaired".

title: Check a Story for Spelling
body:
When you finish a story, read it again slowly, one word at a time, only to check the spelling.
Three spelling patterns cause many mistakes:

1. ie or ei?
   "i before e, except after c", when the sound is "ee":
   believe, piece, field, chief   but after c: receive, ceiling
   (Some words do not follow the rule: weird, seize, and words where the sound is not "ee", such as eight and their.)

2. Plurals of words ending in y or f
   consonant + y: change y to i and add -es: baby, babies; story, stories
   vowel + y: just add -s: day, days; monkey, monkeys
   many words ending in -f or -fe change to -ves: leaf, leaves; knife, knives; wife, wives; thief, thieves
   (but some just add -s: roof, roofs; chief, chiefs)

3. Silent letters
   Some letters are written but not heard: knife, knock, write, wrong, listen, castle, climb, comb, hour, honest, island, answer.
   Say the word in your head the way it is spelt to remember the silent letter.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Afia wrote a continuation of the Cinderella story, beginning where the story ends. Here is one part before and after her spelling check:

Before: "Cinderella beleived the prince was kind. They lived in a castel, and the palace ladys sang for them every evening."

After: "Cinderella believed the prince was kind. They lived in a castle, and the palace ladies sang for them every evening."

1. "beleived": i before e for the "ee" sound, so "believed".
2. "castel": the t is silent but written, and the word ends in -le, so "castle".
3. "ladys": lady ends in a consonant + y, so "ladies".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Finish writing your story first. Then read it again only for spelling.
Step 2: Point to each word as you read, so you do not skip any.
Step 3: For words with ie or ei, check the "i before e, except after c" rule.
Step 4: For plurals, look at the last letters: consonant + y becomes -ies; many -f or -fe words become -ves.
Step 5: For words with silent letters (kn, wr, mb, st, gh, h), check that every letter is written.
Step 6: Circle any word you are not sure about and check it in a dictionary or with a partner.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. ie and ei swapped: "a peice of cloth" should be "a piece of cloth"; "the cieling" should be "the ceiling".
2. Only -s added: "two storys" should be "two stories"; "the thiefs" should be "the thieves".
3. Silent letters left out: "he could not clim the wall" should be "climb"; "an onest man" should be "an honest man".

title: Vérifier l'orthographe d'une histoire
body:
Quand tu as fini une histoire, relis-la lentement, mot par mot, seulement pour vérifier l'orthographe.
Trois règles d'orthographe entraînent souvent des erreurs :

1. ie ou ei ?
   "i avant e, sauf après c", quand le son est "ii" :
   believe, piece, field, chief   mais après c : receive, ceiling
   (Certains mots ne suivent pas la règle : weird, seize, et les mots où le son n'est pas "ii", comme eight et their.)

2. Le pluriel des mots terminés par y ou f
   consonne + y : on change y en i et on ajoute -es : baby, babies ; story, stories
   voyelle + y : on ajoute seulement -s : day, days ; monkey, monkeys
   beaucoup de mots en -f ou -fe deviennent -ves : leaf, leaves ; knife, knives ; wife, wives ; thief, thieves
   (mais certains ajoutent seulement -s : roof, roofs ; chief, chiefs)

3. Les lettres muettes
   Certaines lettres s'écrivent mais ne s'entendent pas : knife, knock, write, wrong, listen, castle, climb, comb, hour, honest, island, answer.
   Prononce le mot dans ta tête comme il s'écrit pour te rappeler la lettre muette.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Afia a écrit une suite de l'histoire de Cendrillon, en commençant là où l'histoire se termine. Voici une partie avant et après sa vérification de l'orthographe :

Avant : "Cinderella beleived the prince was kind. They lived in a castel, and the palace ladys sang for them every evening."

Après : "Cinderella believed the prince was kind. They lived in a castle, and the palace ladies sang for them every evening."

1. "beleived" : i avant e pour le son "ii", donc "believed".
2. "castel" : le t est muet mais s'écrit, et le mot se termine par -le, donc "castle".
3. "ladys" : lady se termine par consonne + y, donc "ladies".

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Finis d'abord d'écrire ton histoire. Ensuite, relis-la seulement pour l'orthographe.
Étape 2 : Montre chaque mot du doigt en lisant, pour n'en sauter aucun.
Étape 3 : Pour les mots avec ie ou ei, vérifie la règle "i avant e, sauf après c".
Étape 4 : Pour les pluriels, regarde les dernières lettres : consonne + y devient -ies ; beaucoup de mots en -f ou -fe deviennent -ves.
Étape 5 : Pour les mots avec des lettres muettes (kn, wr, mb, st, gh, h), vérifie que chaque lettre est écrite.
Étape 6 : Entoure chaque mot dont tu n'es pas sûr et vérifie-le dans un dictionnaire ou avec un camarade.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. ie et ei inversés : "a peice of cloth" doit devenir "a piece of cloth" ; "the cieling" doit devenir "the ceiling".
2. Seulement -s ajouté : "two storys" doit devenir "two stories" ; "the thiefs" doit devenir "the thieves".
3. Lettres muettes oubliées : "he could not clim the wall" doit devenir "climb" ; "an onest man" doit devenir "an honest man".

title: Write a Critical Commentary on a Book
body:
A critical commentary tells readers what you think of a book and WHY. It is not a retelling of the story.

Judge the book against a set of criteria, for example:
  Characters: Are they believable? Do they change?
  Plot: Is it clear and exciting? Does the ending work?
  Setting: Can you picture where and when it happens?
  Language: Is the writing lively, clear, funny or hard to follow?
  Message: What lesson or idea does the book share?

For every judgement, give EVIDENCE from the book: an event, a detail or a short quotation.
Judge only what is inside the book. The cover, the price, the number of pages or who gave you the book are not criteria.

A one-page commentary has three parts:
  1. Introduction: title, author and one or two sentences on what the book is about.
  2. Body: your judgement on each criterion, each with evidence.
  3. Conclusion: your overall verdict and who you would recommend the book to.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body:
Part of Selorm's commentary on "The Night Market":

Weak: "The Night Market is about a girl called Dzifa who helps her mother at the market at night. Then she loses the money, and then she finds it. It is a very nice book with a beautiful cover."

Better: "The Night Market tells how Dzifa learns to be responsible. Dzifa is a believable character: she is careless at first, but after she loses her mother's money she checks the box twice every night. The setting comes alive through details like the smoky lanterns and the cry of the kelewele seller. I recommend it to readers who enjoy stories about family."

1. The weak version only retells events.
2. "Very nice" is a judgement with no evidence.
3. The cover is not a criterion; the better version judges character and setting with evidence.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body:
Step 1: Read the whole book and note pages you liked or did not like.
Step 2: Write down the criteria you will use (characters, plot, setting, language, message).
Step 3: For each criterion, write one judgement in a sentence: "The plot is...", "The main character is...".
Step 4: After each judgement, add evidence: "for example...", "as when...", or a short quotation.
Step 5: Write a short introduction with the title, the author and what the book is about in one or two sentences.
Step 6: End with your overall verdict and who should read the book. Check that it all fits on one page.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body:
Check for three common mistakes.

1. Retelling instead of judging: a paragraph that says "First..., then..., finally..." about the events is a summary, not a critique.
2. Judgement with no evidence: "The characters are wonderful" must be followed by an example from the book that shows why.
3. Judging by things outside the book: "It is good because it is thin" or "because my uncle bought it for me" says nothing about the characters, plot, language or message.

title: Écrire un commentaire critique sur un livre
body:
Un commentaire critique dit aux lecteurs ce que tu penses d'un livre et POURQUOI. Ce n'est pas un résumé de l'histoire.

Juge le livre selon une liste de critères, par exemple :
  Les personnages : sont-ils crédibles ? Changent-ils ?
  L'intrigue : est-elle claire et passionnante ? La fin est-elle réussie ?
  Le cadre : peux-tu imaginer où et quand l'histoire se passe ?
  La langue : l'écriture est-elle vivante, claire, drôle ou difficile à suivre ?
  Le message : quelle leçon ou quelle idée le livre transmet-il ?

Pour chaque jugement, donne une PREUVE tirée du livre : un événement, un détail ou une courte citation.
Juge seulement ce qui se trouve dans le livre. La couverture, le prix, le nombre de pages ou la personne qui t'a donné le livre ne sont pas des critères.

Un commentaire d'une page a trois parties :
  1. Introduction : le titre, l'auteur et une ou deux phrases sur le sujet du livre.
  2. Développement : ton jugement sur chaque critère, chacun avec une preuve.
  3. Conclusion : ton avis général et à qui tu recommanderais le livre.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Exemple résolu
body:
Une partie du commentaire de Selorm sur "The Night Market" :

Faible : "The Night Market is about a girl called Dzifa who helps her mother at the market at night. Then she loses the money, and then she finds it. It is a very nice book with a beautiful cover."

Mieux : "The Night Market tells how Dzifa learns to be responsible. Dzifa is a believable character: she is careless at first, but after she loses her mother's money she checks the box twice every night. The setting comes alive through details like the smoky lanterns and the cry of the kelewele seller. I recommend it to readers who enjoy stories about family."

1. La version faible ne fait que raconter les événements.
2. "Very nice" est un jugement sans preuve.
3. La couverture n'est pas un critère ; la meilleure version juge le personnage et le cadre avec des preuves.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Pas à pas
body:
Étape 1 : Lis tout le livre et note les passages que tu as aimés ou non.
Étape 2 : Écris les critères que tu vas utiliser (personnages, intrigue, cadre, langue, message).
Étape 3 : Pour chaque critère, écris un jugement en une phrase : "The plot is...", "The main character is...".
Étape 4 : Après chaque jugement, ajoute une preuve : "for example...", "as when...", ou une courte citation.
Étape 5 : Écris une courte introduction avec le titre, l'auteur et le sujet du livre en une ou deux phrases.
Étape 6 : Termine par ton avis général et par le public à qui tu conseilles le livre. Vérifie que tout tient sur une page.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA English Language Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Vérifie ta réflexion
body:
Vérifie pour éviter trois erreurs fréquentes.

1. Raconter au lieu de juger : un paragraphe qui dit "First..., then..., finally..." sur les événements est un résumé, pas une critique.
2. Un jugement sans preuve : "The characters are wonderful" doit être suivi d'un exemple du livre qui montre pourquoi.
3. Juger d'après des choses extérieures au livre : "It is good because it is thin" ou "because my uncle bought it for me" ne dit rien des personnages, de l'intrigue, de la langue ou du message.

title: Continue a Number Pattern
body: A number pattern changes by the same amount each time. To find the change, compare two neighbouring numbers. If the numbers get bigger, the rule adds. If they get smaller, the rule subtracts. Check the change between every pair, not just the last two, then use it to find the next number. In 7, 11, 15, 19 each number is 4 more than the one before, so the next number is 23.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA Mathematics Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example
body: Kofi counts bottle tops in bags: 50, 45, 40, 35. Step 1: 45 is 5 less than 50. Step 2: 40 is 5 less than 45, and 35 is 5 less than 40, so the change is the same every time. Step 3: the numbers get smaller, so the rule is subtract 5. Step 4: 35 minus 5 is 30, so the next number is 30.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA Mathematics Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: look at the first two numbers and find how much they change. Step 2: say whether the numbers go up or down. Step 3: check that the same change works for every pair. Step 4: apply the change once more to the last number. Step 5: check your answer fits the pattern.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA Mathematics Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Two slips are common. Some pupils guess the next number without finding the change, for example writing 20 after 12, 15, 18 because it is close. Others add when the pattern goes down, writing 33 after 30, 27, 24 instead of 21. Always find the change, say if it goes up or down, and check it on every pair.

title: Continuer une suite de nombres
body: Une suite de nombres change de la même quantité à chaque fois. Pour trouver ce changement, compare deux nombres voisins. Si les nombres deviennent plus grands, la règle ajoute. Dans 7, 11, 15, 19, chaque nombre a 4 de plus que le précédent, donc le nombre suivant est 23.

title: Exemple résolu
body: Kofi compte des capsules dans des sacs : 50, 45, 40, 35. Étape 1 : 45, c'est 5 de moins que 50. Étape 4 : 35 moins 5 font 30, donc le nombre suivant est 30.

title: Describe the Rule
body: A pattern rule tells what happens to each number to get the next one, such as add 6 or subtract 10. A rule is not one of the numbers in the pattern. Find the change between neighbouring numbers, check it for every pair, then say it with an action and an amount. In 5, 11, 17, 23 each number is 6 more than the one before, so the rule is add 6. Using the rule, the next term is 29.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA Mathematics Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Worked Example with a Table
body: A table shows money saved: Day 1, 4 cedis. Day 2, 7 cedis. Day 3, 10 cedis. Step 1: from 4 to 7 is 3 more. Step 2: from 7 to 10 is also 3 more. Step 3: the amounts go up by the same amount, so the rule is add 3 cedis. Step 4: on Day 4 the saving is 10 plus 3, which is 13 cedis.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA Mathematics Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Step by Step
body: Step 1: find the change from the first number to the second. Step 2: check the same change works for every other pair. Step 3: decide if the numbers go up (add) or down (subtract). Step 4: write the rule as an action and an amount, such as subtract 4. Step 5: test your rule by using it to make the next term.

metadata.curriculumSource: NaCCA Mathematics Curriculum for Primary Schools, Basic 4-6, 2019

title: Check Your Thinking
body: Three slips are common. Some pupils give a number from the pattern as the rule, for example saying the rule of 4, 8, 12, 16 is 16. A rule must say what to do: add 4. Some give only the amount and forget the direction, or say add when the numbers go down. Some check only one pair; always check every pair before you say the rule.

title: Décrire la règle
body: Une règle de suite dit ce qui arrive à chaque nombre pour obtenir le suivant, par exemple ajouter 6 ou soustraire 10. Une règle n'est pas un des nombres de la suite. Trouve le changement entre des nombres voisins, vérifie-le pour chaque paire, puis dis-le avec une action et une quantité. Dans 5, 11, 17, 23, chaque nombre a 6 de plus que le précédent, donc la règle est ajouter 6. Avec cette règle, le terme suivant est 29.

Étape 3 : les montants augmentent toujours de la même quantité, donc la règle est ajouter 3 cedis. Étape 4 : le Jour 4, l'économie est 10 plus 3, soit 13 cedis.
